Pharmacologic class	Penem antibacterial (sulopenem etzadroxil) combined with a renal tubular transport inhibitor (probenecid)
Other product name(s)	sulopenem
Applicant	ITERUM THERAPEUTICS US LTD.

Dosing regimen	One tablet orally twice daily for 5 days
Applicant-proposed indication(s)/population(s)	ORLYNVAH is indicated in adult women ≥18 years of age for the treatment of uncomplicated urinary tract infections caused by the following designated susceptible microorganisms: Escherichia coli, Klebsiella pneumoniae, Proteus mirabilis (b) (4)
SNOMED CT code for proposed indication disease term(s)1	68566005 | Urinary tract infectious disease (disorder)
Regulatory action	Approval
Approved dosage (if applicable)	One tablet orally twice daily for 5 days
Approved indication(s)/population(s) (if applicable)	ORLYNVAH is indicated for the treatment of uncomplicated urinary tract infections (uUTI) caused by the designated microorganisms Escherichia coli, Klebsiella pneumoniae, or Proteus mirabilis in adult women who have limited or no alternative oral antibacterial treatment options.
SNOMED CT code for approved indication disease term(s)1	68566005 | Urinary tract infectious disease (disorder)

L78: ## I. Executive Summary
L79: ## 1. Overview
L80: ## 1.1. Summary of Regulatory Action
L81: On April 25, 2024, the 505(b)(2) NDA 213972 for sulopenem etzadroxil/probenecid oral tablet, a bilayer fixed-dose combination of the penem antibacterial prodrug sulopenem etzadroxil and probenecid (500 mg; 500 mg), a renal tubular transport inhibitor, was resubmitted by Iterum Therapeutics US Ltd. (Applicant) for the proposed indication of treatment of adult women \ge18 years of age with uncomplicated urinary tract infections (uUTI) caused by designated susceptible microorganisms. Sulopenem etzadroxil/probenecid has Qualified Infectious Disease Product (QIDP), Fast Track and Priority Review designations. The Prescription Drug User Fee Act (PDUFA) goal date is October 25, 2024. Throughout this review, the study drug product is referenced as sulopenem etzadroxil/probenecid or oral sulopenem.
L82: NDA 213972 was originally submitted on November 25, 2020, for sulopenem etzadroxil/probenecid for the treatment of uUTI caused by designated microorganisms proven or strongly suspected to be nonsusceptible to a quinolone in adult women. The original NDA was primarily based on Trial IT001-301 (Trial 301), a phase 3, randomized, double-blind, active-controlled trial comparing oral sulopenem to oral ciprofloxacin for the treatment of uUTI in adult women. Independent statistical analyses in this trial indicated that oral sulopenem was inferior to ciprofloxacin for the primary endpoint of overall (or composite) response (including clinical and microbiological responses) in the microbiological modified intent-to-treat ciprofloxacin-susceptible (micro-MITTS) population but achieved statistical superiority in the microbiological modified intent-to-treat ciprofloxacin-resistant (micro-MITTR) population. Data from Trial 302 for the treatment of complicated urinary tract infections (cUTI) and Trial 303 for the treatment of complicated intra-abdominal infections (cIAIs) assessing the safety and efficacy of IV to oral sulopenem formulations versus active comparator regimens were also submitted in the NDA; however, both trials failed to meet their primary endpoints. The original NDA review team concluded that results from the single uUTI trial and lack of confirmatory evidence from Trials 302 and 303 were insufficient to establish substantial evidence of effectiveness (SEE); thus, the NDA received a complete response on July 23, 2021. The Division recommended that the Applicant conduct at least one additional adequate and well-controlled trial in uUTI to support this indication.
L83: In the current NDA resubmission, data were provided from the new Trial IT001-310 (Trial 310), a phase 3, randomized, double-blind, active-controlled, noninferiority (NI) trial comparing oral sulopenem to amoxicillin/clavulanate for the treatment of uUTI caused by designated susceptible microorganisms in adult women. Oral sulopenem was NI with an NI margin of 10% and statistically superior to the comparator in the micro-MITTS (amoxicillin/clavulanate-susceptible) population. The sample size of patients with isolates that were amoxicillin/clavulanate-resistant (micro-MITTR) was too small to allow conclusions regarding efficacy.
L84: Safety data from nearly 3000 subjects across the phase 3 sulopenem development program indicate that oral sulopenem is anticipated to be safe for its intended use. It is expected that potential safety risks can be adequately mitigated through labeling and further evaluated during routine pharmacovigilance.
L85: Because sulopenem etzadroxil/probenecid will, if approved, be the first oral penem antibacterial drug on the U.S. market, the NDA was taken to the Antimicrobial Drugs Advisory Committee on September 9, 2024, to discuss the Applicant's desired indication and consider the information that should be conveyed to medical providers to ensure appropriate use of this drug product. While an oral penem for the treatment of resistant bacteria causing uUTI could potentially address an unmet need, its use in an ambulatory setting where treatment is most commonly empiric raises concern for inappropriate use which may contribute to antimicrobial resistance (AMR). Further, based on the failure of Trials 302 and 303 to meet their primary endpoints, there was concern for potential off-label use of sulopenem etzadroxil/probenecid as a stepdown treatment for cUTI and cIAI following initial intravenous (IV) antibacterial treatment.
L86: Based on the totality of evidence and recommendations from the Advisory Committee (see Section 11), the multidisciplinary review team recommends approval of sulopenem etzadroxil/probenecid with the following Indication: "ORLYNVAH is indicated for the treatment of uncomplicated urinary tract infections (uUTI) caused by the designated microorganisms *Escherichia coli*, *Klebsiella pneumoniae*, or *Proteus mirabilis*, in adult women who have limited or no alternative oral antibacterial treatment options." In addition, the required statement regarding Usage to Reduce Development of Drug-Resistant Bacteria will be strengthened. A Limitations of Use statement that "ORLYNVAH is not indicated for the treatment of: cUTI or cIAI or as step-down treatment after intravenous antibacterial treatment of cUTI or cIAI" will be added. Overall, as delineated in the Benefit/Risk Framework below, the review team concludes that the benefits of oral sulopenem outweigh its associated risks when used as recommended in the approved labeling.
L87: The signatory concurs with the review team's recommendations. There is an unmet need for an oral penem to provide an oral treatment option for adult women with uUTI caused by certain resistant bacteria, such as those with infections caused by bacteria expressing extended-spectrum beta-lactamase enzymes. Trial 301 is considered as two adequate and well-controlled trials based on the statistical analysis plan (SAP), with separate analyses conducted for the micro-MITTS (ciprofloxacin-susceptible) population which failed, and the micro-MITTR (ciprofloxacin-resistant) population which was successful. The interpretable primary analysis of Trial 310 in the micro-MITTS (amoxicillin/clavulanate-susceptible) population was successful. Thus, while the signatory agrees that substantial evidence of effectiveness has been provided, there is some element of uncertainty because of the failed Trial 301 primary analysis in the micro-MITTS (ciprofloxacin-susceptible) population. Consistent with our labeling practices for antibacterial drug products that address unmet need described in our Guidance document, Antibacterial Therapies for Patients with an Unmet Medical Need for the Treatment of Serious Bacterial Diseases – Questions and Answers, (available at (May 2022)) the Indication will read as described above. This Indication and other labeling will address the need to ensure appropriate use of the drug, minimize the risk of contributing to penem resistance in the U.S. population, and avoid use of the drug to treat serious infections such as cUTI or cIAI for which effectiveness has not been established.
L88: Microbiological surveillance as a Post-Marketing Requirement (PMR) mandated by 21 CFR 505(o)(3) will evaluate the possible emergence of resistance to oral sulopenem and cross-resistance to FDA-approved IV carbapenems with the use of sulopenem etzadroxil/probenecid. In addition, FDA will conduct enhanced post-marketing pharmacovigilance to monitor for potential inappropriate use of the product.
L89: ## 1.2. Conclusions on Substantial Evidence of Effectiveness
L90: SEE was established with two or more adequate and well-controlled clinical investigations.
L91: Substantial evidence of effectiveness (SEE) for sulopenem etzadroxil/probenecid for the treatment of uUTI was established based on the results from Trials 301 and 310. For these trials, the SAP pre-specified that the composite primary efficacy endpoint of overall response (combination of clinical and microbiological responses) was analyzed independently in the micro-MITTS (comparator-susceptible) and micro-MITTR (comparator-resistant) populations.
L92: In Trial 301, sulopenem was superior to ciprofloxacin in patients with ciprofloxacin-nonsusceptible pathogens (micro-MITTR population) using the primary efficacy endpoint of overall response. The overall response was 77/160 (48%) for sulopenem and 49/149 (33%) for ciprofloxacin with a difference of 15% (95% CI, 4.4%, 26.1%; p-value 0.0062). Among patients with uUTI caused by a ciprofloxacin-susceptible pathogen (micro-MITTS population), sulopenem was inferior to ciprofloxacin. The overall response was 218/365 (60%) for sulopenem and 296/410 (72%) for ciprofloxacin with a difference of -12.5% (95% CI, -19.1%, -5.9%). The failure of sulopenem in the micro-MITTS population in Trial 301 was driven by lower rates of microbiological success in the sulopenem arm compared to the ciprofloxacin arm.
L93: In Trial 310, oral sulopenem was non-inferior and superior to amoxicillin/clavulanate in the micro-MITTS (i.e., amoxicillin/clavulanate-susceptible) population using the primary efficacy endpoint of overall response (clinical response and microbiological response). The overall response was 296/480 (61.7%) for sulopenem and 243/442 (55.0%) for amoxicillin/clavulanate with a difference of 6.7% (95% CI, 0.3, 13.0; p-value of 0.040). While clinical response was similar between arms, the rate of microbiological response was greater in the sulopenem arm of the micro-MITTS population. The sample size of subjects with isolates that were amoxicillin/clavulanate-resistant (micro-MITTR) was too small to allow conclusions regarding efficacy in this population.
L94: In summary, SEE for sulopenem etzadroxil/probenecid for the treatment of uUTI caused by the designated microorganisms *E. coli*, *K. pneumoniae*, or *P. mirabilis* in adult women who have limited or no alternative oral antibacterial treatment options has been provided by statistical superiority in the micro-MITTR population of Trial 301 along with NI/superiority in the micro-MITTS population of Trial 310. To note, there is some element of uncertainty because of the failed uUTI Trial 301 primary analysis in the micro-MITTS (ciprofloxacin-susceptible) population. Additionally, as discussed in this review, IV to oral sulopenem did not demonstrate efficacy for treatment of cUTI and cIAI in Trials 302 and 303, respectively.
L95: ## 2. Benefit-Risk Assessment
L96: ## 2.1. Benefit-Risk Framework
L97: Table 2. Benefit-Risk Framework
L98: Dimension	Evidence and Uncertainties	Conclusions and Reasons
Analysis of condition	Uncomplicated urinary tract infection or acute cystitis is an acute infection of the bladder in women with normal urinary tract anatomy. Signs and symptoms of uUTI include dysuria, urinary frequency, urinary urgency, and suprapubic pain (August 2019).
Urinary tract infections (UTIs) are the most common bacterial infections in the ambulatory setting in the U.S.; 50-60% of adult women will have at least one UTI during their lifetime (Medina and Castillo-Pino 2019). It is estimated that 10-12% of adult women in the United States have at least one UTI per year, with 20-30% of those having a recurrent infection (Kaye et al. 2021).
The incidence of uUTI has a double peak – first in young, sexually active women aged 15-24 years and then in postmenopausal women (Kaye et al. 2021). Risk factors include sexual intercourse, spermicide use, prior UTI, new sexual partner within the past year, and history of UTI in a first-degree female relative (Hooton 2012).
The most common causative bacterial pathogen in uUTI is Escherichia coli (E.coli) (75-95%). Additional causative pathogens include other species of Enterobacteriales (e.g., Proteus mirabilis (P.mirabilis), Klebsiella pneumoniae (K.pneumoniae)) and Staphylococcus saprophyticus (S.saprophyticus) (Gupta et al. 2011).
AMR among urinary isolates is increasing across the U.S., including resistance related to production of extended-spectrum \beta-lactamases.
uUTI are common bacterial infections in adult women, with E.coli being the most common causative pathogen.
L99: Dimension	Evidence and Uncertainties	Conclusions and Reasons
Current treatment options	Therapy for uUTI is most often empiric. Urine cultures are not typically recommended for the first incidence of uUTI (Kaye et al. 2021).
The Infectious Diseases Society of America recommends the following antibacterial drugs for the treatment of uUTI: nitrofurantoin, trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole (TMP-SMX) (if local resistance rates of uropathogens causing uUTI do not exceed 20%), fosfomycin, or pivmecillinam. Fluoroquinolones (including ciprofloxacin) and \beta-lactams (including amoxicillin/clavulanate) are considered alternative antibacterials for uUTI (Gupta et al. 2011).
Some of the recommended antibacterial drugs have known adverse reactions, including pulmonary toxicity, hepatotoxicity, neuropathy, hypersensitivity reactions, tendinopathy, and QT prolongation.
In the U.S., there is increasing resistance of E. coli to ciprofloxacin and TMP-SMX and increased prevalence of extended-spectrum \beta-lactamase (ESBL) producing E. coli (Kaye et al. 2021). When uUTI are due to antimicrobial resistant pathogens, treatment may require IV antibacterial treatment, necessitating placement of an IV catheter and possibly hospitalization.
There are several FDA-approved antibacterial drugs for the treatment of uUTI. However, increasing antibacterial drug resistance and adverse reactions in some patients may limit treatment options.
uUTI caused by organisms resistant to currently recommended first-line oral antibacterial drugs may require IV antibacterial treatment and hospitalization.
L100: Dimension	Evidence and Uncertainties	Conclusions and Reasons
Benefit	The efficacy of sulopenem etzadroxil/probenecid for the treatment of uUTI was demonstrated in two adequate and well-controlled trials (Trials 301 and 310).
In Trial 301, sulopenem was superior to ciprofloxacin in patients with ciprofloxacin-nonsusceptible pathogens (micro-MITTR population) using the primary efficacy endpoint of overall response. The overall response was 77/160 (48%) for sulopenem and 49/149 (33%) for ciprofloxacin with a difference of 15% (95% CI, 4.4%, 26.1%; p-value 0.0062). Among patients with uUTI caused by a ciprofloxacin-susceptible pathogen (micro-MITTS population), sulopenem was inferior to ciprofloxacin. The overall response was 218/365 (60%) for sulopenem and 296/410 (72%) for ciprofloxacin with a difference of -12.5% (95% CI, -19.1%, -5.9%). The failure of sulopenem in the micro-MITTS population in Trial 301 was driven by lower rates of microbiological success in the sulopenem arm compared to the ciprofloxacin arm.
In Trial 310, oral sulopenem was non-inferior and superior to amoxicillin/clavulanate in the micro-MITTS (i.e., amoxicillin/clavulanate-susceptible) population using the primary efficacy endpoint of overall response (clinical response and microbiological response). The overall response was 296/480 (61.7%) for sulopenem and 243/442 (55.0%) for amoxicillin/clavulanate with a difference of 6.7% (95% CI, 0.3, 13.0; p-value of 0.040). While clinical response was similar between arms, the rate of microbiological response was greater in the sulopenem arm of the micro-MITTS population rather than in the amoxicillin/clavulanate arm.
In the cUTI trial (Trial 302), sulopenem (IV to oral stepdown) was inferior to the active comparator (IV ertapenem with stepdown to oral ciprofloxacin or amoxicillin/clavulanate) based on the primary endpoint of overall response. The overall response was 265/444 (60%) for sulopenem and 296/440 (67%) for the comparator with a difference of -7.6% (95% CI, -13.9, -1.3).
In the cIAI trial (Trial 303), sulopenem (IV to oral stepdown) did not demonstrate noninferiority compared to the active comparator (IV ertapenem with stepdown to oral ciprofloxacin/metronidazole or amoxicillin/clavulanate) based on the primary endpoint of clinical response. The clinical response was 204/249 (82%) for sulopenem and 233/266 (88%) for the comparator with a difference of -6.0% (95% CI, -12.2, 0.2).
Substantial evidence of effectiveness for sulopenem etzadroxil/probenecid for the treatment of uUTI caused by the designated microorganisms E. coli, K. pneumoniae, or P. mirabilis in adult women who have limited or no alternative oral antibacterial treatment options has been provided by statistical superiority in the micro-MITTR population of Trial 301 and noninferiority/superiority in the micro-MITTS population of Trial 310.
Sulopenem etzadroxil/probenecid provides an additional option for the treatment of uUTI in adult women.
IV to oral sulopenem did not demonstrate efficacy for treatment of cUTI and cIAI in Trials 302 and 303, respectively.
L101: Dimension	Evidence and Uncertainties	Conclusions and Reasons
Risk and risk management	The primary safety population consisted of 1932 subjects with uUTI from Trials 301 and 310 who received the proposed dosing regimen of sulopenem etzadroxil/probenecid.
Trial 302 in cUTI and Trial 303 in cIAI, both of which included use of both IV and oral formulations of sulopenem, provided supportive safety data. A total of 2962 subjects received sulopenem among the four phase 3 trials.
Hypersensitivity reactions, including angioedema, were observed in two subjects from a phase 1 study (IT001-101) and Trial 301 after oral sulopenem administration.
There were no deaths in Trial 310; the one death in Trial 301 was due to lung adenocarcinoma and unrelated to sulopenem.
Diarrhea was seen in 10% of subjects who received oral sulopenem, but most episodes were mild. Five (0.3%) occurrences of diarrhea required treatment discontinuation. There were no cases of Clostridium difficile infection (CDI) related to sulopenem.
Elevations in alanine aminotransferase more than three times the upper limit of normal were seen in 0.4% of uUTI subjects, but in general, were not treatment-limiting.
One subject in Trial 302 fulfilled laboratory criteria for Hy's Law but liver enzyme elevations resolved while still on study drug.
Other treatment-emergent adverse events related to sulopenem included headache, nausea, vomiting, and vulvovaginal mycotic infection.
Empiric use of oral sulopenem for treatment of uUTI in an ambulatory setting raises concern for the development of antimicrobial resistance in general and in particular, for cross-resistance to IV carbapenems.
Based on the failure of sulopenem to demonstrate efficacy in Trials 302 for cUTI and 303 for cIAI, potential off-label administration of oral sulopenem as stepdown treatment following IV antibacterial treatment for cUTI or cIAI raises concern for treatment failure.
The four phase 3 trials in uUTI, cUTI, and cIAI provided an adequate safety database for the proposed dosing regimen of oral sulopenem for uUTI treatment.
The safety profile of sulopenem etzadroxil/probenecid appears acceptable. The identified safety risks for sulopenem etzadroxil/probenecid can be adequately mitigated through labeling and further evaluated during routine pharmacovigilance.
Given that sulopenem etzadroxil/probenecid will be the first oral penem antibacterial drug on the U.S. market, effective antimicrobial stewardship and appropriate positioning of the drug in the hierarchy of uUTI treatment options by guidelines committees is critical to mitigate risk of increased carbapenem resistance associated with its use. Microbiological resistance to sulopenem will be monitored for 5 years in a required postmarketing study (PMR).
Limitations of Use to prevent off-label use of oral sulopenem as step-down treatment following IV antibacterial treatment of cUTI or cIAI will be added to the prescribing information (PI).
L102: Abbreviations: AMR, antimicrobial resistance; cIAI, complicated intra-abdominal infection; cUTI, complicated urinary tract infection; IV, intravenous; micro-MITTR, microbiological modified intent-to-treat resistant; micro-MITTS, microbiological modified intent-to-treat susceptible; uUTI, uncomplicated urinary tract infection
L103: ## 2.2. Conclusions Regarding Benefit-Risk
L104: Although multiple antibacterial drugs are FDA-approved to treat uUTI, treatment options can be limited by drug toxicities (e.g., hypersensitivity to \beta-lactams and QT prolongation, central nervous system effects or tendinopathies associated with quinolones) and AMR to first-line drugs including through production of ESBL (Critchley et al. 2019; Dunne et al. 2022). Carbapenem drugs are the mainstay of treatment for infections caused by ESBL-producers, but all approved members of this class require IV administration and are generally reserved for the treatment of culture-proven infections. While an oral penem for treatment of resistant bacteria causing uUTI could potentially address an unmet need, its use in an ambulatory setting where treatment is most commonly empiric raises concern for inappropriate use which may contribute to AMR.
L105: The Applicant submitted data demonstrating safety and effectiveness of sulopenem etzadroxil/probenecid for the treatment of adult women with uUTI due to designated microorganisms.
L106: Trial 301 demonstrated that sulopenem etzadroxil/probenecid is superior to ciprofloxacin for the treatment of subjects with uUTI caused by ciprofloxacin-resistant organisms (micro-MITTR population). The overall response at test of cure (TOC) in the sulopenem etzadroxil/probenecid arm was 48.1% compared with a rate of 32.9% in the ciprofloxacin arm with a treatment difference of 15.3% (95% CI: 4.4%, 26.1%). Of note, this treatment difference is based on analysis by the FDA statistical team utilizing the original SAP submitted by the Applicant and with inclusion of Site 202. After an unblinded interim analysis, the Applicant chose to analyze the primary efficacy endpoint utilizing an updated SAP and excluding Site 202; thus, the treatment difference the Applicant obtained was 26.6% (95% CI: 15.1%, 37.4%). Regardless, the results of both analyses were favorable to oral sulopenem.
L107: Trial 310 demonstrated that sulopenem etzadroxil/probenecid is non-inferior and superior to amoxicillin/clavulanate for subjects with uUTI in the micro-MITTS population. The overall response at TOC in the sulopenem etzadroxil/probenecid arm was 61.7% compared to 55.0% in the amoxicillin/clavulanate arm with a treatment difference of 6.7% (95% CI: 0.3, 13.0), which met the prespecified NI margin of 10%.
L108: The safety database for sulopenem etzadroxil/probenecid, consisting of nearly 3,000 subjects in the four phase 3 trials and more than 1,000 additional subjects in phase 1 and 2 trials, was adequate for the proposed dosing regimen and indication. Overall, sulopenem etzadroxil/probenecid appears to be safe for its intended use; potential safety risks can be adequately mitigated through labeling and further evaluated during routine pharmacovigilance.
L109: Based on the review of all available efficacy and safety data, NDA 213972 for sulopenem etzadroxil/probenecid provides SEE and a favorable benefit-risk profile for the treatment of uUTI caused by the designated microorganisms *E. coli*, *K. pneumoniae*, or *P. mirabilis* in adult women who have limited or no alternative oral antibacterial treatment options.
L110: ## II. Interdisciplinary Assessment
L111: ## 3. Introduction
L112: Sulopenem etzadroxil/probenecid bilayer oral tablet is a fixed-dose combination of the penem antibacterial prodrug (sulopenem etzadroxil) and a renal tubular transport blocking drug (probenecid). Each tablet contains 500 mg sulopenem etzadroxil and 500 mg probenecid. The Applicant's proposed indication is treatment of uUTI caused by designated susceptible microorganisms in adult women \ge18 years of age. The proposed dose is one tablet orally (PO) administered twice daily (BID) for 5 days.
L113: Sulopenem etzadroxil, a new molecular entity, is a \beta-lactam drug closely related to the carbapenems. On oral administration, sulopenem etzadroxil is rapidly hydrolyzed to sulopenem and two other products: formaldehyde and 2-ethylbutyric acid (2-EBA). Probenecid, originally approved in 1951, is co-formulated with sulopenem etzadroxil to increase the systemic exposure of sulopenem.
L114: The Division granted sulopenem QIDP designation for the treatment of uUTIs, complicated urinary tract infections (cUTIs), and complicated intra-abdominal infections (cIAIs) on July 29, 2016, as well as fast track designation for these indications on March 15, 2019.
L115: uUTI is the most common bacterial infection in the ambulatory care setting in the U.S. There are multiple FDA-approved drugs for uUTI treatment (see Benefit-Risk Framework), but their use is challenged by associated drug toxicities and rising antimicrobial resistance.
L116: The Applicant previously developed an intravenous (IV) formulation of sulopenem and studied its efficacy with stepdown to oral sulopenem for cUTI and cIAI. Prior to the original submission of NDA 213972 in 2020, three phase 3 trials were completed - IT001-301 (Trial 301) for uUTI utilizing oral sulopenem, IT001-302 (Trial 302) for cUTI, and IT001-303 (Trial 303) for cIAI, each utilizing IV to oral sulopenem. On November 25, 2020, The Applicant submitted NDA 213972 as a 505(b)(2) submission for sulopenem etzadroxil/probenecid for the proposed indication of treatment of adult women with uUTI caused by designated susceptible microorganisms proven or strongly suspected to be nonsusceptible to a quinolone.
L117: The NDA received a complete response on July 23, 2021, due to lack of substantial evidence of effectiveness (SEE) for sulopenem for the treatment of uUTI. In Trial 301, sulopenem etzadroxil/probenecid was superior to ciprofloxacin based on the primary endpoint of overall response (clinical and microbiological response) in the prespecified subgroup of participants with uUTI caused by a ciprofloxacin-resistant pathogen in the microbiological modified intent-to-treat resistant (micro-MITTR) population. However, in the prespecified subgroup of participants with uUTI caused by a ciprofloxacin-susceptible pathogens [micro-MITTS (microbiological modified intent-to-treat susceptible) population], sulopenem etzadroxil/probenecid was inferior to ciprofloxacin. Also, sulopenem failed to achieve noninferiority (NI) to the active comparator for the primary efficacy endpoints in the cUTI and cIAI studies. The safety profile for sulopenem etzadroxil was found to be acceptable.
L118: Given the sole finding of superiority in the micro-MITTR population with inferiority in the micro-MITTS population in Trial 301 and lack of supportive evidence in the MITT populations
L119: of the cIAI and cUTI trials, it was concluded that there was insufficient evidence to support the effectiveness of sulopenem etzadroxil/probenecid for the treatment of uUTI. The Division recommended an additional trial for uUTI with a different comparator, and that the Applicant conduct further investigations to determine the optimal sulopenem dosing regimen.
L120: Following the complete response, the Applicant halted further development of the IV formulation. The current NDA resubmission includes results from the recommended additional uUTI trial, IT001-310 (Trial 310), in which amoxicillin/clavulanate was chosen as the comparator. Trial 310 was a phase 3, randomized, multicenter, double-blind, double-dummy controlled trial of the efficacy, tolerability, and safety of oral sulopenem etzadroxil/probenecid versus oral amoxicillin/clavulanate for the treatment of uUTI in non-pregnant adult women. Sulopenem etzadroxil/probenecid was non-inferior and statistically superior to the comparator for the primary endpoint of overall response (composite of clinical and microbiological responses) at test of cure (TOC) in the micro-MITTS population (amoxicillin/clavulanate susceptible). Based on the statistical analysis plan, NI was first tested and achieved in the microbiological modified intent-to-treat (micro-MITT) population, but a noninferiority comparison in this population is not considered appropriate due to the inclusion of patients with comparator-resistant isolates. No conclusions regarding efficacy could be drawn in the micro-MITTR population (amoxicillin/clavulanate-nonsusceptible) due to insufficient sample size. Refer to Sections 6 and 7 for detailed reviews of efficacy and safety for Trial 310.
L121: An Advisory Committee (AC) Meeting was held on September 9, 2024, to discuss the overall benefit-risk assessment for the use of sulopenem etzadroxil/probenecid for the treatment of uUTI and to consider information that would be most important to convey to medical providers to ensure appropriate use of sulopenem etzadroxil/probenecid. Details of the Committee's deliberations are provided in Section 11. Based on the Committee's recommendations, the Indication statement in labeling was narrowed to indicate sulopenem etzadroxil/probenecid for the treatment of uUTI caused by the designated microorganisms *E. coli*, *K. pneumoniae*, or *P. mirabilis* in adult women who have limited or no alternative oral antibacterial treatment options.

L146: ## 5. Pharmacologic Activity, Pharmacokinetics, and Clinical Pharmacology
L147: ## 5.1. Nonclinical Assessment of Potential Effectiveness
L148: To support the activity of sulopenem against Enterobacterales, the Applicant conducted in vitro and in vivo pharmacokinetic/pharmacodynamic (PK/PD) index and target determination studies, along with a proof-of-concept study in an in vitro hollow-fiber infection model. For uUTI, there is no established nonclinical model to reliably determine PK/PD targets relevant to the site of infection. Additionally, significant knowledge gaps surrounding urine-specific PK/PD parameters and selection of a bacteriologic endpoint predictive of clinical efficacy limit the use of probability of target attainment (PTA) analyses to predict the efficacy of sulopenem etzadroxil/probenecid for the treatment of uUTI. Therefore, while the nonclinical data support sulopenem's activity against uropathogens, the translational utility of these nonclinical PK/PD findings is limited.
L149: ## 5.1.1. Summary of Nonclinical Pharmacokinetic/Pharmacodynamic Information
L150: Dose fractionation studies were conducted in the murine thigh and in vitro 1-compartment models to determine the PK/PD index that best correlates with sulopenem's activity. Although initial findings from the murine thigh infection model suggested that sulopenem exhibits elements of both time and concentration-dependent killing, results were largely uninterpretable due to concerns with study design, data integrity and the Applicant's atypical analysis of the ensuing results (see Section 14). Subsequent in vitro studies corroborated previous findings that sulopenem does indeed display both time and concentration-dependent activity with coefficient of determination (r^2) values of 0.89 and 0.90 for free sulopenem peak concentration to minimum inhibitory concentration (MIC) free-drug maximum plasma concentration(fC_{max})/MIC and the percentage of the dosing interval that free-drug concentrations exceed the MIC (\%fT&gt;MIC), respectively. Given that traditionally, \%fT&gt;MIC is the index that best correlates with the activity of beta-lactams, the Applicant's eventual use of \%fT&gt;MIC to characterize sulopenem's activity is acceptable.
L151: Similar to the dose fractionation studies, concerns with the Applicant's initial approach for PK/PD target determination in the murine thigh infection model rendered the results unreliable (see Section 14). Subsequent PK/PD target determination studies were conducted in the in vitro 1-compartment model using a panel of 10 *Enterobacteriales* isolates with sulopenem MICs ranging from 0.03 to 0.5 \mug/mL. In this model, the magnitude of median targets for stasis, 1-log kill, and 2-log kill were 40.9, 50.2 and 62.6% fT&gt;MIC, respectively.
L152: Additionally, the Applicant evaluated the bactericidal activity of sulopenem urinary concentrations associated with the proposed 500 mg sulopenem etzadroxil/500 mg probenecid dosage for the treatment of uUTI. The simulated urinary concentrations suppressed the growth of 4 *E. coli* isolates (with sulopenem MICs ranging from 0.03 to 0.5 \mug/mL) and prevented the development of resistance for the entire duration of a 5-day study in a hollow-fiber infection model.

L155: Characteristic	Drug Information
Pharmacologic Activity
Established pharmacologic class	Sulopenem is a penem antibacterial, and probenecid is a uricosuric and renal tubular inhibitor. A new established pharmacologic class for probenecid that reads as "renal tubular transport inhibitor" instead of "renal tubular transport blocking agent" was included in the finalized prescribing information. For additional details see FDA comments sent to the Applicant in DARRTS dated 10/11/2024.
Mechanism of action	Sulopenem inhibits bacterial cell wall synthesis by binding to essential penicillin-binding proteins (PBP). Probenecid is a uricosuric and renal tubular blocking agent that inhibits the OAT3-mediated excretion of sulopenem, thereby providing increased plasma concentrations of sulopenem
Active moieties	The drug product is a bilayer tablet comprised of the prodrug sulopenem etzadroxil and probenecid. Sulopenem etzadroxil is rapidly cleaved to release the active compound, sulopenem.
QT prolongation	
At a concentration of \ge 40 times the peak sulopenem concentrations associated with the recommended dosing regimen, clinically significant QTc interval prolongation was not observed. After a single 500-mg dose, sulopenem does not prolong the QTc interval to any clinically relevant extent. This conclusion was informed by concentration-QTc analysis performed on data from trial A7371007, a single ascending dose study of sulopenem etzadroxil. The predicted \Delta\Delta\text{QTcF} (upper bounds of 90% CI) value was 0.07(4.34) ms at the geometric mean of the C_{\text{max}} (i.e., 109.7 \mu\text{g/mL}) associated with the highest single dose of 2800 mg IV sulopenem administered as a 1 h infusion.
A thorough QTc assessment was not conducted for probenecid either under its original approval in 1951 or as part of the current application. Nonetheless, QTc prolongation is not described as an adverse reaction in the probenecid labeling.

Drug as substrate of transporters	Distribution
The mean apparent volumes of distribution for sulopenem and probenecid are 134 L and 8.81 L, respectively. Sulopenem is 10.7% bound to plasma proteins. Sulopenem is a substrate of OAT3 and sulopenem etzadroxil is a substrate of P-gp. Probenecid is a substrate of BCRP. In a clinical DDI study with a P-gp inhibitor (itraconazole), the effect on the AUC and Cmax of sulopenem was not clinically significant.
Mass balance results	Elimination
Following oral administration of a 2000-mg dose of [14C] sulopenem etzadroxil, 85.1% of the radiolabeled dose was recovered in urine (44.3%) and feces (40.8%) as unchanged sulopenem and metabolites. Sulopenem accounted for 26.9% and 3.1% of the administered dose in urine and feces, respectively.
Clearance	Mean apparent oral clearance values are 77.6 and 2.06 L/h for sulopenem and probenecid, respectively.
Half-life	Mean plasma half-lives are 1.2 and 2.9 h for sulopenem and probenecid, respectively.
Metabolic pathway(s)	Sulopenem etzadroxil is rapidly hydrolyzed after oral administration to sulopenem in the intestines and in systemic circulation. Sulopenem and two inactive metabolites formed by β-lactam cyclic amide bond hydrolysis (M1a and M1b) are the major circulating entities. Sulopenem, M1a and M1b accounted for 32%, 21.8% and 43.6%, respectively, of circulating radioactivity in the mass balance study. No metabolism of sulopenem was observed in vitro with recombinant CYP or UGT enzymes.
Primary excretion pathways (% dose)	Primarily excreted in urine, i.e., 44.3% of oral radiolabeled dose in mass balance studies. 26.9% of total urinary recovery was in the form of unchanged sulopenem.
L158: Characteristic	Drug Information
Intrinsic Factors and Specific Populations
Body weight	No clinically significant differences in PK of sulopenem were observed based on body weight ranging from 38.8 to 140 kg in the subjects enrolled in phase 1 trials and phase 3 Trials 301, 302 and 303. No PK assessments were conducted in Trial 310.
Age	No clinically significant differences in the PK of sulopenem were observed based on age ranging from 18-91 years.
Renal impairment	No dosage adjustment is needed in patients with CrCl \ge15 mL/min. Use is not recommended in patients with CrCl <15 mL/min or those on hemodialysis.
Hepatic impairment	No dosage adjustment is needed in patients with hepatic impairment.
Drug Interaction Liability (Drug as Perpetrator)
Inhibition/induction of metabolism	In vitro, sulopenem etzadroxil is an inhibitor of CYP3A4/5. However, because it is rapidly hydrolyzed to sulopenem, clinically relevant DDIs are not expected with CYP3A4/5 substrates.
Inhibition/induction of transporter systems	Probenecid is a known inhibitor of OAT1 and OAT3 and was observed to inhibit BCRP in vitro. Sulopenem etzadroxil is an inhibitor of BCRP and P-gp. However, because it is rapidly hydrolyzed to sulopenem, clinically significant DDIs are not expected with BCRP or P-gp substrates.

L161: ## 6. Efficacy (Evaluation of Benefit)
L162: ## 6.1. Assessment of Dose and Potential Effectiveness
L163: The Applicant's proposed dosage of 500 mg sulopenem etzadroxil/500 mg probenecid BID orally was evaluated in two phase 3 uUTI trials (Trials 301 and 310). In Trial 301, the proposed dosing regimen, 500 mg sulopenem etzadroxil/500 mg probenecid BID demonstrated superiority to ciprofloxacin 500 mg BID for the treatment of uUTI in patients who presented with a ciprofloxacin-resistant pathogen at baseline but failed to demonstrate noninferiority to ciprofloxacin in patients with a ciprofloxacin-susceptible pathogen at baseline. In Trial 310, 500 mg sulopenem etzadroxil/500 mg probenecid BID was non-inferior to 875 mg amoxicillin/125 mg clavulanate BID for the treatment of uUTI in the amoxicillin/clavulanate susceptible population. Despite the limitations of nonclinical PK/PD data (see Section 5.1), the results of PTA analyses and a 5-day in vitro hollow-fiber infection model study are supportive of the effectiveness of 500 mg sulopenem etzadroxil/500 mg probenecid BID in the treatment of uUTI. The underlying causes of the mixed clinical trial efficacy outcomes are likely multifactorial, and PTA analyses are unable to predict the performance of 500 mg sulopenem etzadroxil/500 mg probenecid BID against different comparators in an efficacy trial.
L164: ## 6.1.1. Support for Proposed Dose of Sulopenem Etzadroxil
L165: ## Probability of Target Attainment Analyses
L166: Urinary drug concentrations are considered important to the successful treatment of uUTIs, while the relative importance of plasma drug concentrations to efficacy is unclear. The Applicant conducted PTA analyses for both plasma and urinary drug concentrations using %fT&gt;MIC targets derived from a murine thigh infection model and an in vitro 1-compartment infection model to support the proposed dosage of 500 mg sulopenem etzadroxil/500 mg probenecid BID and to support a cutoff value of 0.5 µg/mL for Enterobacteriales susceptibility. Due to deficiencies in the murine thigh infection model study design and limited interpretability of the findings, the resulting targets (i.e., 16.6 and 20.3% fT&gt;MIC for stasis and 1-log kill, respectively) were deemed unreliable. Because the in vitro 1-compartment model does not account for bladder tissue architecture or the complexities of urodynamics, it is unclear whether the derived targets are reasonable surrogates for the relevant infection site. Nonetheless, PTA based on the median in vitro targets of 40.9, 50.2 and 62.6% fT&gt;MIC for stasis, 1-log kill, and 2-log kill, respectively, which numerically offered a more conservative appraisal of efficacy than those determined in the murine thigh infection model, were prioritized to support the proposed dosage. PTA results showed that the free plasma concentrations associated with the Applicant's proposed dose regimen resulted in achievement of the in vitro targets in ≥90% of simulated subjects at MICs ranging from 0.031 to 0.25 µg/mL. The Applicant also evaluated the probability of achieving PK/PD targets in urine by simulating 1 h and 2 h bladder voiding patterns. Based on the urine concentrations associated with the Applicant's proposed dose regimen, urine PTA analyses
L167: showed achievement of the in vitro targets in \ge 90\% of simulated subjects at MICs ranging from 2 to 8 \mu\text{g/mL} (see Section 14).
L168: ## **Findings From In Vitro Hollow-Fiber Study**
L169: To further support the proposed dosage of 500 mg sulopenem etzadroxil/500 mg probenecid BID for the treatment of uUTI, the Applicant evaluated the bactericidal activity of urinary concentrations associated with the proposed dosage. The simulated urinary concentrations were demonstrated to suppress the growth of four *E. coli* isolates (with sulopenem MIC values in the clinically relevant range of 0.03 to 0.5 \mu\text{g/mL}) and prevented the development of resistance for the entire duration of a 5-day study in a hollow-fiber infection model (see Section 14).
L170: ## **6.1.2. Support for Proposed Dose/Contribution of Probenecid**
L171: Probenecid lacks antimicrobial activity; instead, it inhibits OAT3-mediated renal clearance of \beta-lactams such as sulopenem, thus resulting in increased plasma drug concentrations. Multiple-dose administration of 500 mg probenecid increased sulopenem plasma area under the concentration-time curve (AUC) by 1.8-fold with a corresponding 1.9-fold reduction in renal clearance. This dose
L172: in the setting of uUTI (where there are uncertainties surrounding the relative importance of urinary versus plasma concentrations), the available data are inconclusive on the contribution of probenecid to efficacy. There are no clinical studies evaluating the efficacy of sulopenem etzadroxil for the treatment of uUTI in the presence and absence of probenecid. Additionally, interpretation of the observed changes in sulopenem urinary PK in the presence of probenecid is limited by the general uncertainties surrounding urine-specific PK/PD parameters and the complexities of sulopenem's PK/PD behavior. Nonetheless, the totality of available clinical and nonclinical data do support the efficacy of the combined sulopenem etzadroxil/probenecid dosage in the treatment of uUTIs.
L173: ## **6.2. Clinical Studies/Trials Intended To Demonstrate Efficacy**
L174: ## **6.2.1. Results of Pooled Analyses, Trials 301 and 310**
L175: Trial IT001-301 comparing sulopenem to ciprofloxacin for treatment of uUTI in adult women was reviewed for the initial NDA submission and is not included in this review. Please refer to the previous NDA 213972 Multidisciplinary Review and Evaluation dated July 22, 2021, for a full discussion of the design, analysis, and results from this trial and Section 16.1 for a summary of this trial. The current NDA resubmission is based on the most recent phase 3 trial (Trial IT001-310 or Trial 310 for short) which had a different comparator than was used in the previously reviewed Trial IT001-301 and is reviewed in this section. No pooled analyses are presented. Because the Division of Anti-Infectives recommends that Limitations of Use in
L176: labeling be included for cUTI and cIAI, the results of Trials 302 (cUTI) and 303 (cIAI) are discussed briefly in Section 16.
L177: ## 6.2.2. Trial 310
L178: ## 6.2.2.1. Design, Trial 310
L179: Trial 310 was a phase 3, multicenter, double-blinded, double-dummy, randomized, controlled study to compare oral sulopenem to oral amoxicillin/clavulanate for the treatment of uUTI in adult women. Eligible adult women were randomized 1:1 to receive either oral sulopenem etzadroxil/probenecid 500 mg/500 mg BID for 5 days or oral amoxicillin/clavulanate 875 mg/125 mg BID for 5 days. Subjects were followed-up at Day 12 TOC visit and Day 28 (final visit).
L180: ## 6.2.2.2. Eligibility Criteria, Trial 310
L181: Subjects had to meet the following criteria to be eligible for the study:
L182: - Female subjects \ge 18 years of age with \ge 24 hours and \le 96 hours of urinary symptoms attributable to a UTI
- Two of the following signs and symptoms of uUTI: urinary frequency, urinary urgency, pain or burning on micturition, suprapubic pain
- A mid-stream urine specimen with:a machine-read dipstick positive for nitrite AND any positive leukocyte esterase OR
- evidence of pyuria alone.
L183: Subjects who met any of the following specified criteria were excluded from the study, for example, presence of signs and symptoms suggestive of acute pyelonephritis defined as: fever (temperature &gt; 38^\circ Celsius), chills, costovertebral angle tenderness, flank pain, nausea, and/or vomiting.
L184: See Section 15 for full inclusion and exclusion criteria.
L185: ## 6.2.2.3. Statistical Analysis Plan, Trial 310
L186: The primary efficacy endpoint was overall success (combined clinical and microbiologic success) on Day 12 (\pm 1 days)/TOC in micro-MITT, micro-MITT comparator-susceptible (micro-MITTS) and micro-MITT comparator-resistant or nonsusceptible (micro-MITTR) populations. The micro-MITT population included all randomized patients who received at least one single dose of study medication and had a positive study entry urine culture defined as \ge 10^5 colony-forming units (CFU)/mL of a uropathogen (Enterobacterales or *Staphylococcus saprophyticus* (*S. saprophyticus*) only) and no more than 2 species of microorganisms identified in the study entry urine culture, regardless of colony count. Comparator susceptibility was based on MIC [susceptible: MIC \le 8/4 mg/L; nonsusceptible: intermediate (MIC 16/8 mg/L) or resistant (MIC \ge 32/16 mg/L)] to the components of the comparator study drug, amoxicillin and clavulanate, respectively.
L187: For the definitions of overall success, clinical success, and microbiological success endpoints, please see Section 15.
L188: ## Analysis of the Primary Efficacy Endpoint
L189: To control for inflation of the overall type I error rate, the hierarchical testing procedure of Westfall and Krishen (Westfall and Krishen 2001) was proposed by the Applicant and used to test the hypotheses of the primary efficacy endpoint in these populations in the sequential order described below.
L190: - NI in the micro-MITT population.
- NI in the micro-MITTS population or superiority in the micro-MITTR population.
- Superiority test of overall success in the micro-MITT population.
L191: Testing was to proceed to the next comparison only if the null hypothesis in the comparison was rejected. For pre-specified sequential hypothesis testing, no adjustment to the alpha level was required. However, in the second step of the hierarchy, the trial did not adjust for multiplicity in testing in the micro-MITTS and micro-MITTR populations because at the time of study design the analyses in these populations were considered to address separate questions as if they were separate studies under a single protocol for logistical reasons.
L192: Two-sided 95% CIs for the treatment difference in success proportions (sulopenem-active control) would be determined using the method of Miettinen and Nurminen. NI was established if the lower bound of the CI was greater than -10% and superiority was established if the lower bound of the CI was greater than 0.
L193: The FDA had communicated the following comment regarding the planned analysis: “We strongly recommend testing NI in the micro-MITTS population as the primary endpoint. An alternative is hierarchical testing for (i) NI in the micro-MITTS population followed by (ii) superiority in the micro-MITT population. It would be an important review issue if the trial is unable to demonstrate noninferiority in the micro-MITTS population, which is not currently assessed in the first level of the planned hierarchical testing. We note that the trial is adequately powered for the analysis of noninferiority in the micro-MITTS population.”
L194: Because the hierarchical testing rejected the null hypothesis in the first level of testing for noninferiority in the micro-MITT (as will be subsequently discussed), the analysis of the primary endpoint in the micro-MITTS in the second level of the hierarchy was considered to have the statistical interpretability of a prespecified primary analysis.
L195: In addition, the FDA finds the NI testing in a population that included patients with isolates that were not susceptible to the comparator (Step 1), uninterpretable for regulatory purposes.
L196: ## Secondary Efficacy Endpoints
L197: Clinical response and microbiologic response were analyzed. Overall success, clinical success, and microbiologic success by baseline pathogen and monomicrobial/polymicrobial infection were analyzed.
L198: Overall response by baseline uropathogen resistance class(es) were presented.
L199: ## **Interim Analysis**
L200: A blinded interim analysis for sample size re-estimation was to be performed when clinical and microbiologic response data at Day 12 (\pm 1 day)/TOC were available for approximately 50% of the subjects (approximately 983 subjects). The sample size of the study would be computed to ensure that there was sufficient power for the primary efficacy endpoint in the micro-MITTS population. It was anticipated that this would ensure the study was sufficiently powered to test the primary endpoint in the micro-MITT and micro-MITTR populations as well.
L201: Following the blinded interim analysis, the Data Monitoring Committee recommended that in order to maintain 80%-90% power, the trial should continue to enroll to achieve a minimum of 1966 subjects (original sample size in protocol) up to a maximum of 2428 subjects (to achieve 90% power). On October 23, 2023, enrollment was completed with 2222 randomized patients as the Applicant considered that adequate statistical power had been achieved.
L202: ## **6.2.2.4. Results of Analyses, Micro-MITTS and Micro-MITTR Populations, Trial 310**
L203: The study was conducted in the U.S. between October 18, 2022 and November 21, 2023. The clinicaltrials.gov identifier for the study was NCT05584657. In the following subsections, the intent-to-treat (ITT) population will be discussed briefly, followed by results in the micro-MITTS population and micro-MITTR population. As noted above, because the hierarchical testing rejected the null hypothesis in the first level of testing, the analysis of the primary endpoint in the micro-MITTS in the second level of the hierarchy was considered to have the statistical interpretability of a prespecified primary analysis.
L204: ## **Disposition, Baseline Demographics and Baseline Characteristics**
L205: ## **Disposition**
L206: The following Table 8 summarizes the disposition of subjects. A total of 2222 subjects were randomized and included in the ITT population of all randomized subjects. Four subjects in each arm were excluded from a modified intent-to-treat (MITT) population for not receiving study drug. A total of 44.6% of ITT subjects were included in the micro-MITT population (with a nominally significantly higher proportion in the sulopenem than in the control group). A total of 922 and 67 of subjects were included in the micro-MITTS population and micro-MITTR population, respectively.
L207: Overall, approximately 95% of the ITT subjects completed study drug treatment, while 4% discontinued treatment prematurely. The primary reasons for discontinuation of treatment were noncompliance with study drug and withdrawal by subject. Approximately 95% of the ITT subjects completed the study. The primary reasons for study discontinuation were loss to follow-up (1.8%) and withdrawal by subject (3.0%). The two treatment groups were comparable with respect to the reasons for treatment discontinuation or study discontinuation.

L252: In the micro-MITTS population, a total of 6.2% of the subjects (comparable in the two treatment groups) reported concomitant antibacterial drug use (Table 16). L272: ## Distribution of Baseline Study Uropathogens by Antibiotic Resistance
L273: Distribution of baseline study uropathogens by antibiotic resistance is shown in **Table 20**. A total of 8.9% of micro-MITTS subjects had at least 1 baseline Enterobacterales pathogen that was extended-spectrum β-lactamase-positive, as determined by having a ceftriaxone MIC of &gt;1 µg/mL. A total of 13%, 30.7%, 26.9% of subjects' isolates were non-susceptible to nitrofurantoin, trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole and quinolones, respectively. Susceptibility was comparable (not nominally statistically significant) between the two treatment groups.

L278: ## Primary and Key Secondary Efficacy Results
L279: ## Primary Efficacy Analysis Results
L280: In the micro-MITTS population, the overall success proportions were 61.7% and 55.0% in the sulopenem and amoxicillin/clavulanate treatment groups, respectively, with a difference of 6.7% [95% CI: 0.3%, 13.0%] and a two-sided p-value of 0.040 for superiority. The results demonstrated NI using a -10% NI margin and superiority of sulopenem to the active control. The treatment effect for overall success was driven by microbiological success, as the clinical success proportions were similar between the two treatment groups.

L328: ## Sensitivity Analyses of Primary Efficacy Endpoint
L329: ## **Contaminated Urine Sample Treated as Failure**
L330: At TOC in the micro-MITTS population, there were 23 and 24 subjects in the sulopenem and active control groups, respectively, that were coded by the Applicant as “Eradication” with ≥3 organisms present (indicating contamination at collection). Thirteen and 18 of these subjects were coded as success for the overall response. If these successes were changed to failures, then the treatment effect was slightly higher, as shown in Table 30.
L331: ## **Complete Eradication (&lt;100 CFU/mL)**
L332: The overall response at TOC when using complete eradication (&lt;100 CFU/mL) as the definition of microbiologic success was lower in both groups, but the treatment effect was similar to that observed in the primary analysis (6.5% versus 6.7%) (Table 30).
L333: ## **Concomitant Use of Antibacterial Drugs**
L334: Five and two subjects in the sulopenem and the control group, respectively, who received concomitant antibacterial drugs were considered as successes in the primary efficacy analysis. If those 7 subjects were considered as failures, the difference between the two groups reduced from 6.7% in the primary analysis to 6.1%, only demonstrating NI.

L367: In view of the failure of sulopenem to meet the primary endpoint in Trial 302 for cUTI, there is concern for possible off-label use of oral sulopenem as stepdown therapy following initial IV antibacterial treatment of cUTI. Please see Section 16.4 for a discussion of results from Trial 302.
L368: ## Study Results, Trial 303 for cIAI
L369: In view of the failure of sulopenem to meet the primary endpoint in Trial 303 for cIAI, there is concern for possible off-label use of oral sulopenem as stepdown therapy following initial IV antibacterial treatment of cIAI. Please see Section 16.5 for a discussion of results from Trial 303.

L372: ## 7. Safety (Risk and Risk Management)
L373: ## 7.1. Potential Risks or Safety Concerns Based on Nonclinical Data
L374: Nonclinical studies submitted to support the safety evaluation for this NDA include the following studies with sulopenem etzadroxil: safety pharmacology studies (neurofunctional, in vitro and in vivo cardiovascular, and pulmonary function assessments), pharmacokinetic and toxicokinetic assessments (absorption, distribution, metabolism, and excretion), general toxicology studies (1-month studies in rats and monkeys), in vitro and in vivo genetic toxicology studies, and developmental and reproductive toxicology studies (male and female fertility study in rats, embryo-fetal development studies in mice, rats, and rabbits, a pre-postnatal development study in rats and a juvenile toxicology study in rats). Also, a 14-day combination toxicology study with orally administered sulopenem etzadroxil and probenecid was conducted in rats. Additional nonclinical safety studies with sulopenem, the active metabolite of sulopenem etzadroxil, that were evaluated in support of the NDA include an in vitro hERG assessment, in vitro plasma-protein binding, CYP450 inhibition, mass balance, and metabolite profiling studies, and a full battery of genetic toxicology studies. Additional information regarding genetic toxicity findings for probenecid was obtained from historical probenecid product labels previously approved by the FDA.
L375: ## 7.1.1 Target Organs of Toxicity
L376: ## Kidney
L377: Adult rats were administered sulopenem etzadroxil in oral doses of 100, 400, and 2000 mg/kg/day in the 1-month toxicology study in rats. Renal effects included minimal vacuolation of the tubular epithelium, tubular hypertrophy, and a potentially adverse effect, i.e., a low incidence of tubular degeneration. These effects occurred primarily in high-dose males and females in the 2000 mg/kg/day group and to a lesser extent in mid-dose males receiving 400 mg/kg/day.
L378: In a definitive juvenile toxicity study, oral administration of sulopenem etzadroxil in doses of 25, 75, and 225 mg/kg/day to juvenile rats for 85 days beginning on postnatal Day 5 and continuing to postnatal Day 90, was associated with more varied and severe renal histopathology findings
L379: compared to the findings in adult rats in the 1-month toxicology study. Renal histopathology in juvenile male and/or female rats included slight degeneration of tubular epithelium, renal infarcts, and intratubular concretions. The findings in juvenile rats occurred at lower sulopenem etzadroxil doses and exposures than the doses associated with renal findings in adult rats in the 1-month study, and the findings were poorly reversible or, in the case of tubular concretions, irreversible after a 2-week recovery period (see Sections 5.4 and 5.5.6 in the NDA 213972 Multidisciplinary Review dated July 22, 2021, for more information). The results are consistent with a potential for more severe renal toxicity in juvenile rats compared to adults and suggest increased monitoring for renal toxicity may be warranted for clinical administration of sulopenem etzadroxil to pediatric patients.
L380: ## **Gastrointestinal Tract**
L381: Sulopenem etzadroxil-related findings in gastrointestinal (GI) tissues were observed in the 14-day combination-toxicology study with sulopenem etzadroxil plus probenecid in rats (mixed cell infiltrates, hyperplasia of glandular epithelium and edema in the large intestine) and the 1-month study in monkeys (minimal mucosal hyperplasia). The sulopenem etzadroxil doses at which GI effects were observed in the 14-day combination toxicology study in rats (800 mg/kg/day) and the 1-month study in monkeys (400 mg/kg/day) are approximately 7- and 6-times, respectively, the clinical sulopenem exposure for the maximum recommended human dose of sulopenem etzadroxil based on plasma AUC comparison (see Sections 5.4, 5.5.1 and 5.5.2 in the NDA 213972 Multidisciplinary Review dated July 22, 2021).
L382: ## **Immune/Hematopoietic Systems**
L383: In the 1-month toxicology study, monkeys also exhibited positive Coombs test results that tended to increase with the sulopenem etzadroxil dose and likely contributed to antibody mediation of minimal erythrocyte loss and compensatory erythropoiesis in monkeys. The lowest sulopenem etzadroxil dose (400 mg/kg/day) at which these effects were observed is approximately 6-times the clinical sulopenem exposure for the maximum recommended human dose of sulopenem etzadroxil based on plasma AUC comparison (see Sections 5.4 and 5.5.1 in the NDA 213972 Multidisciplinary Review dated July 22, 2021).

L395: ## 7.1.2 Developmental and Reproductive Toxicity
L396: Oral administration of sulopenem etzadroxil to pregnant females was associated with maternal and fetal toxicity in embryo-fetal development studies in mice, rats, and rabbits.
L397: In mice, sulopenem etzadroxil administered to pregnant females in oral doses of 100, 400, and 2000 mg/kg/day during the period of organogenesis was associated with maternal toxicity (clinical signs and reduced maternal body weights) and fetal toxicity including reduced fetal weights and a fetal malformation. Maternal clinical signs including respiratory distress, abdominal distension, decreased motor activity and reduced maternal body weight gain occurred in the 2000 mg/kg/day group. In the same group, reduced fetal weights were observed, and a fetal malformation, cleft palate, occurred with an increased fetal and litter incidence relative to control values.
L398: Sulopenem etzadroxil administered in oral doses of 100, 400, and 2000 mg/kg/day to pregnant females during the period of organogenesis in a rat embryo-fetal development study was associated with maternal weight loss and reduced maternal weight gain and reduced fetal body weights. Maternal toxicity occurred in the mid- and high-dose groups receiving 400 and 2000 mg/kg/day, respectively. Fetal weight loss occurred in the 2000 mg/kg/day group.
L399: In rabbits, oral doses of sulopenem etzadroxil (5, 15, and 50 mg/kg/day) administered to pregnant females during the period of organogenesis were associated with reduced maternal weight gain occurring in a dose-dependent manner in all the treatment groups. In addition, post-implantation loss was increased and reductions in the number of viable fetuses, gravid uterine weights, and fetal body weights occurred in the mid- and high-dose groups receiving 15 and 50 mg/kg/day, respectively.

L409: ## 7.2. Potential Risks or Safety Concerns Based on Drug Class or Other Drug-Specific Factors
L410: Oral sulopenem etzadroxil is the pro-drug of the penem antibacterial drug, sulopenem and is hydrolyzed rapidly to sulopenem upon oral ingestion. Penem antibacterials are a class of beta-lactams structurally similar to carbapenems. If approved, sulopenem would be the first oral penem on the U.S. market so there are no in-class comparators. In general, carbapenems have a favorable safety profile and are well-tolerated. Common adverse reactions associated with their use include headache, nausea, diarrhea, vomiting, rash, and injection site reactions. Labeled Warnings and Precautions for carbapenems (imipenem-cilastatin, ertapenem, meropenem) include hypersensitivity reactions, seizures and other adverse central nervous system experiences, *Clostridioides difficile*-associated disease, severe cutaneous adverse reactions, thrombocytopenia in patients with renal dysfunction, development of drug-resistant bacteria and drug-drug interactions (DDIs) with valproic acid resulting in reduction of its plasma concentrations and increased seizure potential.
L411: Reported postmarketing adverse events (AEs) for carbapenems include anaphylaxis, hepatitis and hepatic failure, hematologic adverse reactions including pancytopenia and hemolytic anemia, central nervous system disturbances, muscular weakness, Stevens-Johnson syndrome, toxic epidermal necrolysis, drug reaction with eosinophilia and systemic symptoms, erythema multiforme, acute generalized exanthematous pustulosis, drug fever, and acute renal failure.
L412: Probenecid has been in use since the 1950s and is generally well-tolerated with a favorable safety profile. Labeled Warnings and Precautions for probenecid include exacerbation of gout, increased plasma concentration of methotrexate, severe allergic reactions including anaphylaxis, hematuria, renal colic, costovertebral pain, formation of uric acid stones, and antagonism of the uricosuric action of probenecid with concomitant use of salicylates. Adverse reactions observed with probenecid include headache, dizziness, precipitation of acute gouty arthritis, hepatic necrosis, nausea, vomiting, anorexia, sore gums, genitourinary AEs including uric acid stones and nephrotic syndrome, hypersensitivity reactions, aplastic anemia, leukopenia, hemolytic anemia, anemia, dermatitis, alopecia, and flushing.
L413: The risks and safety concerns for oral sulopenem are anticipated to be similar to carbapenems as summarized above except that because sulopenem etzadroxil/probenecid is an oral tablet, injection site reactions would not be expected. Adverse events of special interest monitored by the Applicant during the uUTI development program included diarrhea and renal disorders; infusion-related events were monitored in Trials 302 and 303 utilizing sulopenem IV but will not be discussed further in this review.
L414: ## 7.3. Potential Risks or Safety Concerns Identified Through Postmarket Experience
L415: Not applicable. Sulopenem etzadroxil/probenecid is not approved in the U.S. or in any foreign market; therefore, no postmarketing experience is available for sulopenem etzadroxil/probenecid.

L422: ## 7.4. FDA Approach to the Safety Review
L423: The primary safety analysis for the resubmitted NDA was conducted on data derived from the phase 3 uUTI Trial 310. Additional analyses were conducted on the combined phase 3 uUTI study populations from Trials 301 and 310. During the first review cycle, safety data from Trials 301, 302 and 303 were analyzed, along with phase 1 studies (conducted by the Applicant and Pfizer) and phase 2 studies (conducted by Pfizer). While specific safety findings from these three trials (301, 302 and 303) are presented in this review when relevant, please refer to the NDA Multi-Disciplinary Review and Evaluation {NDA 213972} dated July 22, 2021 for complete details. Identified safety issues during the previous review cycle included hypersensitivity reactions (angioedema), elevated alanine aminotransferase (ALT), and gastrointestinal adverse reactions.
L424: No major data quality or integrity issues were identified for Trial 310. Coding of verbatim terms to the Medical Dictionary for Regulatory Activities (MedDRA) preferred terms (PTs) was generally acceptable. A treatment-emergent adverse event (TEAE) was defined by the Applicant as an AE that newly appeared or worsened in severity following study drug initiation. A TEAE was considered drug-related if the AE was possibly or probably related to study drug. Safety evaluations included recording of AEs, vital signs, and collection of laboratory results. While the TOC visit was Day 12 (+/-1 day), AEs were collected through the final study visit (Day 28 \pm 2 days). MedDRA version 26.1 was used for Trial 310 (MedDRA version 21.0 was used for Trials 301, 302, and 303; MedDRA version 22.0 was used for the phase 1 studies). AEs were classified by investigators as mild (does not interfere with the patient's usual function), moderate (interferes to some extent with the patient's usual function), or severe (interferes significantly with the patient's usual function). An AE was defined as a serious adverse event (SAE) if the event:
L425: - Resulted in death,
- Was life-threatening,
- Required hospitalization or prolongation of hospitalization,
- Resulted in persistent or significant disability/incapacity,
- Resulted in congenital anomaly/birth defect,
- Was assessed as being a medically important event based on medical and scientific judgement. Such medically important events may not be immediately life-threatening or result in death or hospitalization but may require medical or surgical intervention to prevent one of the above outcomes.
L426: The clinical data scientist performed standard safety analyses including FDA medical queries (FMQs) to identify safety signals. In this review, the terms AE and TEAE are used interchangeably and sulopenem etzadroxil/probenecid is also referenced as oral sulopenem.
L427: ## 7.5. Adequacy of the Clinical Safety Database
L428: The safety database is adequate. Trial 301 in the original NDA submission included 825 subjects who received sulopenem etzadroxil/probenecid for the treatment of uUTI. Thirteen subjects (8
L429: from the sulopenem arm, 5 from the ciprofloxacin arm) in Trial 301 were from site 218 and excluded from the FDA's safety database (b) (7)(A). Trial 310 added an additional 1107 subjects resulting in a total clinical safety database of 1932 subjects who received oral sulopenem etzadroxil/probenecid for the treatment of uUTI (Table 37).
L430: Additional safety data were available from 1030 subjects who received IV sulopenem and oral sulopenem etzadroxil/probenecid in the phase 3 cUTI and cIAI trials as well as 2006 subjects from twenty-four phase 1 and phase 2 studies who received IV and oral formulations of sulopenem.
L431: The numbers of subjects, dosing, and duration of exposure in Trial 310 (in addition to the previously reviewed studies) are sufficient to conduct a safety review.

L438: ## **Baseline Demographic and Clinical Characteristics**
L439: In Trial 310, baseline demographic and clinical characteristics were similar between treatment arms (Table 38). All subjects were female and from the United States. The median age in the sulopenem arm was 50 years and 48 years in the comparator arm. In both arms, most subjects (around 80%) were less than 65 years old. There were slightly more subjects (7.2%) in the sulopenem arm who were aged 75 years or older compared to the amoxicillin/clavulanate arm (5.8%). In both arms, the majority of subjects were white and Hispanic or Latino. A greater number of subjects (39.3%) in the sulopenem arm had a BMI &gt;30 kg/m2 than in the amoxicillin/clavulanate arm (36.5%). The number of subjects with CrCl &gt;60 mL/min was comparable between arms, but there were more subjects (1.7%) in the amoxicillin/clavulanate arm with a CrCl &lt;30 mL/min compared to sulopenem subjects (0.8%). There was a higher percentage of subjects with a CrCl of 30-60 mL/min in the sulopenem arm (18.0%) compared to subjects in the amoxicillin/clavulanate arm (15.4%).

L474: ## 7.6.1.4. Adverse Events Leading to Treatment Discontinuation, Trial 310
L475: The proportion of subjects with TEAEs leading to treatment discontinuation was comparable in both treatment arms (0.7% in the sulopenem arm and 0.4% in the amoxicillin/clavulanate arm). In the sulopenem arm, these included the following PTs, most of which (except chills, headache and syncope) were related to the Gastrointestinal Disorders system organ class (SOC): nausea (n = 4), gastroesophageal reflux disease ([GERD] n = 3), diarrhea (n = 3), constipation (n = 1), flatulence (n = 1), abdominal pain (n = 1), chills (n = 1), headache (n = 1), and syncope (n = 1).

L482: The proportion of subjects who terminated the study early was approximately 5% in both treatment arms with the majority of discontinuations being lost to follow-up or withdrawal by subject. However, there were three subjects in the sulopenem arm who discontinued the study due to an AE. Sulopenem subjects with AEs leading to treatment or study discontinuation are briefly described below:
L483: - Subject (b) (6) had an AE of mild worsened acid reflux. The subject took a single dose of sulopenem etzadroxil/probenecid on study Day 1 and experienced worsened acid reflux. Sulopenem was discontinued and she was prescribed Tums. The AE recovered/resolved on the same day. The investigator assessed the event as probably related to study drug. The FDA reviewer agrees with the investigator's assessment.
- Subject (b) (6) had AEs of moderate diarrhea, worsened acid reflux, and nausea that began on Day 2. Nexium and Zantac were prescribed, and sulopenem was discontinued on Day 3. All three AEs recovered/resolved on Day 4. The investigator considered nausea possibly related to study drug and diarrhea and worsened acid reflux as probably related. The FDA reviewer agrees that the three AEs were probably related to sulopenem.
- Subject (b) (6) had AEs of mild constipation, nausea, and headache. The subject took a single dose of sulopenem on Day 1 and developed these three AEs on the same day. No therapy was prescribed. Sulopenem was discontinued on Day 1 with resolution of the AEs on Day 3. The AEs resulted in study discontinuation. The investigator considered the AEs as possibly related to sulopenem. The FDA reviewer agrees that nausea and headache were
L484: possibly related to sulopenem but notes that constipation is unlikely to be related to sulopenem.
L485: - Subject (b) (6) had an AE of severe vasovagal syncope on Day 1 after a single dose of sulopenem. The AE resolved the same day and resulted in treatment and study discontinuation. The AE was considered possibly related to sulopenem by the investigator, and the FDA reviewer agrees.
- Subject (b) (6) had AEs of moderate diarrhea, mild nausea, and mild chills starting on Day 2. Sulopenem was discontinued on Day 4, after six total doses. Nausea resolved on Day 4 and chills and diarrhea resolved on Day 6. The investigator considered nausea and diarrhea to be possibly related to study drug and chills unlikely related to study drug. The FDA reviewer agrees with this assessment.
- Subject (b) (6) had AEs of mild diarrhea and nausea that began on Day 1. Sulopenem was discontinued on Day 2 after 3 total doses. Diarrhea and nausea resolved on Day 4 but led to study discontinuation. The investigator assessed the two AEs as possibly related to sulopenem. The FDA reviewer agrees with this assessment.
- Subject (b) (6) had an AE of mild abdominal pain that occurred on Study Day 1. Sulopenem was discontinued the same day after two total doses. No therapy was prescribed for abdominal pain, and the AE resolved on Day 3. The investigator considered the AE unlikely related to study drug. Although the narrative is limited, the FDA reviewer disagrees and notes that abdominal pain could potentially be related to sulopenem.
- Subject (b) (6) had AEs of mild flatulence and acid reflux that occurred on Day 5. Sulopenem was discontinued on Day 5 after eight total doses. The AEs resolved without therapy. The two AEs were assessed as possibly related to sulopenem, and the FDA reviewer agrees.
L486: The most common adverse reactions leading to discontinuation (nausea, diarrhea, and gastroesophageal reflux) will be included in Section 6 of the Prescribing Information.
L487: ## 7.6.1.5. Treatment-Emergent Adverse Events, Trial 310
L488: TEAEs occurred in 18.9% of the subjects in the sulopenem arm and 12.3% of subjects in the amoxicillin/clavulanate arm. As shown in Table 44, this difference in TEAEs was largely driven by diarrhea (8.1% in the sulopenem arm versus 4.1% in the amoxicillin/clavulanate arm). The following TEAEs (listed in decreasing order of frequency) occurred more commonly in the sulopenem etzadroxil/probenecid arm and were seen in \ge 1\% of subjects: diarrhea (8.1%), nausea (4.3%), vulvovaginal mycotic infection (3.0%), headache (2.2%), vomiting (1.4%), and gastroesophageal reflux disease (1.0%). Fatigue (0.5%) and urine odor abnormal (0.4%) occurred in the sulopenem etzadroxil/probenecid arm, but not in the amoxicillin/clavulanate arm. Abdominal pain occurred in 0.6% of subjects in the sulopenem arm and in 1.0% of subjects in the amoxicillin/clavulanate arm.
