L506: ## Diarrhea
L507: Diarrhea was the most common TEAE in the sulopenem etzadroxil/probenecid arm and had a higher incidence (8.1% versus 4.1%) than in the amoxicillin/clavulanate arm. In most patients (7.5%), diarrhea was considered to be related to study drug. The mean duration of diarrhea in the sulopenem group was 2.9 days, and the mean duration from end of sulopenem treatment to resolution of diarrhea was 4.1 days. There were no cases of *Clostridioides difficile* infection in the sulopenem etzadroxil/probenecid arm. There was one subject with *Clostridioides difficile* infection in the amoxicillin/clavulanate arm.
L508: Most cases of diarrhea in the oral sulopenem arm were mild or moderate, but there were three cases (0.3%) of severe diarrhea. The subjects with severe diarrhea were not administered therapy for diarrhea and did not discontinue study drug. One of the subjects had diarrhea for one day and the other two subjects had diarrhea for three days. As discussed above in Section 7.6.1.4, three patients discontinued sulopenem due to mild or moderate diarrhea.
L509: ## Vomiting
L510: Vomiting was more common in the sulopenem etzadroxil/probenecid arm, occurring in 1.4% of subjects compared to 0.4% in the comparator arm. Most cases of vomiting were considered mild, and none were severe. No patients discontinued sulopenem etzadroxil/probenecid due to vomiting. The mean duration of vomiting in the sulopenem arm was 1.7 days.
L511: ## Gastroesophageal Reflux Disease
L512: The incidence of GERD was higher in the sulopenem etzadroxil/probenecid arm, occurring in 1% of subjects compared to 0.1% in the comparator arm. Most cases of GERD were mild. There were no severe cases of GERD; however, as described above in Section 7.6.1.4, GERD led to discontinuation of sulopenem in three subjects. The mean duration of GERD was 3.1 days in the sulopenem arm.
L513: ## Fungal Infection
L514: The number of subjects having an AE of fungal infection was higher in the sulopenem etzadroxil/probenecid arm (3.0%) than in the amoxicillin/clavulanate arm (1.2%). All cases were under the PT vulvovaginal mycotic infection. AEs were either mild or moderate and did not lead to treatment discontinuation.
L515: ## Fatigue
L516: Five subjects (0.5%) experienced fatigue in the sulopenem etzadroxil/probenecid arm whereas no subjects experienced fatigue in the comparator arm. Four of the five subjects experienced mild fatigue and one experienced moderate fatigue. The mean duration of fatigue was 2.7 days. No subjects discontinued study drug due to fatigue.
L517: ## Urine Odor Abnormal
L518: The AE of urine odor abnormal only occurred in the sulopenem arm. Four subjects (0.4%) experienced this AE. All cases were considered mild, and none resulted in treatment discontinuation. This AE was also seen in Trial 301 and phase 1 studies of sulopenem. Per the NDA Multi-disciplinary Review and Evaluation {NDA 213972} dated July 22, 2021, the Applicant reported that sulfur-containing sulopenem metabolites are the likely cause of the abnormal urine odor.
L519: ## 7.6.1.6. Laboratory Findings, Trial 310
L520: In Trial 310, there were no significant differences between treatment arms in baseline average chemistry and hematology values or significant interval changes in mean values between baseline and TOC.
L521: As shown in Table 46, the frequency of patients with one or more chemistry analyte values with specified elevated or low values was comparable between the two arms.

L550: ## 7.6.1.7. Assessment of Drug-Induced Liver Injury, Trial 310
L551: There were no significant differences between the two treatment arms in the proportions of patients with abnormal liver chemistry values (ALT, aspartate aminotransferase [AST], alkaline phosphatase [AP], total bilirubin). No subjects in the sulopenem arm had elevations in AP &gt;1.5X upper limit of normal (ULN) compared to two (0.2%) subjects in the amoxicillin/clavulanate arm. One (0.1%) subject in the sulopenem arm had an elevated bilirubin level &gt;2X ULN compared to 3 (0.3%) subjects in the amoxicillin/clavulanate arm.

L581: ## Subjects With Elevated Liver Enzymes Postbaseline
L582: Narratives for subjects in the sulopenem arm with ALT or AST values &gt;3x ULN or Bilirubin &gt;2x ULN are discussed below. The first three subjects had normal liver function tests at baseline,
L583: while the last subject had abnormal liver function tests at baseline. Please also refer to Section 7.6.4.7.
L584: - Subject (b) (6) was a 74-year-old woman who received five days of sulopenem etzadroxil/probenecid. On Day 12, ALT had increased to 192 U/L, AST had increased to 87 U/L, and gamma-glutamyl transferase (GGT) had increased to 248 U/L. AP and bilirubin were normal. At Day 28, AST and ALT had normalized and GGT trended down to 119 U/L (normal range 7-38 U/L). The subject was asymptomatic but had underlying non-alcoholic steatohepatitis and was taking Crestor and metformin. Sulopenem may have contributed to the increase in GGT, AST, and ALT, but attribution of causality is confounded by the subject's comorbidities and concomitant medications.
- Subject (b) (6) was a 23-year-old woman with ALT and AST elevated at 92 U/L and 231 U/L, respectively, at the Day 12 visit. Additionally, lactate dehydrogenase was elevated at 510 U/L. GGT, AP, and bilirubin levels were normal. On Day 15, ALT and AST were trending down and lactate dehydrogenase had normalized. Liver enzymes were normal on Day 22. The subject was asymptomatic and her only other medication was Lo Loestrin Fe. Investigations included negative viral hepatitis serologies, negative urine toxicology screen, normal % carbohydrate-deficient transferrin, and normal CK-18 M30 Apoptosense. Given the time course and lack of an alternative cause, sulopenem was potentially the cause of the elevation in liver enzymes.
- Subject (b) (6) was a 27-year-old woman who received 5 days of sulopenem etzadroxil/probenecid. On Day 12, total bilirubin and direct bilirubin were elevated at 2.83 mg/dL and 0.49 mg/dL, respectively. ALT, AST, GGT, and AP were normal. Labs were repeated on Day 37 and the bilirubin had normalized. The subject was asymptomatic and her only concomitant medication was an oral contraceptive (Yasmine). Urine toxicology screen and hepatitis serologies were negative. Testing for % carbohydrate-deficient-transferrin was normal. The etiology of the asymptomatic hyperbilirubinemia is unclear, but Gilbert syndrome is a consideration.
- Subject (b) (6) was a 38-year-old woman who received 5 days of sulopenem etzadroxil/probenecid. At baseline, ALT (236 U/L), AST (180 U/L), and GGT (123 U/L) were elevated. At Day 5, these lab values remained abnormal with decreases in ALT and AST values and slight increase in GGT. At Day 12, ALT, AST and GGT remained elevated. She had a past history of elevated liver function tests with no clear etiology. As these laboratory abnormalities were present at baseline, sulopenem was likely not the cause.
L585: ## 7.6.1.8. Vital-Sign Analyses, Trial 310
L586: Review of mean values and mean changes in vital signs from baseline to Day 12 did not reveal significant differences between the two arms.
L587: ## 7.6.1.9. Subgroup Analyses, Trial 310
L588: All subjects in Trial 310 were female. In the sulopenem arm, the frequency of AEs was overall balanced across age groups. AEs occurred with a similar frequency between white and Black subjects within both arms. The small number of subjects of other races preclude further
L589: conclusions about race-based AE imbalances. In the sulopenem arm, AEs were less frequent (14.4%) in Hispanic or Latino subjects than in non-Hispanic/Latino subjects (27.9%). The reason for this finding is unclear and differs from Trial 301 where AEs were more frequent in Hispanic or Latino subjects (28.9%) than in non-Hispanic/Latino subjects (22.7%). The frequency of AEs was similar in sulopenem subjects with CrCl 30-60 mL/min and sulopenem subjects with CrCl &gt;60 mL/min. The number of subjects with CrCl &lt;30 mL/min was too low to draw conclusions. Sulopenem-treated subjects with a BMI of &lt;25 had the highest frequency of AEs compared with subjects with higher BMIs; this may be a chance finding as a biologically plausible cause is not apparent.

L593: ## 7.6.2. Summary of Safety Results, Trial 301
L594: The safety data from Trial 301 were reviewed in the initial review cycle for NDA 213972. The Agency's safety database excluded 13 subjects (8 in the sulopenem arm and 5 in the ciprofloxacin arm) from Site 218
L595: (b) (7)(A)
L596: (b) (7)(A) The Applicant included these subjects in their safety database. For completeness, a summary of safety findings from Trial 301 is provided below. For detailed analysis, please refer to the NDA Multi-disciplinary Review and Evaluation {NDA 213972} dated July 22, 2021. Identified safety issues during the previous review cycle included hypersensitivity reactions, elevated ALT, and GI adverse reactions.
L597: A total of 825 subjects in the sulopenem arm were included in the safety database of Trial 301. More subjects in the sulopenem arm (25.1%) experienced a TEAE than subjects in the ciprofloxacin arm (14.0%), largely driven by TEAEs in the Gastrointestinal disorders SOC (17% in the sulopenem arm, 7.9% in the ciprofloxacin arm) and to a lesser extent by TEAEs under the SOCs of Infections and infestations (4.6% in the sulopenem arm, 2.6% in the ciprofloxacin arm), Nervous system disorders (3.8% in the sulopenem arm, 2.8% in the ciprofloxacin arm), and Renal and urinary disorders (1.5% in the sulopenem arm, 0.1% in the ciprofloxacin arm). The following TEAEs occurred in 1% or more of subjects in the sulopenem arm and were more frequent in the sulopenem arm compared to the ciprofloxacin arm (listed in descending order): diarrhea (12.5%), nausea (3.9%), headache (2.2%), abdominal pain (2.2%), vomiting (1.6%), vulvovaginal mycotic infection (1.3%), dizziness (1.1%), and urine odor abnormal (1.0%). A total of 13 (1.6%) subjects in the sulopenem arm had a TEAE leading to study drug discontinuation compared to 8 (1.0%) subjects in the ciprofloxacin arm. The following TEAEs led to sulopenem discontinuation: vomiting (n=3), abdominal pain (n=2), diarrhea (n=2), dizziness (n=2), nausea (n=1), angioedema (n=1), dyspnea (n=1), and hypertension (n=1).
L598: Given that there was a notable imbalance in diarrhea between arms, further analysis was conducted. Diarrhea occurred in 103 (12.5%) subjects in the sulopenem arm and 21 (2.6%) in the ciprofloxacin arm. In the sulopenem arm, all diarrhea was either mild (10.2%) or moderate (2.3%). The FDA reviewer noted that the average duration of diarrhea was longer by about one day in subjects in the sulopenem arm compared to subjects in the ciprofloxacin arm, and subjects who took sulopenem with food had a shorter duration of diarrhea (a difference of 2 days on average) compared to subjects who did not take all their sulopenem doses with food.
L599: There was one death in Trial 301 and this subject is described in Section 7.6.4.2 Six subjects (0.7%) in the sulopenem arm (described in Section 7.6.4.3 and two subjects (0.2%) in the ciprofloxacin arm experienced SAEs.
L600: On review of mean chemistry and hematology laboratory values at baseline and Day 12 (TOC), the proportions of sulopenem subjects with postbaseline abnormalities, including liver enzyme elevations, were low and no significant differences were noted between treatment arms. There were no cases meeting Hy's Law criteria in the sulopenem arm, and no imbalances were noted in peak AST elevations between arms. The FDA reviewer, Dr. Mukil Natarajan, noted that several of the subjects with ALT elevations had baseline abnormal ALT values that were likely due to underlying conditions such as fatty liver disease. Dr. Natarajan concluded that sulopenem may cause elevation of ALT.
L601: No significant differences in vital signs were seen between the two arms. Electrocardiograms were not collected in the phase 3 trials as there was adequate data on sulopenem and cardiac conduction from the phase 1 Study A7371007, which was reviewed by the QT Interdisciplinary Review Team in 2017.
L602: Subgroup analyses revealed that subjects with Hispanic/Latino ethnicity, BMI&gt;30, and those in the United States were more likely to have a TEAE compared to the overall population. Among these groups, the difference in the incidence of TEAEs between the arms was largely accounted for by diarrhea. Most subjects of Hispanic/Latino ethnicity and BMI&gt;30 were enrolled in the United States. The FDA reviewer suspected the higher incidence of diarrhea could be due to different physiological responses based on ethnicity or obesity or could be due to differences in AE reporting by country/site. The FDA reviewer noted that the rate of TEAEs in Ukraine was notably lower than in the United States or Russia with no TEAEs of diarrhea reported from subjects in Ukraine.
L603: The integrated assessment of safety included data from Trials 301, 302, and 303 as well as phase 1 and 2 studies. The following safety issues were identified:
L604: - **Angioedema:** As discussed in Section 7.6.4.1, one sulopenem subject in Trial 301 experienced angioedema. In addition, a subject in a phase 1 study experienced angioedema after a dose of sulopenem etzadroxil/probenecid. Hypersensitivity will be included as a warning in the labeling.
- **Gastrointestinal AEs:** GI AEs, including diarrhea, nausea, and abdominal pain, were common among subjects taking sulopenem. Diarrhea was the most common AE among sulopenem subjects, and in general was mild and not treatment-limiting. Taking sulopenem etzadroxil/probenecid with food appeared to shorten the duration of diarrhea. GI AEs are to be included in Section 6 of labeling.
- **Elevations in ALT:** As noted in Section 7.6.4.7, elevations in ALT were more common among sulopenem subjects compared to ciprofloxacin subjects in Trial 301 and in the integrated phase 3 population (Trials 301, 302, and 303). Please refer to Section 7.6.4.7. Elevated transaminases will be noted in Section 6 of labeling.
L605: The safety findings from Trial 310 were consistent with the safety findings from Trial 301. No new safety signals were identified in Trial 310.
L606: ## 7.6.3. Summary of Safety in Phase 1 and Phase 2 Clinical Studies
L607: The phase 1 and 2 studies were reviewed during the initial review cycle (see the NDA Multi-disciplinary Review and Evaluation {NDA 213972} dated July 22, 2021). Safety signals identified in phase 1 studies were diarrhea, nausea, abdominal pain, headache, dizziness, rash, and abnormal urine odor. Additionally, as noted above, one subject who received oral sulopenem etzadroxil/probenecid experienced angioedema of the face and lips and discontinued study drug. The safety signals in the phase 3 trials were consistent with the observed AEs in the phase 1 studies.
L608: In the Pfizer-conducted phase 2 studies, there were three deaths in subjects who received sulopenem. Dr. Natarajan reviewed the narratives. Two deaths were due to underlying malignancy and not related to sulopenem. The third death was related to myocardial infarction and pneumonia which were unlikely to be related to sulopenem.
L609: ## 7.6.4. Safety Results, Pooled Analyses, Trials 301 and 310
L610: ## 7.6.4.1. Overview of Treatment-Emergent Adverse Events Summary, Pooled Analyses, Trials 301 and 310
L611: An overview of TEAEs, SAEs and drug discontinuations in the ISP (Trials 301 and 310) is provided in Table 53. Six (0.3%) subjects in the sulopenem arm had a SAE. All six subjects were enrolled in Trial 301. One SAE, angioedema, was judged as related to sulopenem etzadroxil/probenecid and led to treatment discontinuation; the remaining SAEs are described in Section 7.6.4.3. The single death was due to underlying lung adenocarcinoma and was not related to study drug (see Section 7.6.4.2). TEAEs resulting in treatment discontinuation were reported in 21 (1.1%) subjects in the sulopenem group with the majority of the TEAEs being gastrointestinal AEs, including diarrhea, nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, and gastroesophageal reflux disease (see Section 7.6.4.4). The overall incidence of TEAEs was higher (21.5%) in the sulopenem group than in the comparator groups (amoxicillin/clavulanate, 12.3%; ciprofloxacin, 14.0%). In all three groups, the majority of TEAEs were mild or moderate with severe AEs being uncommon.

L623: ## 7.6.4.3. Serious Treatment-Emergent Adverse Events, Pooled Analyses, Trials 301 and 310
L624: In the uUTI ISP, six subjects (0.3%) who received sulopenem etzadroxil/probenecid experienced SAEs compared to five (0.5%) and 2 (0.2%) in the amoxicillin/clavulanate and ciprofloxacin arms, respectively. All six sulopenem subjects were enrolled in Trial 301. In the sulopenem arm, the SAEs included angioedema, lung adenocarcinoma, presyncope, small intestinal obstruction, abdominal pain upper, chest pain, pyelonephritis acute, and urosepsis. Only the SAE of angioedema was attributed to sulopenem etzadroxil/probenecid. As presyncope, small intestinal obstruction, abdominal pain and chest pain occurred on Day 21 or later, the clinical reviewer judged these events as less likely to be related to sulopenem. The SAE of lung adenocarcinoma was not related to sulopenem etzadroxil/probenecid as discussed above. Pyelonephritis and urosepsis were attributed to an obstructing kidney stone rather than to study drug. For further details, please refer to the NDA Multi-disciplinary Review and Evaluation {NDA 213972} dated July 22, 2021.

L652: ## 7.6.4.6. Laboratory Findings, Pooled Analyses, Trials 301 and 310
L653: No major laboratory abnormalities were noted in the sulopenem arm of the ISP. Distribution of abnormal chemistry laboratory findings as shown in Table 59, are similar between the sulopenem and comparator arms. There was a slightly higher percentage of subjects with level 2 (≥200 mg/dL) glucose elevation in the sulopenem arm (4%) compared with the amoxicillin/clavulanate (3.3%) or ciprofloxacin (2.7%) arms. However, the percentage of subjects with level 3 (≥250 mg/dL) glucose elevations were balanced among the three arms. While elevations in potassium were balanced between the sulopenem arm and ciprofloxacin arms, a higher percentage of sulopenem subjects had Level 1 (&gt;5.5 mEq/L) and Level 2 (&gt;6
L654: mEq/L) elevations in potassium compared to amoxicillin/clavulanate arm subjects. Overall, there do not appear to be major differences between sulopenem and the comparators with respect to chemistry laboratory findings. The imbalances noted in potassium and glucose values are not likely to be significant in the context of uUTI treatment.

L711: Subject (b) (6) in the sulopenem arm from Trial 310 had cholestasis and is discussed in further detail in Section 7.6.1.7. There were 9 (0.5%) subjects in the sulopenem arm (6 from Trial 301 and 3 from Trial 310) that had ALT and/or AST \ge 3\times the upper limit of normal. The 3 subjects from Trial 310 (subjects (b) (6)) are discussed in further detail in Section 7.6.1.7. The six subjects from 301 (subjects (b) (6)) were reviewed during the initial NDA submission (See NDA Multi-disciplinary Review and Evaluation {NDA 213972} dated July 22, 2021).
L712: Six of the 9 subjects listed above in the oral sulopenem arm of the phase 3 uUTI population had postbaseline ALT elevations of \ge 3\times to &lt;5\times ULN (subjects (b) (6) from Trial 301 and subjects (b) (6) from Trial 310). Of these six subjects, four had abnormal ALT values at baseline, including one patient with underlying fatty liver disease and one patient with a history of abnormal liver function tests. In three of the four subjects, the ALT remained elevated at TOC (no further information was available on these patients) while one subject achieved a normal ALT at TOC. Two subjects had normal ALT values at baseline; one had underlying nonalcoholic steatohepatitis and was also on a statin and metformin. Elevated ALT was noted at TOC but normalized at Day 28. The other subject had no underlying medical conditions or concomitant medications and remained asymptomatic but was noted to have elevated ALT at TOC; follow-up laboratory tests were not obtained. Attribution of causality to sulopenem etzadroxil/probenecid in most of these patients cannot be ruled out but is confounded by baseline elevations in ALT or underlying conditions.
L713: One subject in the sulopenem etzadroxil/probenecid arm of Trial 301 (subject (b) (6)), a 28-year-old woman with a medical history significant for obesity and use of an oral contraceptive pill, had postbaseline ALT elevation &gt;5\times ULN. Liver function tests were normal at baseline except for a mild elevation of AP at 125 U/L. At the TOC visit, the AP had increased further (223 U/L), and ALT was elevated to 208 U/L (normal range 6 to 41 U/L). The subject was asymptomatic. Laboratory testing was repeated 5 days later with a decrease in ALT to 46 U/L and a downward trend in the AP to 169 U/L. The cause of the ALT elevation was not known, but potentially could have been related to sulopenem etzadroxil/probenecid.
L714: In the sulopenem arm of the four phase 3 trials, 9 (0.3%) subjects and 1 (&lt;0.1) subject had ALT elevations of &gt;5\times ULN and &gt;10\times ULN, respectively. Of these subjects, one was in Trial 301 as described above and eight subjects were in Trials 302 and 303. On review of the narratives of these eight subjects, attribution of causality to sulopenem appeared confounded by the subjects' underlying medical conditions and/or concomitant medications.
L715: One subject from Trial 302 (Subject (b) (6)) discontinued IV sulopenem due to the AE of toxic hepatitis. The subject was a 47-year-old woman with pyelonephritis who had normal ALT, AP and bilirubin at baseline and mild elevation of AST. On Study Day 5, while on IV sulopenem, ALT and AST were &gt;3\times ULN. On Day 7, the subject was diagnosed with probable toxic hepatitis, and sulopenem was discontinued. AST and ALT trended down at Day 10 with normalization of values at TOC. Sulopenem may have contributed to the elevations in liver enzymes, but attribution of causality is confounded by the concomitant medications of paracetamol and methimazole.
L716: One subject in Trial 302 ( (b) (6)) with schizoaffective disorder on valproic acid had normal AST, ALT and bilirubin values at baseline but met laboratory criteria for Hy's Law with an ALT of 269 U/L, AST of 313 U/L and total bilirubin of 2.8 mg/dL after completing 5 days of IV
L717: sulopenem. However, study drug was continued, and the subject was switched to oral sulopenem etzadroxil/probenecid on Days 6 and 7 with near normalization in liver enzymes by Day 10. Penem antibacterial drugs are known to be associated with decreased valproic acid levels (which were noted in this subject). While IV sulopenem may have caused elevated liver enzymes in this patient, the abnormalities resolved while on oral sulopenem which may suggest hepatic adaptation.

L728: ## 7.6.4.9. Subgroups, Pooled Analyses, Trials 301 and 310
L729: All subjects in Trials 301 and 310 were female. Within the sulopenem arm, TEAEs were evenly distributed across age groups, but occurred more frequently than in comparator arms. In contrast, AEs occurred more frequently in subjects ≥75 years of age compared to other age groups in the amoxicillin/clavulanate arm. AEs occurred with similar frequency in white and Black subjects among treatment arms. The small number of subjects of other races preclude further conclusions based on race. The frequency of AEs in subjects from Ukraine compared to the frequency of AEs in subjects from the United States or Russia was markedly lower in both the sulopenem and
L730: ciprofloxacin arms. The reason for this difference is unclear but may be related to differences in reporting among the different populations. In the sulopenem arm, there were no major differences in occurrences of AEs by BMI category. The frequency of AEs was similar in sulopenem subjects with CrCl 30-60 mL/min and sulopenem subjects with CrCl &gt;60 mL/min. The number of subjects with CrCl &lt;30 mL/min was too low to draw conclusions.

L737: ## 8. Therapeutic Individualization
L738: ## 8.1. Intrinsic Factors
L739: ## 8.1.1. Hepatic Impairment
L740: The effect of hepatic impairment has not been evaluated for either IV or oral sulopenem. Sixty-five patients across all 4 phase 3 trials (301, 302, 303, and 310) had a history of hepatic disease, including hepatic steatosis and nonspecific liver disorder. However, none of these patients had a Child-Pugh categorization of the severity of their hepatic impairment and the safety of sulopenem etzadroxil/probenecid in these patients was comparable to the rest of the phase 3 trial population. In vitro, sulopenem is not metabolized by recombinant CYP or UGT enzymes. Additionally, the mass balance study (Study A8811006) indicated that biliary excretion does not play a role in sulopenem elimination. Therefore, hepatic impairment is not expected to have a clinically significant effect on sulopenem exposures, and no dosage adjustment is recommended based on hepatic impairment.
L741: ## 8.1.2. Renal Impairment
L742: The Applicant did not propose any alternative dosage recommendations for the use of sulopenem etzadroxil/probenecid in patients with renal impairment. In the mass balance study, approximately 26.9% of total radioactivity was recovered in urine as unchanged sulopenem following oral administration of a 2000 mg dose of [^{14}C] sulopenem etzadroxil. In the dedicated renal impairment study (A8811009), when compared to subjects with normal renal function, sulopenem plasma AUC_{0-\infty} increased 2.0-, 3.0- and 7.4-fold in subjects with mild (CrCl 60 to &lt;90 mL/min), moderate (CrCl 30 to &lt;60 mL/min) and severe (CrCl 15 to &lt;30 mL/min) renal impairment, respectively, following administration of a 1000 mg dose of sulopenem etzadroxil. Because sulopenem exhibits dose proportionality within the dose range of 400 to 2000 mg, similar fold increases in AUC are anticipated for the Applicant's proposed 500 mg dose of sulopenem etzadroxil. Although assessment of the effect of renal impairment on sulopenem PK was conducted in the absence of probenecid, the observed exposure changes with sulopenem etzadroxil are expected to approximate the fold changes in exposure with administration of the bilayer tablet due to the decline in probenecid's effectiveness as an OAT3 inhibitor as renal function declines.
L743: From an efficacy perspective, there is theoretical concern for a reduction in efficacy with declining renal function given that renal impairment is associated with decreases in renal clearance and ultimately, urinary concentrations of sulopenem. In Trial 301, overall response at the TOC visit was lower in subjects with CrCl &lt;60 mL/min compared to those with CrCl \ge60 mL/min. However, in Trial 310, overall response was comparable for subjects with CrCl above and below this threshold (Table 69). Of note, CrCl &lt;60 mL/min was not a pre-specified
L744: criterion for treatment group randomization, and thus, other confounders may have contributed to the observed outcomes in Trial 301. Therefore, the totality of information is inconclusive on the effect of renal impairment on sulopenem's efficacy in the treatment of uUTI and the need for an alternative dosage strategy.

L748: From a safety perspective, data from trial A8811009 and phase 3 Trials 301 and 310 did not associate mild, moderate or severe renal impairment with a higher incidence of TEAEs as compared with subjects with normal renal function. Given these observations, sulopenem's short plasma half-life of 1.2 h and the proposed 5-day duration of therapy, 500 mg sulopenem etzadroxil/500 mg probenecid BID is expected to be safe in patients with CrCl \ge15 mL/min. However, there are no PK or safety data in patients with CrCl &lt;15 mL/min or those on hemodialysis to inform dosage recommendations in these subpopulations. Moreover, uUTI in patients on hemodialysis may not be considered uncomplicated. Therefore, use of 500 mg sulopenem etzadroxil/500 mg probenecid bilayer tablet is not recommended in patients with CrCl &lt;15 mL/min and those on hemodialysis.
L749: ## 8.1.3. Other Intrinsic Factors
L750: Population PK analysis involving PK data from phase 1 trials and phase 3 Trials 301, 302 and 303 indicated that sex, body weight (38.8 to 140 kg) and age (18 to 91 years) did not have a clinically significant effect on the PK of sulopenem.
L751: ## 8.2. Extrinsic Factors
L752: ## 8.2.1. Food Effect
L753: Following administration of the to-be-marketed sulopenem etzadroxil/probenecid bilayer tablet formulation to healthy adult volunteers, area under the concentration-time curve estimated to infinity (AUC0-\infty) and maximum plasma concentration (Cmax) increased 48% and 45%, respectively, with a high fat meal (800-1000 calories; 50% fat) compared to fasted conditions. The Applicant proposes that the bilayer tablet should be taken with food (b) (4) because food increases the oral bioavailability and tolerability of sulopenem. This recommendation is consistent with the instructions provided to Trial 301 and 310 participants. Because neither trial recorded the type of food consumed, caloric content or timing of food intake, fed status was poorly defined. Study 310 only provided a comparison of efficacy outcomes based on fed status. Nonetheless, Trial 301 did provide a comparison of safety and efficacy outcomes under fed and fasted conditions. In this trial, while the incidence of clinically
L754: significant treatment-emergent diarrhea was comparable under fed (7.1%) and fasted conditions (7.4%) (Table 70), food appeared to decrease the mean duration of treatment-emergent diarrhea from 5.6 days to 3.7 days. The lack of a notable difference in the incidence of diarrhea is consistent with the safety findings from the dedicated food effect Study 105, where the incidence of GI-related TEAEs following administration of the bilayer tablet were identical (7.1%) in the fed and fasted states. In both Trial 301 and 310, food did not appear to significantly impact efficacy as administration of the bilayer tablet in the fed or fasted states resulted in comparable overall response rates of 63.5% and 62.8%, respectively, at the TOC visit for the entire microbiologically-evaluable population. Additionally, in PTA analyses, simulated sulopenem exposures under fed conditions yielded target attainment at MIC values that were either comparable or a single-fold dilution higher than under fasted conditions. Based on the findings that food increases bioavailability and may improve tolerability by shortening the duration of clinically significant treatment-emergent diarrhea, the clinical pharmacology review team recommends administering the sulopenem etzadroxil/probenecid bilayer tablet with food.

L761: ## 8.2.2. Summary of In Vitro Drug-Drug Interaction Studies
L762: In vitro studies indicated that sulopenem is a substrate of OAT3, and the prodrug sulopenem etzadroxil is a substrate of P-gp and inhibitor of CYP3A4/5, P-gp, breast cancer resistance protein (BCRP), OAT1 and OAT3. No clinical studies of sulopenem etzadroxil as an OAT1/3,
L763: CYP3A4/5, BCRP and P-gp inhibitor were conducted by the Applicant. Given that sulopenem etzadroxil is rapidly hydrolyzed upon oral administration and was undetected in plasma in the human mass balance study (A8811006), the potential for clinically relevant DDIs with OAT1/3 is considered to be low. Because sulopenem etzadroxil is administered orally, it has the potential to inhibit CYP3A4/5, BCRP and P-gp in the gut. The sulopenem etzadroxil half-maximal inhibitory concentration (IC_{50}) for inhibition of CYP3A4/5 could not be calculated within the concentration range studied in vitro and was estimated to be &gt;150 \mu M. Although the IC_{50} values for BCRP (IC_{50} = 20.4 \mu M) and P-gp (IC_{50} = 1.91 \mu M) are likely to be exceeded by more than 10-fold in the GI tract following administration of a single 500 mg dose of sulopenem etzadroxil, the Applicant's in vitro stability and release studies indicated that sulopenem etzadroxil is rapidly degraded in simulated intestinal fluid. Therefore, sulopenem etzadroxil's inhibition of BCRP and P-gp is expected to be transient. Similarly, regardless of the magnitude of the in vitro IC_{50} for CYP3A4/5 inhibition, sulopenem etzadroxil's effect as a CYP3A4/5 inhibitor is also expected to be transient and not to result in clinically significant DDIs with CYP3A4/5 substrates.
L764: Probenecid is a known OAT1/3 inhibitor and was found to be a substrate and inhibitor of BCRP in vitro. No clinical evaluations of probenecid as a BCRP substrate and inhibitor were performed. The in vitro IC_{50} of probenecid as a BCRP inhibitor was 814 \mu M, resulting in an I_{gut} to IC_{50} ratio of 10, which is the threshold for characterizing an orally administered drug as a BCRP inhibitor in the 2020 FDA Guidance for Industry, *In Vitro Drug Interaction Studies-Cytochrome P450 Enzyme- and Transporter-Mediated Drug Interactions* (January 2020). However, because of probenecid's low aqueous solubility (0.06 mg/mL), the probability of clinically significant BCRP-mediated DDIs with probenecid is low.
L765: ## 8.2.3. Summary of Clinical Drug-Drug Interaction Studies
L766: ## 8.2.3.1. Effect of P-gp Inhibitors on Sulopenem PK
L767: Because sulopenem etzadroxil was identified as a P-gp substrate in vitro, the Applicant conducted a clinical DDI study to evaluate the effect of P-gp inhibitors on sulopenem exposure using oral itraconazole. In Study IT001-103, administration of a clinical dose of 200 mg itraconazole (2 x 100 mg capsules) daily for 3 days in the fasted state, followed by concomitant administration of sulopenem etzadroxil/probenecid on Day 4 in the fed state resulted in a non-clinically significant increase in sulopenem exposure. Therefore, no dosage adjustment is required for coadministration of sulopenem etzadroxil/probenecid with P-gp inhibitors.
L768: ## 8.2.3.2. Effect of Antacids and Proton Pump Inhibitors on Sulopenem PK
L769: Results of in vitro solubility studies indicated that sulopenem etzadroxil is a Biopharmaceutical Classification System Class IV drug (i.e., low permeability and low solubility) that does not exhibit pH-dependent solubility within a pH range of 1.2 to 6.8. Based on this information, coadministration of gastric pH modifiers would not be expected to impact sulopenem's exposure. However, per the Applicant, in vitro stability studies indicated that sulopenem etzadroxil was
L770: unstable in simulated gastric fluid (containing pepsin) but stable in simulated enzyme-free intestinal fluid. Therefore, gastric pH modifiers were predicted to decrease sulopenem etzadroxil's vulnerability to acid degradation and thus increase the bioavailability of sulopenem. Given that the stability of sulopenem etzadroxil was evaluated in gastric fluid in the presence of pepsin, it is unclear that its degradation was precipitated exclusively by low gastric pH. The Applicant conducted a clinical DDI study (A8811018) using pantoprazole, a proton pump inhibitor (PPI), and aluminum hydroxide, an antacid. Administration of 40 mg pantoprazole for 3 days, followed by coadministration with sulopenem etzadroxil on Day 4 under fasted conditions did not significantly impact sulopenem exposure. Therefore, no dosage adjustment is necessary for coadministration with a PPI. Administration of a single dose of 600 mg aluminum hydroxide with sulopenem etzadroxil under fasted conditions decreased AUC_{0-last} and C_{max} by less than 20%. According to the FDA guidance on conducting DDI studies with gastric-acid reducing agents, PPIs present the worst-case scenario for pH-dependent DDIs due to their long-lasting effects on gastric pH. Thus, the negative finding from Study A8811018 indicates an overall lack of pH-dependent DDI. Therefore, no dosage adjustment is required for coadministration with antacids.
L771: ## 8.2.3.3. Effect of Sulopenem Etzadroxil/Probenecid on Valproic Acid PK
L772: Concomitant administration of carbapenem antibacterial drugs and valproic acid has been associated with clinically significant reductions in serum valproic acid concentrations, resulting in a loss of seizure control. Because sulopenem (a penem) is structurally similar to carbapenems, the Applicant conducted a DDI study (Study 104) with valproic acid using the sulopenem etzadroxil/probenecid bilayer tablet, a standalone sulopenem immediate release tablet, and IV sulopenem. In this study, multiple dose administration of 500 mg sulopenem etzadroxil with valproic acid decreased valproic acid AUC and C_{max} by approximately 25% and 19%, respectively. Similarly, coadministration of 1000 mg IV sulopenem with valproic acid also resulted in reductions of valproic acid plasma AUC and C_{max} of 33% and 28%, respectively. However, when administered concomitantly with sulopenem etzadroxil and probenecid, less than 10% reduction in valproic acid plasma exposures were observed. These results indicate that probenecid negates the reduction in valproic acid plasma concentrations caused by sulopenem. These findings were corroborated in the Applicant's phase 3 cUTI trial in one patient in the sulopenem arm who received concomitant valproic acid treatment. Following the IV sulopenem treatment phase of the study (i.e., Days 1-5), valproic acid plasma/serum levels decreased to 21000 ng/mL (in serum) from a baseline of 54800 ng/mL (in plasma). However, following the switch to oral step-down therapy with sulopenem etzadroxil/probenecid, valproic acid levels recovered to 50100 ng/mL (in plasma) and 50600 ng/mL (in serum) at the end of treatment visit.

8.1 Pregnancy	Sulopenem Etzadroxil
Sulopenem etzadroxil was orally administered during organogenesis in embryo-fetal studies in mice, rats, and rabbits. In pregnant mice, an increased litter incidence of a fetal malformation, cleft palate, was observed with an oral dose of sulopenem etzadroxil associated with a sulopenem exposure approximately 23 times the clinical sulopenem exposure for the MRHD of 1000 mg/day sulopenem etzadroxil. No maternal toxicity or fetal malformations occurred in mice with doses \le400 mg/kg/day (approximately 3 times the clinical sulopenem exposure for the MRHD of sulopenem etzadroxil based on plasma AUC comparison).
In pregnant rats and rabbits, orally administered sulopenem etzadroxil was not associated with fetal malformations at any dose, but in rats, maternal toxicity and reduced fetal body weights occurred at sulopenem etzadroxil doses associated with sulopenem plasma exposures approximately 2 and 6 times, respectively, the clinical sulopenem exposure for the MRHD of sulopenem etzadroxil. The doses at which no maternal toxicity or fetal toxicity occurred in rats were, respectively, 100 mg/kg/day and 400 mg/kg/day (less than or equal to and approximately 2 times, respectively, the clinical sulopenem exposure for the MRHD of sulopenem etzadroxil based on plasma AUC comparison).
In rabbits, maternal toxicity, reduced numbers of viable fetuses, and reduced fetal body weights occurred at sulopenem etzadroxil doses associated with sulopenem plasma exposures approximately 0.1 and 0.2 times, respectively, the clinical sulopenem exposure for the MRHD of sulopenem etzadroxil. Maternal body weight gain and food consumption were decreased in all the sulopenem etzadroxil dose groups. The dose at which no fetal toxicity occurred was 5 mg/kg/day (approximately 0.1-times the clinical sulopenem exposure for the MRHD of sulopenem etzadroxil based on plasma AUC comparison).
In a pre-postnatal study in rats, sulopenem etzadroxil was administered by oral gavage to pregnant females from gestation day 6 through the lactation period to LD 20 in maternal doses of 100, 300, and 1000 mg/kg/day. No adverse effects on the survival, growth, behavior, or reproduction of first-generation offspring occurred with any of the sulopenem etzadroxil doses up to the high dose of 1000 mg/kg/day (approximately 10-times
L788: Labeling Section	Nonclinical Data
the MRHD of sulopenem etzadroxil based on body surface area comparison).
Probenecid
Available published data over several decades of probenecid use in pregnant woman have not identified a drug-associated risk of miscarriage, major birth defects, or adverse maternal or fetal outcomes. No embryo-fetal development studies with probenecid have been conducted in animals. Probenecid crosses the placental barrier and appears in cord blood.

8.2 Lactation	
Human Data
Sulopenem Etzadroxil
There are no data on the presence of sulopenem etzadroxil or its metabolite in human milk, the effects on the breastfed infant, or the effects on milk production.
Probenecid
Probenecid is present in human milk based on a case report. There are no reports of adverse effects in infants associated with probenecid exposure through breastmilk. There is no information on the effects of probenecid on milk production.
Animal Data
Sulopenem Etzadroxil
The active metabolite of sulopenem etzadroxil, sulopenem, was present in rat milk after oral dosing of sulopenem etzadroxil to lactating female rats. When a drug is present in animal milk, it is likely that the drug will be present in human milk.

13.1 Carcinogenesis, Mutagenesis, Impairment of Fertility	
Impairment of Fertility
Sulopenem Etzadroxil
Male and female fertility and early embryonic development were examined in rats (20/sex/group) orally administered sulopenem etzadroxil in daily doses of 100, 400, or 2000 mg/kg beginning 28 days prior to mating and throughout the mating period in males and for 14 days before mating, throughout the mating period, and until GD 7 in females. There were no treatment-related effects on estrous cycle length, mating and fertility rates, implantation, conceptus viability, sperm concentration and motility, or accessory male sex gland weights. No adverse effects on male and female fertility or early embryonic development in female rats were observed at doses up to 2000 mg/kg/day (approximately 10- and 12-times in male and female rats, respectively, the clinical sulopenem exposure for the MRHD of sulopenem etzadroxil based on plasma AUC comparison).

L802: ## Human Pregnancy Data
L803: Pregnant women were excluded from all clinical studies of sulopenem. However, one pregnancy occurred in the sulopenem arm of Trial 310. A 22-year-old woman (Subject [REDACTED](b) (6)) received 5 days of sulopenem etzadroxil/probenecid. The baseline urine pregnancy test was negative as was a urine pregnancy test on Day 28. On Day 41, a serum pregnancy test was positive. Possible conception dates were determined to be 12-22 days after the sulopenem course was completed; therefore, it was unlikely the subject was pregnant while receiving sulopenem. The subject gave birth to a full term healthy female baby.
L804: There was also one pregnancy in the sulopenem arm of Trial 301. A 26-year-old woman had a negative screening urine pregnancy test at the trial site but three days later, the central laboratory reported the pregnancy test as positive. Study drug was stopped. The subject had an uneventful pregnancy and gave birth to a healthy male baby 8 months later.
L805: During the initial review of NDA 213972, DPMH was consulted to assist with the Pregnancy and Lactation subsections of labeling. In their consult response dated May 4, 2021, DPMH noted that as a penem antibacterial drug, sulopenem is very similar to carbapenems, and teratogenic risks and adverse maternal and fetal outcomes have not been identified with carbapenem use during
L806: pregnancy. Additionally, based on decades of experience with carbapenems, sulopenem is not expected to cause harmful effects in breastfed infants. DPMH also observed that available published studies over several decades of probenecid use in pregnancy have not identified a drug-related risk of miscarriage, congenital malformations, or adverse maternal or fetal outcomes. Therefore, DPMH did not recommend a postmarketing pregnancy study or postmarketing lactation study for sulopenem etzadroxil/probenecid.
L807: ## 9. Product Quality
L808: ## Approval
L809: This NDA was recommended for approval from the Product Quality perspective in the first review cycle (refer to the Office of Pharmaceutical Quality (OPQ) Integrated Quality Assessment # 1, dated June 1, 2021, in the Document Archiving Reporting and Regulatory Tracking System. The drug product is a pink, oval-shaped, film coated, immediate release, bilayer tablet, containing 500 mg sulopenem etzadroxil and 500 mg probenecid, and conventional excipients of compendial grade. With the current NDA resubmission (SDN# 71, dated April 25, 2024), several changes and updates have been proposed in Module 3, such as removal of blister packaging originally proposed for the drug product. The OPQ review team has assessed the NDA 213972 resubmission with respect to chemistry, manufacturing, and controls and has determined that it meets all applicable standards to support the identity, strength, quality, and purity that it purports. The currently proposed commercial packaging configurations for the drug product include high density polyethylene bottles only (10-count and 30-count) with child-resistant caps. Based on the overall stability data package submitted in the original NDA and the resubmission, the proposed expiration dating of 60 months is granted for the drug product to be stored at room temperature (20-25°C). All proposed commercial manufacturing and testing facilities have been found acceptable and an overall “Approve” recommendation was entered into Panorama by the Office of Pharmaceutical Manufacturing Assessment on September 6, 2024. As such, OPQ recommends approval of this NDA from a quality perspective (refer to the OPQ Integrated Quality Assessment # 2, dated September 25, 2024, in DARRTS).

L813: The Applicant has provided attestation that Trial 310 was conducted in compliance with good clinical practice (GCP) guidelines and all local regulatory requirements were followed. The trial protocol and amendments and informed consent documentation were reviewed by institutional
L814: review boards. The Applicant certified that none of the investigators for Trial 310 had any financial interests or arrangements with the Applicant.
L815: In the original NDA submission, the Applicant provided attestation that Trial 301 was conducted in compliance with good clinical practice guidelines and all local regulatory requirements were followed. The trial protocol and amendments were reviewed by institutional review boards. The Applicant certified that none of the investigators for Trial 301 had any financial interests or arrangements with the Applicant.
L816: A review of clinical sites for Trial 310 was conducted by the Office of Scientific Investigations (OSI) to ensure data quality. Three sites (Site 115 in California, Site 129 in Arkansas, and Site 251 in Florida) were inspected based on high enrollment and high treatment response. Per the Clinical Inspection Summary by Dr. John Lee, the data from the inspected sites appear to be acceptable in support of the proposed indication for sulopenem etzadroxil/probenecid. The primary and key secondary efficacy endpoint data were verifiable, and no significant underreporting of AEs was observed. The trial appeared to have been conducted in compliance with good clinical practice principles and regulations at Sites 115 and 129. A GCP deficiency (lack of consistent documentation of adequate contraception history and negative pregnancy testing) was noted at Site 251 but was unlikely to be important to efficacy analysis of study data. For additional details, please refer to Section 22 and the clinical inspection summary written by Dr. John Lee from OSI, dated October 7, 2024, in DARRTS.
L817: For Trial 301, routine PDUFA surveillance inspections were conducted for four clinical investigators. In addition, combined PDUFA/for-cause inspections of two clinical sites (Sites 202 and 218) were conducted to address specific data reliability concerns raised by the Applicant. The Applicant listed several reasons for their exclusion of Site 202: (1) pulse-field gel electrophoresis (PFGE) analysis of some urinary isolates identified from the baseline urine bacterial cultures were either genetically indistinguishable or closely related; (2) a high contamination rate of urine samples; and (3) artificial intelligence software that suggested intentional patient nonadherent behavior. The FDA inspection could not confirm that a single urine sample was used to enrolled multiple subjects at Site 202. In addition, it was concluded that the medication adherence software results may have been misinterpreted as many subjects with “red flag” events were well-documented to have taken the dose. Finally, the decision to exclude Site 202 was made after unblinding of the interim analysis. FDA concluded that there did not appear to be sufficient cause to exclude data from Site 202. (b) (7)(A)
L818: For these reasons, FDA agreed with the Applicant that data from Site 218 should be excluded. For details on clinical site inspections for Trial 301, please refer to the NDA Multi-Disciplinary Review and Evaluation {NDA 213972} dated July 22, 2021, and the clinical inspection summary written by Dr. Cheryl Grandinetti from OSI, dated June 18, 2021, in DARRTS.
L819: ## 11. Advisory Committee Summary
L820: Because oral sulopenem etzadroxil/probenecid, if approved, would be the first oral penem on the U.S. market, the Division took NDA 213972 to an Antimicrobial Advisory Committee meeting
L821: on September 9, 2024 to discuss concerns for possible inappropriate use of this drug in an ambulatory setting which may lead to increasing antimicrobial resistance as well as considerations that should be communicated to prescribers in order to ensure appropriate use of sulopenem etzadroxil/probenecid.
L822: The following discussion questions were posed to the AC:
L823: - The Applicant is seeking an indication for sulopenem etzadroxil/probenecid in adult women \ge 18 years of age for the treatment of uUTI caused by designated susceptible microorganisms. Discuss the overall benefits and risks for the use of sulopenem etzadroxil/probenecid for this indication.
- Considering the totality of the evidence in this application, discuss considerations that would be important for medical providers to know to ensure appropriate use of sulopenem etzadroxil/probenecid.
L824: Although there were no voting questions, the AC members discussed concerns for potential downstream risks to both individual patients and to society from antimicrobial cross-resistance to carbapenems arising from unrestricted empiric use of oral sulopenem for uUTI in an ambulatory setting. The potential lack of mechanisms for effective antimicrobial stewardship in an ambulatory setting in general was discussed. Given the totality of evidence presented in the FDA Briefing Document and the concerns outlined above, the AC members recommended restricting the indication and providing limitations of use statements.

L826: ## 12. Summary of Regulatory History
L827: On March 1, 2016, Iterum Therapeutics US Ltd. (Sponsor) submitted IND 129849, for sulopenem etzadroxil (PF-03709270 sulopenem oral prodrug) tablets.
L828: A type C Guidance meeting was held on February 27, 2017, to discuss the development program for PF-03709270. The Sponsor stated that following completion of the ongoing phase 1 clinical program the Sponsor would select the prodrug to move forward into clinical development.
L829: An End of Phase 2 meeting was held on July 21, 2017, to discuss the design of Trial 301 for the treatment of uncomplicated urinary tract infection (uUTI). During this meeting, the Division emphasized that the clinical response component of the overall response endpoint (combined clinical and microbiological responses) should be defined as the resolution of all urinary tract infection (UTI) symptoms present at trial entry. Discussion also included considerations of evaluation of sulopenem versus ciprofloxacin based on assessment of non-inferiority (NI) in the micro-MITTS (ciprofloxacin-susceptible) population and assessment of superiority in the micro-MITTR population (ciprofloxacin-resistant population). The Division noted that the primary analysis population in an NI analysis should only include patients with pathogens susceptible to the proposed comparator.
L830: A type B, chemistry, manufacturing and controls (CMC) meeting was held on August 28, 2017. During this meeting the data needed to demonstrate comparability between the sources of the drug substance, frequency of microbial testing, impurity testing, dissolution methods, suitability of batch manufacture and the overall CMC-development program to support NDA submission was discussed.
L831: On September 19, 2017, the Sponsor submitted their initial pediatric study plan (iPSP) to IND 129849 and an Agreed iPSP letter was issued on February 26, 2018.
L832: On October 27, 2017, PF-03709270/probenecid (sulopenem etzadroxil/probenecid) bilayer tablet was granted Qualified Infectious Disease Product (QIDP) designation for uUTI, complicated urinary tract infection (cUTI), and complicated intra-abdominal infection (cIAI) and Fast Track designation for these same indications on March 15, 2019.
L833: On December 8, 2017, in follow-up to a meeting request to discuss the statistical analysis plan for study IT001-301, the Division provided the Sponsor with comments on the proposed framework for hypothesis testing and interim analysis. The Division commented that discordant results in the two primary analyses (assessment of NI in the microbiological modified intent-to-treat ciprofloxacin- susceptible (micro-MITTS) population and assessment of superiority in the microbiological modified intent-to-treat ciprofloxacin-resistant (micro-MITTR) population) could be problematic and that there would need to be an understanding of the reasons for discrepant findings. Further, such results may also have labeling implications.
L834: On December 27, 2017, the Sponsor submitted a Special Protocol Assessment (SPA) for Protocol IT001-301, entitled: "A prospective, Phase 3, randomized, multi-center, double-blind
L835: study of the efficacy, tolerability, and safety of oral sulopenem etzadroxil/probenecid versus oral ciprofloxacin for treatment of uncomplicated urinary tract infections in adult women.” The Division issued a Special Protocol-Agreement letter for Protocol IT001-301 on February 6, 2018.
L836: A SPA modification request was submitted on June 18, 2018. The modification included a request to increase the sample size, update inclusion criteria, add urine pharmacokinetic (PK) assessments to be consistent with FDA Guidance for uUTI, and to include a recommendation to dose sulopenem etzadroxil/probenecid with food. A Special Protocol Modification Agreement letter was issued on July 10, 2018.
L837: On August 6, 2018, the Sponsor notified FDA of the change in designation of the Sponsor to an affiliated entity, and noted the change from Iterum Therapeutics, US, Ltd. to Iterum Therapeutics International, Ltd.
L838: On February 13, 2020, a type-B Pre-NDA, CMC meeting was held to discuss the content and structure of Section 2.3 (Overall Quality Summary) and Module 3, Quality section of the forthcoming NDA.
L839: On September 28, 2020, a type B meeting was held to discuss the Pre-NDA submission. The Division stated that a determination of substantial evidence of effectiveness and adequate safety to support a labeled indication for the treatment of adult women with uUTI due to quinolone-resistant pathogens would be a review issue. The Sponsor enquired about a limited patient population uUTI indication and proposed submission of the NDA under the LPAD pathway. There were no agreements for late submission(s), therefore the NDA application was expected to be complete at the time of submission.
L840: On November 25, 2020, Iterum Therapeutics US Ltd. (Applicant) submitted NDA 213972 for oral sulopenem etzadroxil/probenecid for the proposed indication of treatment of uUTI caused by designated susceptible microorganisms proven or strongly suspected to be nonsusceptible to a quinolone. NDA 213972 was filed on January 21, 2021, and the NDA received a Priority Review designation. The basis for the NDA submission was the single uUTI Trial 301. Data from Trials 302 (for cUTI) and 303 (for cIAI) were submitted as supportive data only, as both trials failed to meet their primary endpoints.
L841: On February 25, 2021, the Division provided an update on the NDA review during the Mid-Cycle Communication teleconference; on May 26, 2021, the Late-Cycle Meeting was held with the Applicant to discuss substantive review issues. No Advisory Committee meeting was held during the first cycle review.
L842: The NDA received a complete response action on July 23, 2021, due to lack of substantial evidence of effectiveness (SEE). While sulopenem etzadroxil/probenecid demonstrated superiority to ciprofloxacin for the overall (clinical and microbiological) response rate in the micro-MITTR population, the product was inferior in the micro-MITTS population. Additionally, the cUTI Trial 302 and cIAI Trial 303, conducted with IV sulopenem followed by oral sulopenem etzadroxil/probenecid stepdown therapy, failed to meet their primary endpoints and thus, were not considered to provide supportive evidence of effectiveness. FDA recommended that the Applicant conduct an additional trial for uUTI using a different comparator.
L843: On September 23, 2021, a type-A, Post Action meeting was held to discuss and clarify the deficiencies outlined in the complete response letter and on December 21, 2021, a type B,
L844: Guidance meeting was held wherein the Division and the Applicant discussed the design of a new study protocol for the indication of uUTI.
L845: A type B guidance meeting was held on March 10, 2022, to discuss clinical development plans to support approval of sulopenem etzadroxil/probenecid tablets for the treatment of uUTI under the LPAD pathway. The Applicant proposed a NI study using amoxicillin/clavulanate as the comparator. The Division commented that a first-line treatment, such as nitrofurantoin, may be a better choice for the comparator to assess the efficacy of sulopenem etzadroxil/probenecid.
L846: On March 16, 2022, in follow-up to a type B guidance meeting request, the Division issued Written Response Only comments to the Applicant to address questions on the developmental plans for PK/pharmacodynamic (PD) studies.
L847: On June 1, 2022, the Applicant submitted a SPA request for Protocol IT001-310 titled, “A prospective, Phase 3, randomized, multi-center, double-blind study of the efficacy, tolerability, and safety of oral sulopenem etzadroxil/probenecid versus oral amoxicillin/clavulanate for treatment of uncomplicated urinary tract infections (uUTI) in adult women.” A Special Protocol-Agreement letter was issued for Protocol IT001-310 on July 7, 2022.
L848: During development the Applicant submitted multiple requests to amend the Agreed iPSP. On September 25, 2023, the Division issued the final Amended Agreed iPSP Agreement letter. The Applicant submitted the Agreed Amended iPSP in the NDA to address the requirements of the Pediatric Equity Research Act (PREA). The Applicant requested a deferral in children ages 2 to &lt;18 years and a partial waiver in children ages &lt;2 years.

L861: ## Nonclinical PK/PD Studies
L862: ## Identification of PK/PD Index for Sulopenem
L863: PK/PD index and target determination for sulopenem were previously conducted using neutropenic and immune-competent murine thigh infection models. As with other beta-lactams, the percent of time that free drug concentrations remain above the minimum inhibitory concentration (%fT&gt;MIC) was expected to be the PK/PD driver of sulopenem's efficacy. However, the Applicant's dose fractionation studies failed to illustrate definitively the index most relevant to efficacy, instead suggesting that the relevant index is pathogen-specific. Because the relevant PK/PD index for antibacterial drugs is typically pathogen independent, the discordance between pathogens was partly illustrative of the complexities of sulopenem's PK/PD properties. However, ambiguities within the study methodology and inconsistencies with data analysis raised concerns about the reliability and interpretability of study findings. Refer to NDA 213972 Multi-disciplinary Review and Evaluation dated July 22, 2021, for further details. As a result of these observations, the Applicant was asked to conduct additional dose fractionation studies to better understand sulopenem's PK/PD behavior. Because sulopenem has a short murine half-life of ~5 min, completion of PK/PD studies in the murine model of infection is technically challenging. Therefore, the review team agreed that the Applicant may conduct subsequent PK/PD studies in an in vitro model of infection.
L864: Using a wild-type strain of *E. coli* (NCTC 13441), a series of duplicate dose-fractionation studies were conducted in a 1-compartment in vitro infection model using 5 different total sulopenem daily doses of 62.5, 125, 250, 500 and 2000 mg divided equally according to q4h, q8h or q12h dosing regimens. To approximate oral absorption, sulopenem was infused into the in vitro system over 2 h. A Hill-type model was fit to the resulting PK and PD (i.e., changes in bacterial burden) to determine which of the 3 traditional PK/PD indices best correlates with sulopenem's activity. %fT&gt;MIC held the strongest correlation with sulopenem's activity based on r^2 values (Figure 4), followed closely by free-drug maximum plasma concentration/MIC. These findings suggest that sulopenem exhibits both time and concentration-dependent bacterial killing.
L865: **Figure 4. Relationships Between f_{AUC}/MIC, fC_{max}/MIC, %fT&gt;MIC and Change in Bacterial Burden**
L866: Source: Figure 5 of Applicant's ICPD Report on In Vitro Pharmacokinetics and Pharmacodynamics of Sulopenem
Abbreviations: AUC_{0-24h}, area under the concentration-time curve from time 0 to 24 h; CFU, colony-forming units; C_{max}, maximum plasma concentration; f_{AUC}, free-drug area under the concentration-time curve; fC_{max}, free-drug maximum plasma concentration; ICPD, Institute for Clinical Pharmacodynamics; MIC, minimum inhibitory concentration; q4h, every 4 hours; q8h, every 8 hours; q12h, every 12 hours
L867: *Reviewer's comment: %fTime&gt;MIC was selected as the PK/PD index for sulopenem as it is the index typically attributed to the beta-lactam drug class. However, the fact that free-drug maximum plasma concentration/MIC is also highly correlated with bacterial killing suggests sulopenem's dosing could be also optimized by maximizing maximum plasma concentration.*
L868: ## **Determination of PK/PD Targets for Sulopenem**
L869: Instead of a separate set of dose-ranging studies dedicated to target determination, the Applicant relied upon the results of the dose fractionation studies against a set of Gram-positive and Gram-negative pathogens to determine the magnitude of %fT&gt;MIC (the assumed PK/PD index for sulopenem) required for stasis and 1-log kill. The atypical approach to target determination and concerns with reliability of data precluded use of this data to inform probability of target attainment (PTA) analyses.
L870: Dose-ranging studies were conducted in duplicate in the 1-compartment in vitro infection model against a panel of 10 Enterobacterales (i.e., 6 *E. coli* and 4 *K. pneumoniae*) with sulopenem MICs of 0.03 to 0.5 \mu\text{g/mL}. Free sulopenem exposures associated with doses ranging from 7.81 to 2000 mg q12h were simulated in the model to determine the magnitude of sulopenem %fT&gt;MIC required to achieve stasis, 1-log and 2-log kill. Similar to the dose fractionation studies, sulopenem was infused into the in vitro system over 2 h to simulate oral absorption, and a Hill-type model was fitted to the resulting data to determine individual as well as pooled targets for each of the bacteriologic endpoints of interest. 1-log kill was achieved in all but 1 isolate,
L871: while 2-log kill was achieved in only 4 of the 10 isolates. The median %ofT&gt;MIC targets were 40.9, 50.2 and 62.6% for stasis, 1-log and 2-log kill, respectively.
L872: ## **Proof-of-Concept Study in a Hollow Fiber Infection Model**
L873: In a series of studies conducted in a hollow fiber infection model, sulopenem urinary exposures associated with 500 mg q12h regimen were simulated against 4 extended-spectrum \beta-lactamase (ESBL)-positive *E. coli* isolates with sulopenem MICs 0.03 to 0.06 \mug/mL. The selected isolates were resistant to levofloxacin and susceptible to meropenem to allow for the use of levofloxacin 750 mg q24h and meropenem 2 g q8h as negative and positive controls, respectively. For all 4 isolates, sulopenem exposures associated with 500 mg q12h produced a sustained reduction in bacterial burden from baseline and suppressed the development of resistance. Representative results for 1 of the isolates, *E. coli* 845741, are shown in Figure 5.
L874: **Figure 5. Hollow Fiber Results Displaying Total and Drug-Resistant [4X Sulopenem and Meropenem] Subpopulations in No Treatment Control, Sulopenem, Meropenem, and Levofloxacin**
L875: Source: Figure 22 of Applicant's ICPD Report on In Vitro Pharmacokinetics and Pharmacodynamics of Sulopenem
Abbreviations: CFU, colony-forming units; ICPD, Institute for Clinical Pharmacodynamics; IV, intravenous; MIC, minimum inhibitory concentration; MEM, meropenem; q4h, every 4 hours; q8h, every 8 hours; q12h, every 12 hours; SLP, sulopenem
L876: *Reviewer's comment: For levofloxacin and meropenem, the Applicant's hollow fiber studies simulated plasma drug exposures instead of urinary exposures. Per the Applicant, use of these exposures was intended to establish the sensitivity of the model in discerning positive and negative results, and not intended to facilitate a head-to-head comparison of urinary drug activity across the 3 drugs.*

L881: ## 14.5. Pharmacometrics Assessment
L882: ## 14.5.1. Review Summary
L883: The Applicant previously developed a population PK (PopPK) model using plasma PK data from nine phase 1 and three phase 3 trials, in which sulopenem etzadroxil was administered either as a monolayer tablet, the to-be-marketed bilayer tablet and a powder-in-bottle (PIB) formulation with or without probenecid. Briefly, the PopPK model was previously reviewed in detail and found to reasonably describe the concentration-time profiles of sulopenem in healthy subjects and subjects with uUTI. Additionally, the PopPK model was considered acceptable in generating exposure parameters (i.e., area under the concentration-time curve during the dosing interval and maximum plasma concentration) to support labeling statements. However, potential correlations between intrinsic and extrinsic factors (i.e., renal function, food effects, and formulations) (with or without probenecid) may confound the evaluation and interpretation of covariate effects on sulopenem PK, and as such, careful consideration should be exercised when interpreting simulations (e.g., PTA) based on the correlated covariates. Refer to the NDA 213972 Multi-disciplinary Review and Evaluation dated July 22, 2021, for details on the PopPK model evaluation and utility.
L884: In the current submission, the PopPK model was extended to describe the disposition of sulopenem in urine (i.e., fraction of elimination from the central compartment to urine compartment) based on urinary exposure data obtained from a subset of the studied PK population (i.e., healthy subjects). Additionally, urine PTA was conducted to predict the proportion of subjects achieving specified target exposures in the urine. Although the updated PopPK model is generally acceptable for characterizing sulopenem urine PK in phase 1 Trial 101 and phase 3 Trial 302, the model did not reasonably describe the phase 3 Trial 301 urine data. It is unclear whether this is due to a difference in sulopenem urine PK between healthy subjects and those with uUTI. Further, there are uncertainties regarding the assumed bladder voiding frequencies that limit the interpretability of the urine PTA results. Nonetheless, the plasma-based PTA results support a susceptible breakpoint of up to 0.5 mcg/mL.
L885: ## 14.5.2. Introduction
L886: The objectives of the PopPK analysis were to:
L887: - Develop a PopPK model to describe the disposition of sulopenem in plasma and urine
- Evaluate the impact of clinically relevant covariates on the PK of sulopenem
- Predict the probability of PK/PD target attainment in plasma and urine
L888: ## 14.5.3. Model Development
L889: The clinical Pharmacology Review Team previously reviewed the model development, evaluation of model performance and covariate analysis; refer to NDA 213972 Multi-disciplinary Review and Evaluation dated July 22, 2021. Briefly, the PopPK model is based on data from 12 studies as summarized in (Table 73); there are no PK data available from Trial 310. A summary of the number of observations from each trial and demographic information are provided in Table 74, Table 75 and Table 76. Phase 1 studies included rich PK sampling while sparse samples were obtained in the phase 3 trial participants. A graphical illustration of the initial model, which was a 3-compartment model with non-linear elimination developed using only plasma PK data, is shown in Figure 6.
L890: For urine observations, urine concentration and volume data were collected for 243 subjects in Trials 101, 301, and 302 (Table 76). The final and updated PopPK model was based on urine measurements results from Day 1 of Trial 101, where the urine collection process was well-controlled and yielded reliable urine concentration and volume data (i.e., with sampling at 2 h intervals through 12 h post dosing in 32 subjects) in healthy subjects. In total, 32 unique subjects contributed 159 urine concentration and urine volume observations. Because urine PK data were available for only a subset of subjects in the PK population, the Applicant limited their analyses to estimation of urine-specific parameters (i.e., urine fraction, inter-individual variability in urine fraction, and a residual error of the urine concentration data) by fixing the plasma PopPK model parameters to individual's empirical Bayes estimates.

L910: The previously reviewed plasma PopPK model was modified to specify a urine compartment, resulting in a 3-compartment model with nonlinear elimination (at concentrations exceeding those associated with the proposed dosage) mathematically described by:
L911: ## **Figure 7. Updated PopPK Model Equation**
L912: \frac{dA_{central}}{dt} = \frac{k_{tr1} + k_{tr2}}{2} - k_{12} \cdot A_{central} + k_{21} \cdot A_{peripheral2} - k_{13} \cdot A_{central} + k_{31} \cdot A_{peripheral3} - k_e \cdot A_{central}\frac{dA_{peripheral2}}{dt} = k_{12} \cdot A_{central} - k_{21} \cdot A_{peripheral2}\frac{dA_{peripheral3}}{dt} = k_{13} \cdot A_{central} - k_{31} \cdot A_{peripheral3}\frac{dA_{urine}}{dt} = k_e \cdot A_{central} \cdot UrineFraction
L913: where the micro-constants of the mass transfer are defined as
L914: k_{tr1} = \frac{N_{tr}+1}{MTT_{tr}}; \quad k_e = \frac{T_M \cdot C_S}{K_M + C_S}; \quad k_{12} = \frac{Q_1}{V_1}; \quad k_{21} = \frac{Q_2}{V_2}; \quad k_{13} = \frac{Q_3}{V_1}; \quad k_{31} = \frac{Q_3}{V_3}.
L915: and urine concentrations defined as
L916: Conc_{urine} = \frac{A_{urine}}{V_{urine}}
L917: Source: Section A.12.3 of Applicant's Population PK and PTA Analysis Report
Abbreviations: PK, pharmacokinetic; PTA, probability of target attainment
L918: To update the previous PopPK model, implementation of the urine observations assumed complete voiding of the bladder (i.e., urine compartment) with the observed urine volume reflecting the total amount produced within the collection interval (i.e., between two observations). The final model PK parameters and inter-subject variabilities (IVs) are shown in
L919: **Table 77** and **Table 78**, respectively. Parameters were generally estimated with precision (relative standard errors &lt;50%). The estimated urine fraction was 48% (95% CI, 40% to 56%; based on logit-transformed point estimate, e^{\text{THETA}31}/(1+e^{\text{THETA}31})) of the plasma clearance rate with an IIV variance estimate of 0.219 (i.e., 49.5% coefficient of variation with 20.3% shrinkage) and proportional residual error variance estimate of 0.29 (residual standard error 19%; shrinkage, 2.8%).
L920: Using the final model parameter estimates and assuming no difference between healthy volunteers and patients, urine PK was simulated for Trials 101, 301 and 302 population. Prediction-corrected visual predictive check plots for the sulopenem urinary concentrations in the presence or absence of food and probenecid indicate that although the updated model tends to reasonably capture the central tendency for data in Trials 101 and 302, there are underpredictions for the respective 95th percentiles of the observed urine data in these two studies. Furthermore, the relatively wide 95% CI of the predicted 5th percentiles for the observed urine data in Trials 101 and 302 are likely due to small sample size and high variability (**Figure 8**). For Trial 301, the updated PopPK model underpredicts the urine exposures, and it is unclear which factor(s) (i.e., potential difference in urine PK between subjects in Trial 101 and Trial 301, shorter urine PK collection period in Trial 301, or relatively higher variabilities of the nominal urine concentration compared to those of Trials 101 and 302) may account for the underpredictions. Because of these limitations, the urine PTA findings based on the updated PopPK model should be interpreted with caution.

L933: ## 14.5.4. Probability of Target Attainment in Plasma and Urine
L934: The final PopPK model was subsequently used to simulate and estimate PTAs for both plasma and urine using Monte Carlo simulations. Patient covariates incorporated in the PopPK model (i.e., body weight, sex, and creatinine clearance [CrCl]) were obtained by re-sampling
L935: individuals, with replacement, from the analysis dataset (from Trials 101, 301, and 302), resulting in the covariate distributions summarized in Table 79. Although in the current regulatory setting, uUTI is generally considered to occur in women with normal genitourinary anatomy inclusion of data from male trial participants (who are expected to exhibit lower sulopenem exposures than females based on model predictions) was reasonable to allow a more conservative estimation of PTA (Section 2.1). To account for the impact of bladder emptying, two voiding frequencies (i.e., 1 h and 2 h) were evaluated. However, it is unclear whether these voiding patterns are readily generalizable in clinical settings. The urine production rate (L/h) used in the simulations was based on literature reports indicating normal urine production rates of 0.5-1.5 mL/kg/h. A value of 1 mL/kg/h appeared to best align with observed urine production rates in 101, 301, and 302 (calculated as measured urine volume (L) divided by time in between observations).

L945: ## 14.6. Pharmacogenetics
