L947: ## 15. Study/Trial Design
L948: Inclusion criteria, exclusion criteria, analysis populations, and efficacy endpoints of Trial 310 are described below.
L949: ## Inclusion Criteria
L950: Patients had to meet the following criteria to be eligible for the study:
L951: - Female patients \ge 18 years of age with \ge 24 hours and \le 96 hours attributable to a UTI
- Two of the following signs and symptoms of uUTI: urinary frequency, urinary urgency, pain or burning on micturition, suprapubic pain
- A mid-stream urine specimen with:a machine-read dipstick positive for nitrite AND any positive leukocyte esterase
- OR
- evidence of pyuria alone as defined by either:a machine-read dipstick positive for large leukocyte esterase
- OR
- at least 10 white blood cells per cubic millimeter on microscopic analysis of unspun urine
- OR
- white blood cell count \ge 10 cells/HPF in the sediment of a spun urine
- Has given written informed consent to participate in the study
L952: ## Exclusion Criteria
L953: Patients who met any of the following criteria were excluded from the study:
L954: - Presence of signs and symptoms suggestive of acute pyelonephritis defined as: fever (temperature &gt; 38^\circ Celsius), chills, costovertebral angle tenderness, flank pain, nausea, and/or vomiting
- Receipt of antibacterial drug therapy potentially effective as treatment of uUTI within the prior 7 days
- Concurrent use of non-study treatments that would have a potential effect on outcome evaluations in patients with uUTI, including analgesics (e.g., non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, aspirin, paracetamol etc.), phenazopyridine, and cranberry products. Note: Patients could be included if these medications were previously taken and had ceased at the time of Screening onward.
- Any anatomical abnormality of the urinary tract, including surgically modified urinary tract anatomy, and obstructive uropathy due to nephrolithiasis, stricture, tumor, or fibrosis
- Ongoing urinary retention
L955: - Neurogenic bladder
- Current resident of a long-term care facility
- Instrumentation of urinary tract in the previous 30 days
- An indwelling urinary catheter, ureteral stent or other foreign material in the urinary tract
- Any history of trauma to the pelvis or urinary tract
- Current urine culture, if available while evaluating eligibility, that was positive for more than 2 microorganisms regardless of colony count (contaminated), or confirmed a fungal UTI
- Receiving hemodialysis, hemofiltration, peritoneal dialysis, or had a renal transplant
- Immunocompromised as evidenced by any of the following:Known HIV positive, with either a recent (in the past 6 months) AIDS-defining condition or a CD4 + T lymphocyte count &lt;200/\text{mm}^3
- Known neutropenia (defined as absolute neutrophil count &lt;1000 \text{ cells}/\text{mm}^3)
- Systemic or hematological malignancy requiring chemotherapeutic or radiation/immunologic interventions within 6 weeks prior to randomization or anticipated to begin prior to completion of study
- Immunosuppressive therapy, including maintenance corticosteroid therapy (&gt;40 \text{ mg}/\text{day} equivalent prednisolone for 5 days or more in the 30 days prior to randomization)
- Known liver function abnormalities as defined by the following laboratory criteria:Alanine aminotransferase or aspartate aminotransferase &gt;3\times upper limit of normal, and/or
- Total bilirubin &gt;2\times upper limit of normal
- Females of child-bearing potential who were unable to take adequate contraceptive precautions, had a positive pregnancy test result within 24 hours of study entry, were otherwise known to be pregnant, or were currently breastfeeding
- Poorly controlled diabetes mellitus, including the presence of ketoacidosis and hyperosmolar hyperglycemia
- History of seizures
- History of blood dyscrasias
- History of uric acid kidney stones
- Acute (current) gouty arthritis
- Concomitant administration of valproic acid
- History of allergy or hypersensitivity to carbapenems, \beta-lactams or probenecid, as formulated with their excipients
- Unlikely to survive the 4-week study period or had a rapidly progressive or terminal illness, including septic shock, associated with a high risk of mortality
- The use of any other investigational drug in the 30 days prior to the first dose of study drug, or prior participation in any sulopenem clinical trial
L956: Urine samples, including results from urine tests, collected as part of routine standard of care, prior to obtaining informed consent, may have been used to assess eligibility for enrollment into study and/or for baseline urine culture.
L957: ## **Analysis Populations**
L958: **Intent-to-Treat (ITT):** all randomized patients regardless of whether or not the patient received study drug.
L959: **Modified ITT (MITT):** randomized patients who received at least a single dose of study medication.
L960: **Micro-MITT:** all MITT patients with a positive study entry urine culture defined as \ge 10^5 colony-forming units (CFU)/mL of a uropathogen (*Enterobacteriales* or *S. saprophyticus* only) and no more than 2 species of microorganisms identified in the study entry urine culture, regardless of colony count.
L961: The primary comparisons for regulatory approval were in two mutually exclusive subpopulations of the microbiological modified intent-to-treat (micro-MITT) population defined by a baseline characteristic, the micro-MITTS and micro-MITTR populations:
L962: - **Micro-MITTS population:** the subset of patients whose baseline pathogens were determined to be susceptible (\text{MIC} \le 8/4 \text{ mg/L}) to the comparator study drug, amoxicillin/clavulanate.
- **Micro-MITTR population:** the subset of patients whose baseline pathogen was determined to be non-susceptible [intermediate (\text{MIC} 16/8 \text{ mg/L}) or resistant (\text{MIC} \ge 32/16 \text{ mg/L})] to the comparator study drug, amoxicillin/clavulanate.
L963: ## **Efficacy Endpoints**
L964: ## **Primary Efficacy Endpoint**
L965: The primary efficacy endpoint was overall success (combined clinical and microbiologic success) on Day 12 (\pm 1 days)/test of cure (TOC) in the micro-MITT, micro-MITTS and micro-MITTR populations.
L966: A patient was defined as an overall success if the following criteria were met:
L967: - The patient was alive
- The patient received no rescue therapy for uUTIIf an antibiotic active against the urinary tract pathogen was given for other reasons, then the patient would be considered indeterminate
- The patient had resolution of the symptoms of uUTI present at trial entry and no new uUTI symptoms (based on the Patient Symptom Assessment Questionnaire)
- Urine culture taken on Day 12 (\pm 1 day)/TOC demonstrated &lt;10^3 CFU/mL of the baseline uropathogen based on results of quantitative cultures performed on collected urine specimens.
L968: All other patients would be considered as failures unless data were unavailable to determine whether the patient was a success or a failure. In this case, the patient would be considered as having an indeterminate response. Patients with an indeterminate response were included in the denominator for determination of the overall success rate.
L969: For overall response, if the urine culture was contaminated, baseline pathogen(s) was/were considered eradicated. For microbiologic response, contaminated results were considered a negative culture and therefore an eradication. We will conduct additional analysis to address the effect of contamination coded as eradication for the primary efficacy endpoint.
L970: ## Secondary Efficacy Endpoints Included
L971: ## **Microbiologic Response**
L972: In the protocol, microbiological response was assessed using the following definitions:
L973: **Table 80. Definition of Microbiologic Response**
L974: Response	Definition
Success	The urine culture demonstrates <10^3 CFU/mL of the baseline uropathogen (also referred to as eradication) at the time-point of analysis
Persistence	A uropathogen present at baseline grew at \ge 10^3 CFU/mL at the time-point of analysis
Persistence with increasing MIC	A urine culture taken after at least 2 full days of treatment grew \ge 10^3 CFU/mL of the baseline uropathogen and displayed \ge 4-dilutions higher MIC, as compared to baseline, to study drug received at the time-point of analysis
Indeterminate	Patient was lost to follow-up, or an assessment was not undertaken such that no urine culture was obtained (or culture results could not be interpreted for any reason) at the time-point of analysis
L975: Source: Page 47 of the Study Protocol
L976: Abbreviations: CFU, colony-forming units; MIC, minimum inhibitory concentration
L977: ## **Patient-Determined Clinical Response**
L978: A patient was defined as a clinical success if the following criteria were met:
L979: - The patient was alive
- The patient received no rescue therapy for uUTIIf an antibiotic active against the urinary tract pathogen was given for other reasons, the patient was considered indeterminate.
- The patient had resolution of the symptoms of uUTI present at trial entry and no new uUTI symptoms based on the Patient Symptom Assessment QuestionnaireBaseline symptoms associated with another known condition (e.g., overactive bladder) do not need to be resolved
L980: All other patients were considered as failures unless data were unavailable to determine if the patient was a success or a failure. In this case, the patient was considered as having an indeterminate response. Patients with an indeterminate response were included in the denominator for determination of the response rate.
L981: ## **Investigator-Determined Clinical Response**
L982: The following clinical response definitions were used by the investigators:
L983: - **Clinical success:** all pre-therapy signs and symptoms of the index infection had resolved such that no additional antibiotics were required.
- **Clinical failure:** patients who met any one of the following criteria:Death related to uUTI prior to end of trial (EOT), TOC, and final visit (FV), respectively
- Persistence or progression of any pre-therapy uUTI signs and symptoms or use of additional antibiotics for the current infection
- Patient previously met criteria for failure and received rescue antibiotics
- **Indeterminate:** Data not available for evaluation of efficacy for any reason, including but not limited to:Patient lost to follow-up or assessment not undertaken such that a determination of clinical response could not be made at either the EOT, TOC or FV, respectively
- Death prior to EOT, TOC, or FV, respectively, where uUTI was clearly non-contributory
L984: ## **16. Efficacy**
L985: The results from Trial 301, the micro-MITT and ITT populations of Trial 310, Trial 302 for cUTI, and Trial 303 for cIAI are included in this section. Trials 301, 302 and 303 were included in the initial NDA submission; therefore, only a brief summary of these three trials is included in this review.
L986: ## **16.1. Summary of Trial 301 in uUTI**
L987: A total of 1660 adult women with uUTI were randomized and received trial medications in this multinational, randomized, double-blind clinical trial comparing oral sulopenem etzadroxil 500 mg and probenecid 500 mg twice daily (BID) for 5 days to oral ciprofloxacin 250 mg BID for 3 days. The micro-MITT population, which included all patients who had at least one uropathogen isolated at baseline (\ge 10^5 CFU/mL), consisted of 1105 patients; the median age was 53 years; median weight in the randomized population was 70.4 kg. Patients were enrolled from the United States (55%) and Eastern Europe (45%). Patients were Caucasian (90%), African American (9%) or of other races (1%).
L988: Composite response (combined microbiological response and clinical cure) was determined by comparing the response rate of sulopenem to ciprofloxacin at the TOC visit (12 days after randomization) in two primary populations: Micro-MITTS (micro-MITT population with baseline pathogens susceptible to ciprofloxacin, MIC \le 1 \mug/mL) and Micro-MITTR (micro-MITT population with baseline pathogens non-susceptible to ciprofloxacin, MIC \ge 2 \mug/mL).
L989: Clinical cure was defined as the resolution of patient-reported uUTI symptoms and no new uUTI symptoms. Microbiological response was defined as a reduction of all baseline uropathogens to less than 103 CFU/mL in the urine.
L990: Sulopenem demonstrated efficacy in the micro-MITTR population but did not demonstrate efficacy in the micro-MITTS population.

L995: ## 16.2. Study Results, Micro-MITT Population, Trial 310
L996: The Applicant listed the micro-MITT population as Step 1 in the hierarchical testing procedure and reported the results. Therefore, we include the results from this population in the review. As the micro-MITT population was mainly composed of micro-MITTS subjects, the results were very similar to those in the micro-MITTS population.
L997: ## Disposition
L998: Overall, approximately 96% of the 990 micro-MITT subjects completed study drug treatment, while 4% discontinued treatment prematurely. The primary reasons for discontinuation of treatment were non-compliance with study drug (1.1%) and withdrawal by subject (1.2%). The primary reasons for discontinuation of study were loss to follow-up (2.0%) and withdrawal by subject (2.3%).

L1081: ## 16.4. Trial 302 for cUTI
L1082: Trial 302 was a phase 3, multicenter, double-blind, randomized trial designed to compare the efficacy, tolerability, and safety of IV sulopenem followed by oral sulopenem etzadroxil/probenecid with that of IV ertapenem followed by oral ciprofloxacin or amoxicillin/clavulanate for the treatment of cUTI in both men and women.
L1083: Subjects were randomized 1:1 to receive either IV sulopenem 1000 mg once daily for at least 5 days (five doses) followed by oral sulopenem etzadroxil 500 mg co-administered with oral probenecid 500 mg BID to complete 7 to 10 total days of treatment versus ertapenem IV 1000 mg once daily for at least 5 days (five doses) followed by oral ciprofloxacin 500 mg or
L1084: amoxicillin/clavulanate 875 mg BID to complete 7 to 10 total days of therapy. Duration of treatment could be extended up to a total of 14 days for patients with bacteremia at baseline.
L1085: The primary efficacy endpoint was overall response (resolution of symptoms and clearance of the baseline uropathogen) at Day 21 (TOC). The primary analysis population was the micro-MITT, defined as subjects who received at least a single dose of study medication, had the disease under study (with two of the five baseline cUTI symptoms), and a positive study entry urine culture within 48 h prior to the first dose. The study entry urine culture had to have no more than two species of uropathogens (Enterobacteriales only, susceptible to sulopenem [MIC \le 1] and ertapenem [MIC \le 0.5]) at \ge 10^5 CFU/mL, except in the situation where one of the organisms cultured from the urine was also isolated from blood cultures drawn at baseline. Patients with a study pathogen isolated from baseline blood cultures were included in the micro-MITT population regardless of the patient's baseline urine culture result.
L1086: The Applicant's efficacy results were based on definitions of microbiological responses using the same definition for "persistence" as in Trial 301, i.e., a uropathogen present in baseline urine culture which grew at \ge 10^3 CFU/mL at TOC with further specification as follows: "The genus/species and susceptibility profiles need to match. For the Baseline and TOC visits, additional molecular testing by pulsed field gel electrophoresis or whole-genome sequencing may be performed for confirmation." FDA requested reanalysis of the data for Trials 301, 302, and 303 (for cIAI), based on definitions of microbiological response without using additional molecular testing. The results from the two analyses from the initial and updated reports were consistent, but only the results using the initial statistical analysis plan (SAP) are reported here.
L1087: The two treatment groups were comparable with respect to demographic characteristics. The majority of subjects were female (about 55%). The mean age was about 59 years (range 18 to 94 years). The majority of subjects had acute pyelonephritis (57.1% in the sulopenem arm; 56.9% in the ertapenem arm). *E. coli* was the most common organism isolated (76.1% on sulopenem; 78.6% on ertapenem).
L1088: As shown in the following Table 96, Trial 302 failed to show noninferiority using a -10% noninferiority margin. IV sulopenem followed by oral (PO) sulopenem etzadroxil/probenecid was significantly worse than the active comparator, IV ertapenem followed by PO ciprofloxacin or amoxicillin/clavulanate.

L1093: In the sulopenem group, 87% of all subjects in the micro-MITT population stepped down from IV sulopenem to PO sulopenem etzadroxil/probenecid and the overall response rate in these subjects was 61.2% [i.e., (154+26+53+5)/(248+55+80+6)]; the response rates by ciprofloxacin and amoxicillin/clavulanate susceptibility are shown in Table 97. In the ertapenem group, 67.5%
L1094: (297/440) of subjects stepped down to oral therapy with either ciprofloxacin or amoxicillin/clavulanate; of these subjects, 50% (220/440) stepped down to ciprofloxacin PO with an overall response rate of 82.3% (181/220) while 17.5% (77/440) of subjects stepped down to amoxicillin/clavulanate with an overall response rate of 54.5% (42/77). Comparisons of outcomes between subjects who stepped down to oral therapy in the two groups are limited by being post-randomization subgroup analyses. The fact that more subjects stepped down to oral therapy in the sulopenem group suggested that subjects receiving oral sulopenem etzadroxil/probenecid were not necessarily comparable to subjects receiving oral ciprofloxacin or oral amoxicillin/clavulanate at the time of stepdown. Nevertheless, the results in Table 97 suggest that an efficacy decrement of stepdown sulopenem etzadroxil/probenecid compared to stepdown ciprofloxacin in the subgroup with ciprofloxacin-susceptible pathogens may have contributed to the unfavorable trial conclusions. Such an efficacy decrement would be consistent with the Trial 301 results seen for uUTI.

L1115: ## **Efficacy Conclusions From Trial 302**
L1116: Trial 302 did not provide evidence for the efficacy of IV sulopenem followed by oral sulopenem etzadroxil/probenecid for the treatment of cUTI. In the primary efficacy analysis of overall clinical and microbiological response at the TOC visit, IV sulopenem followed by oral sulopenem etzadroxil/probenecid did not demonstrate noninferiority compared to the control group treated with IV ertapenem followed by oral ciprofloxacin or oral amoxicillin/clavulanate. Further, the sulopenem group was statistically inferior to the control group. Results for overall response in the two treatment groups were similar at Day 5 (the minimum duration of IV therapy) and the EOT but differed by the TOC visit on Day 21. The efficacy decrement was driven by a difference in microbiologic response rates, as clinical response rates were similar between the sulopenem and ertapenem treatment groups. There was remaining uncertainty regarding whether any efficacy decrements were due to the intravenous or oral sulopenem because while the randomized comparisons were designed to evaluate intravenous-to-oral regimens, results were suggestive of an efficacy decrement of stepdown sulopenem etzadroxil/probenecid compared to stepdown ciprofloxacin in subjects with ciprofloxacin-susceptible pathogens. Such an efficacy decrement is consistent with the Trial 301 results seen for uUTI where the noninferiority of oral sulopenem etzadroxil/probenecid to oral ciprofloxacin in ciprofloxacin-susceptible isolates was not demonstrated.
L1117: ## **16.5. Trial 303 for cIAI**
L1118: Trial 303 was a phase 3, multicenter, double-blind, randomized trial designed to compare the efficacy, tolerability, and safety of IV sulopenem followed by oral sulopenem etzadroxil/probenecid with that of IV ertapenem followed by oral ciprofloxacin and metronidazole or amoxicillin/clavulanate for the treatment of cIAI.
L1119: A total of 674 subjects were randomized (1:1) to receive either IV sulopenem 1000 mg once daily for at least 5 days (five doses) followed by sulopenem etzadroxil 500 mg co-administered with oral probenecid 500 mg twice daily to complete 7 to 10 total days of treatment or ertapenem IV 1000 mg once daily for at least 5 days (five doses) followed by oral ciprofloxacin 500 mg twice daily and metronidazole 500 mg four times a day or amoxicillin/clavulanate 875 mg twice daily to complete 7 to 10 total days of therapy. Duration of treatment could be extended up to a total of 14 days. The results are shown in Table 101. After initial unblinding of the study, imbalances in outcome by treatment were identified by the Applicant. Subsequently, the Applicant conducted a post hoc analysis by re-examining and re-analyzing the data. FDA did not agree with the Applicant's post hoc analysis after the study data were unblinded. Trial 303 failed to show NI using a -10% margin, either based on the primary analysis or the post hoc analysis.

L1148: ## 19. Clinical Microbiology
L1149: ## 19.1. Nonclinical Microbiology
L1150: Please refer to the previous Multidisciplinary Review dated July 22, 2021, for the evaluation of in vitro and in vivo microbiology data presented in the initial NDA submission. No new in vitro and in vivo studies were conducted for this resubmission.
L1151: ## Clinical Studies for the uUTI Indication
L1152: The Applicant conducted two phase 3 uUTI clinical trials (IT001-301 or Trial 301 and IT001-310 or Trial 310) to determine the safety and efficacy of oral sulopenem etzadroxil/probenecid for this indication. For the treatment of adult women with uUTI, oral sulopenem etzadroxil/probenecid was compared with oral ciprofloxacin in Trial 301, while in Trial 310, oral sulopenem etzadroxil/probenecid was compared with oral amoxicillin/clavulanate.
L1153: Data from Trial 301 were reviewed for the initial NDA submission and are not included in this review. Please refer to the previous Multidisciplinary Review and Evaluation dated July 22, 2021. There are no pooled analyses, as only one phase 3 trial, Trial 310 is included in this resubmission. Therefore, this review only covers the uUTI Trial 310 and the Agency's recommendation on sulopenem broth microdilution MIC and disk diffusion breakpoints (BPs) for the uUTI-indicated Enterobacterales species.
L1154: ## **uUTI Phase 3 Clinical Study: IT001-310 or Trial 310**
L1155: In Trial 310, oral sulopenem etzadroxil/probenecid was compared with oral amoxicillin/clavulanate for the treatment of adult women with uUTI. The primary endpoint was overall response on Day 12 (\pm 1 day) which was the TOC visit.
L1156: ## **Definitions of Analysis Populations**
L1157: **Intent-to-Treat:** The ITT population included all randomized patients regardless of whether the patient received study drug.
L1158: **Modified ITT:** The MITT group included all randomized patients who received at least a single dose of study medication. Patients were analyzed according to the treatment group to which they were randomized.
L1159: **Microbiologic-MITT (or micro-MITT):** Micro-MITT patients were MITT patients with a positive study entry urine culture defined as \ge 10^5 CFU/mL of a uropathogen (*Enterobacterales* or *S. saprophyticus* only) and no more than two species of microorganisms identified in the study entry urine culture, regardless of colony count.
L1160: **Micro-MITTS:** The micro-MITTS population comprised micro-MITT patients with a baseline uropathogen susceptible to the comparator drug, amoxicillin/clavulanate (defined as MIC \le 8/4 mg/L per Clinical and Laboratory Standards Institute [CLSI] breakpoints [CLSI M100]), and no baseline pathogen non-susceptible to amoxicillin/clavulanate.
L1161: **Micro-MITTR:** The micro-MITTR population comprised micro-MITT patients with a baseline uropathogen non-susceptible (intermediate [MIC 16/8 mg/L per CLSI M100] or resistant [MIC \ge32/16 mg/L per CLSI M100]) to the comparator drug, amoxicillin/clavulanate.
L1162: In the ITT populations, a total of 522/1111 (47%) and 468/1111 (42.1%) patients were in the micro-MITT populations of the sulopenem arm and amoxicillin/clavulanate arm, respectively. The micro-MITT population included both micro-MITTS (patients with a baseline pathogen susceptible to amoxicillin/clavulanate) and micro-MITTR (patients with a baseline pathogen non-susceptible to amoxicillin/clavulanate) populations. In Trial 310, the micro-MITTR population was very small (3% total in both arms) compared to the micro-MITTR (18%) in Trial 301.
L1163: ## Microbiological Sampling
L1164: ## Methods for Microbiological Collection, Culture, and Identification
L1165: For microbiological culture and analysis, mid-stream clean-catch urine specimens were collected from patients at Screening (Baseline), Day 3, Day 5 (EOT), Day 12 (TOC), Day 28, and for any study-related visits. Urine samples were received at International Health Management Associates in boric acid tubes within 48 hours of collection, either ambient or refrigerated.
L1166: Baseline/screening urine samples were cultured on blood agar plates, and MacConkey plates using a 1 \muL loop. Samples from all other visits were cultured on blood agar plates, CAN, and MacConkey plates using a 1 \muL and a 10 \muL loop. All culture plates were incubated at 35°C for 18 to 24 hours in non-CO2 incubators.
L1167: ## Target Pathogens
L1168: For Study IT001-310, the following organisms were considered a uropathogen when isolated from an acceptable urine culture specimen:
L1169: Monomicrobial or polymicrobial infections caused by:
L1170: - Enterobacterales
- *Staphylococcus saprophyticus*
- *Pseudomonas aeruginosa*
- *Enterococcus* spp.
L1171: The latter two organisms were considered non-target pathogens. All target and non-target pathogens were identified by Matrix-Assisted Laser Desorption Ionization–Time of Flight (MALDI-TOF), had aspartate aminotransferase testing by broth microdilution, and were saved when considered significant. Disk diffusion testing was performed on only Enterobacterales and *S. saprophyticus*. The micro-MITT population for this study only included patients with uUTIs caused by Enterobacterales. A study urine culture that was positive for more than two species of microorganisms was considered contaminated, regardless of colony count.
L1172: ## Microbiological Outcome Measures
L1173: The microbiological definitions used in the assessment of the per-pathogen microbiological response at baseline and post-baseline are summarized in Table 104 and Table 105.
L1174: **Table 104. Microbiological Assessment of Baseline Pathogens at TOC**
L1175: Response	Definition
Eradication	A urine culture obtained at the timepoint of analysis demonstrated <10^3 CFU/mL of the baseline uropathogen
Persistence	A uropathogen from urine present at baseline regardless of susceptibility grew at \ge 10^3 CFU/mL at the timepoint of analysis*.
Persistence with Increasing MIC	A urine culture taken after at least 2 full days of treatment grew \ge 10^3 CFU/mL of the baseline uropathogen and displayed \ge 4-fold higher MIC to study drug received at the timepoint of analysis.
Indeterminate	Patient was lost to follow-up, or an assessment was not undertaken such that no urine culture was obtained (or culture results could not be interpreted) at the timepoint of analysis (contaminated results are considered a negative culture and therefore an eradication6).
L1176: Source: NDA submission
L1177: *The genus/species and susceptibility profiles need to match. Additional molecular testing by pulsed field gel electrophoresis or whole genome sequencing was performed as needed for confirmation.
L1178: Abbreviations: CFU, colony-forming units; MIC, minimum inhibitory concentration
L1179: **Table 105. Microbiological Definitions of Post-Baseline Pathogens**
L1180: Response	Definition
Superinfection	A uropathogen not present at baseline grew with \ge 10^5 CFU/mL from the first dose of study drug through the EOT visit in the setting of recurrent/persistent/new uUTI symptoms requiring non-study systemic antibacterial treatment* (patient-determined clinical failure at EOT).
New Infection	Isolation of a non-baseline pathogen from a culture post-EOT visit from a urine culture specimen with \ge 10^5 CFU/mL in a patient with one or more new uUTI signs/symptoms requiring new systemic antibacterial treatment* after the EOT visit (patient-determined clinical failure post-EOT).
Recurrence	In a patient with clinical and microbiological success at EOT, isolation of a baseline pathogen from a urine culture specimen with \ge 10^5 CFU/mL post-EOT visit, along with new or recurrence of one or more uUTI signs/symptoms requiring new systemic antibacterial treatment* after the EOT visit (patient-determined clinical failure post-EOT).
Colonization	Isolation of a microorganism from the urine culture after EOT in a patient without one or more signs and symptoms of uUTI and not requiring new systemic antibiotic therapy* (patient-determined clinical success post-EOT).
L1181: Source: NDA submission
L1182: *Excluding linezolid, daptomycin, vancomycin, azithromycin, metronidazole, josamycin, macrolide, nifuratel, tergynan, fluconazole, cystone, butoconazole nitrate, clindamycin hydrochloride, clotrimazole, tinidazole, and clarithromycin, as well as "antibiotics and chemotherapeutics for dermatological use" and "ophthalmologicals" since they have no activity against the pathogens in the study.
L1183: Abbreviations: CFU, colony-forming units; EOT, end of treatment; uUTI, uncomplicated urinary tract infection

L1205: ## Clinical and Microbiological Outcomes, Trial 310

L1207: ## Overall Response at TOC: micro-MITT Population, Trial 310
L1208: The primary efficacy endpoint for this study was the overall response at the TOC (Day 12) Visit. Overall success was observed in 60.9% of patients receiving sulopenem etzadroxil/probenecid, compared to 55.6% of patients in the amoxicillin/clavulanate treatment group [treatment difference (95%CI): 5.4% (-0.8, 11.5)]. Sulopenem demonstrated noninferiority to amoxicillin/clavulanate in the micro-MITT population and is summarized in Table 109.

L1286: ## Sulopenem Activity Against AmpC and ESBL Isolates With Known \beta-Lactamase (*bla*) Genes in Trials 301 and 310
L1287: A total of 336 phenotypically resistant baseline uUTI isolates from Trials 301 and 310 were further analyzed by multiplex PCR to screen for *bla*-genes encoding ESBLs, AmpC \beta-lactamases, and carbapenemases. Table 116 and Table 117 summarize the clinical and microbiological responses to sulopenem in AmpC- and predominant ESBL-producing isolates in Trials 301 and 310, respectively. Against 208 AmpC and ESBL isolates in Trial 301, sulopenem had MIC_{50}/MIC_{90} values of 0.06/0.12, 0.03/0.06, and 0.03/0.06 mcg/mL against AmpC (n=12), CTX-M (n=105), and TEM-OSBL (n=38) genotypes, respectively. The clinical responses were 33.3%, 66.7%, and 63.2% and microbiological responses were 50%, 49.5%, and 50% against AmpC, CTX-M, and TEM-OSBL, respectively. Similarly, against 128 AmpC- and ESBL-producing isolates in Trial 310, sulopenem MIC_{50}/MIC_{90} values were 0.06/0.12, 0.03/0.06, 0.03/0.06 mcg/mL against AmpC (n=14), CTX-M (n=78), and TEM-OSBL (n=22) genotypes, respectively. Against AmpC, CTX-M, and TEM-OSBL, the clinical responses were 71.4%, 84.6%, and 72.7% and the microbiological responses were 85.7%, 62.8%, and 50%, respectively. Among all ESBL genotypes, CTX-M-15 was the most frequently identified from 107/336 (31.8%) baseline ESBL-producing isolates.

L1345: ## **Correlation of Microbiological Success to MIC Values of Baseline *E. coli*, *K. pneumoniae*, and *P. mirabilis* Isolates From uUTI Trials 301 and 310**
L1346: Microbiological success at the TOC visit, in relation to MIC values of total baseline *E. coli*, *K. pneumoniae*, and *P. mirabilis* isolates from the sulopenem treatment group in the micro-MITT population of both uUTI clinical trials (301 and 310), are summarized below:
L1347: - Among a total of 876 baseline *E. coli* isolates from Trials 301 and 310, the MIC range was ≤0.008 to 1.0 mcg/mL; the MIC90 values against *E. coli* isolates from surveillance and clinical studies were 0.03 and 0.06 mcg/mL, respectively. Overall microbiological eradication/success at TOC was achieved in 661/876 (75.5%) isolates. While the cumulative microbiological success rate of 75.4% (660/875) was achieved up to the highest MIC 0.25 mcg/mL, 5/7 (71.4%) isolates were eradicated at this MIC. No baseline *E. coli* isolates with MIC 0.5 mcg/mL or ≥2 mcg/mL were available; only one baseline *E. coli* isolate with sulopenem MIC of 1 mcg/mL was available and eradicated. Therefore, we recommend a susceptible BP of 0.25 mcg/mL as more appropriate to cover most of the *E. coli* population.
- Among a total of 108 baseline *K. pneumoniae* isolates from Trials 301 and 310, the MIC range was 0.015 to 8.0 mcg/mL; the MIC90 values against *K. pneumoniae* isolates were 0.12 mcg/mL and 0.06 to 0.12 mcg/mL from surveillance and clinical studies, respectively. Overall microbiological eradication/success at TOC was achieved in 81/108 (75%) isolates. While the cumulative microbiological success rate of 74.5% (79/106) was achieved up to the highest MIC 0.25 mcg/mL, 1/2 (50%) isolates were eradicated at this MIC. No baseline *K. pneumoniae* isolates with MIC 0.5 and 1.0 mcg/mL were available. However, 2 baseline isolates with MIC 4 mcg/mL and 8 mcg/mL were available and eradicated. Therefore, we recommend a susceptible BP of 0.25 mcg/mL as more appropriate to cover most of the *K. pneumoniae* population.
- Among a total of 31 baseline *P. mirabilis* isolates from Trials 301 and 310, the MIC range was ≤0.015 to 0.5 mcg/mL; the MIC90 values against *P. mirabilis* isolates from surveillance and clinical studies were 0.5 and 0.25 to 0.5 mcg/mL, respectively. Overall microbiological
L1348: eradication/success at TOC was achieved in 20/31 (64.5%) isolates. While the cumulative microbiological success rate of 67.9% (19/28) was achieved up to the highest MIC 0.25 mcg/mL, 13/14 (92.9%) isolates were eradicated at this MIC. Three baseline *P. mirabilis* isolates with MIC 0.5 mcg/mL were available but only one isolate was eradicated. No baseline *P. mirabilis* isolates with MIC \ge 1.0 mcg/mL were available. Therefore, we recommend a susceptible BP of 0.25 mcg/mL as more appropriate to cover most of the *P. mirabilis* population.
L1349: ## PK/PD Data and PTA Predictions in Plasma
L1350: The lack of an established nonclinical model for uUTIs and uncertainties surrounding: 1) urine specific PK/PD parameters, 2) appropriate bacteriologic endpoint for use in PTA analyses, and 3) the relative importance of plasma versus urine drug concentrations limited the Agency's reliance on the Applicant's PK/PD package to support the proposed STIC. Because of concerns with the reliability of the results of the murine thigh infection model PK/PD studies, results of the in vitro PK/PD target determination studies were prioritized in the Agency's PTA evaluations. PTA analyses showed that the free plasma concentrations associated with the proposed dose regimen resulted in achievement of the in vitro targets in \ge 90\% of simulated subjects up to an MIC 0.25 mcg/mL. In urine, PTA analyses showed achievement of the in vitro targets in \ge 90\% of simulated subjects up to an MIC of 8 mcg/mL. Given the aforementioned knowledge gaps and their implications for the translatability of nonclinical PK/PD findings to clinical efficacy, the Agency prioritized the more conservative findings from plasma-based PTA analysis in support of a sulopenem susceptible BP of 0.25 mcg/mL against Enterobacterales.
L1351: In summary, the FDA review team recommends sulopenem Susceptible (S)/Intermediate (I)/Resistant (R) MIC BPs of \le 0.25/0.5/\ge 1.0 mcg/mL against Enterobacterales (*E. coli*, *K. pneumoniae*, and *P. mirabilis* only) that are [REDACTED] (b) (4) than the Applicant's proposed S/I/R BPs of [REDACTED] (b) (4) mcg/mL.
L1352: The corresponding disk diffusion zone diameter BPs have been calculated by following CLSI error rate criteria. The Agency-recommended broth microdilution (MIC) and disk diffusion interpretive criteria (BPs) for sulopenem are summarized in Table 120.

L1390: ## 20. Mechanism of Action/Drug Resistance
L1391: ## 20.1. Mechanism of Action
L1392: Sulopenem is a penem antibacterial drug that inhibits bacterial cell wall synthesis by binding to penicillin-binding proteins (PBPs). A competitive binding assay was conducted with ^{3}\text{H}-penicillin in *E. coli* strain W-7 that showed sulopenem (CP-65,207) had the highest affinity for PBP2, with concentrations as low as 0.004 mcg/mL (Gootz et al. 1989). The assay also showed that the relative order of affinity for PBPs of sulopenem in *E. coli* was PBP2 &gt; PBP1A &gt; PBP1B &gt; PBP4 &gt; PBP3 &gt; PBP5/6. Additionally, it was determined through a hydrolysis study that sulopenem (CP-65207) was highly stable to some cephalosporinases, including plasmid-encoded enzymes TEM-1, SHV-1, and PSE-2.
L1393: Similar to other carbapenems, sulopenem showed bactericidal killing by time-kill assay at concentrations \ge 4\times the MIC against *E. coli* and *K. pneumoniae*.
L1394: **Figure 24. Autoradiograph of Competitive Binding of Unlabeled Sulopenem (CP-65,207) vs. ^{3}\text{H}-penicillin G for *E. coli* W-7 PBPs**
L1395: Source: (Gootz et al. 1989) AAC, Figure 3
Lanes 1 through 10, Test system with concentrations of CP-65,207 between 0 and 4.2 pLg/ml; lane 11, radiolabeled molecular weight standards.
Abbreviations: *E. Coli*, *Escherichia coli*; PBP, penicillin-binding proteins
L1396: ## 20.2. Drug Resistance
L1397: In general, the mechanisms for \beta-lactam resistance in gram-negative bacteria include the following:
L1398: - Hydrolysis by penicillinases, cephalosporinases, oxacillinases and carbapenemases;
- Reduced uptake across the outer membrane due to decreased expression or loss of porin channels;
- Extrusion of drugs by multidrug resistance efflux pumps;
- Mutation of PBP targets (e.g., PBPs).
L1399: High-level \beta-lactam resistance is achieved when multiple mechanisms are combined in a single cell, e.g., production of a carbapenemase in a cell that lacks porin(s) and has overexpressed efflux pumps.
L1400: In vitro, development of resistance to sulopenem was evaluated in spontaneous mutation frequency studies using two *E. cloacae* isolates and in serial passage studies using clinical isolates of *E. coli* and *K. pneumoniae*.
L1401: In spontaneous mutation frequency studies, sulopenem resistant mutants were selected in vitro at a frequency of 1 \times 10^{-8} with a \le 2-fold MIC increase from the parent *E. cloacae* strain. In the serial passage mutation studies, MIC values increased 16-fold during 15 serial passages in two out of the three tested *E. coli* isolates and were unchanged for the third isolate. MIC values increased 8-fold during serial passage for one of the two *K. pneumoniae* isolates tested, and MIC values increased from 0.5 to 256 mcg/mL for the other isolate.
L1402: Similar to other carbapenems, resistance to sulopenem occurs primarily due to enzymatic inactivation by carbapenemases, but also can be caused by \beta-lactamase production, efflux pump
L1403: expression, and changes in porins and/or PBPs (Papp-Wallace et al. 2011; Harting 2019; Papp-Wallace 2019) Aside from the \beta-lactam class of antimicrobial drugs, sulopenem is not expected to demonstrate cross-resistance to any other class.

L1405: Following the complete response of the original NDA application, the Applicant halted development of the IV sulopenem formulation (Please see Sections 3 and 8.3).

L1426: **Protocol IT001-310, Site 251:** 81 subjects were screened, 77 were enrolled, and 63 completed the study. The study conduct at this clinical investigator site was audited for adherence to the study protocol, IRB oversight, site monitoring, staff training, study medication disposition, and clinical investigator financial disclosure.
L1427: Subject case records were reviewed for all subjects, including detailed review for 31 subjects. The major study data were verified against source records for all enrolled subjects, to include treatment assignment, major efficacy endpoints, AEs, PDs, and use of non-study rescue antibiotics or other concomitant medications.
L1428: The inspection was noteworthy for documentation of subject selection that appeared to be NOT adequately rigorous, typically for Exclusion Criterion 15 (pregnancy potential). Adequate contraception history and negative pregnancy testing were not consistently documented in as many as one-third (26/77) of the women enrolled.
L1429: GCP deficiencies important to study data quality were not observed. ICFs were signed for all subjects. The study records showed complete financial disclosure, adequate AE and PD
L1430: reporting, and acceptable drug accountability. The major efficacy and safety endpoint data were verifiable.
L1431: Reviewer's [Dr. John Lee's] comment: *Specifically, the following GCP deficiencies were observed. All observations appear unlikely to have any impact on the efficacy or safety of the study results.*
L1432: - *Inclusion Criteria 3 (leukocyte esterase): Six subjects were enrolled based on positive leukocyte esterase urine dipstick testing (LE-UDT) not further specified as 4+ positive (large) LE-UDT.*
- *Exclusion Criteria 15 (pregnancy potential): For all subjects, a negative urine pregnancy test result was obtained, and a screening interview was conducted to verbally confirm (and document) adequate contraception during study participation, but: (1) pregnancy testing was not always obtained within the protocol-specified timeframe, and (2) the specific method of ongoing contraception was often not recorded. All subjects were contacted as needed to retroactively obtain and record the missing information about the specific contraception method. No subject became pregnant during the study.*
- *Exclusion 13 (neutropenia): One subject was enrolled with an absolute neutrophil count (ANC) of 0.99 \times 10^3/\mu\text{L}, just under (at) the protocol-specified minimum of 1.0 \times 10^3/\mu\text{L}. Repeat testing (Day 12) confirmed an ANC well above the protocol-specified minimum.*

L1435: ## 23. Labeling: Key Changes
L1436: This Prescribing Information (PI) review includes a high-level summary of the rationale for major changes to the finalized PI as compared to the Applicant's draft PI submitted on April 25, 2024 (Table 126). The PI was reviewed to ensure that PI meets regulatory/statutory requirements, is consistent (if appropriate) with labeling guidance, conveys clinically meaningful and scientifically accurate information needed for the safe and effective use of the drug, and provides clear and concise information for the healthcare practitioner.
L1437: Based on discussions with the Office of New Drug Policy (ONDP), Regulatory Policy Advisors Team and Labeling Policy Team (email from ONDP dated 9/30/2024), it was noted that due to the specific concerns regarding ORLYNVAH use and possible increase in antimicrobial resistance, ONDP agreed with DAI/OID's position that parts of the language under 21 CFR 201.24 (Labeling for systemic antibacterial drug products) are not appropriate to include in the ORLYNVAH PI. Omission and/or revision of parts of the language under 21 CFR 201.24 seems particularly critical from a public health standpoint for ORLYNVAH given the concerns about inappropriate use of ORLYNVAH (which could lead to drug resistance) and antibacterial drug stewardship. See Table 126 below for descriptions of omissions/revisions made to the language under 21 CFR 201.24 in Section 17 (Patient Counseling Information) and subsections 1.2 (Usage
L1438: to Reduce Development of Drug-Resistant Bacteria) and 5.5 (Development of Drug-Resistant Bacteria) of the full prescribing information (FPI). Similar edits were made to the Highlights section of the PI (not shown in Table 126) to align with these edits made to the FPI.

L1598: ## 1. Executive Summary
L1599: ## 1.1. Product Introduction
L1600: Sulopenem etzadroxil/probenecid bilayer oral tablet is a fixed-dose combination of a penem antibacterial prodrug (sulopenem etzadroxil) and a renal tubular transport blocking drug (probenecid). The role of probenecid is to increase the systemic exposure of the antibacterial drug, sulopenem. Each tablet contains 500 mg sulopenem etzadroxil and 500 mg probenecid. Sulopenem etzadroxil is a new molecular entity while probenecid was approved in the 1950s. The Applicant's proposed indication is the treatment of adult women \ge 18 years of age with uncomplicated urinary tract infections (uUTI) caused by designated susceptible microorganisms proven or strongly suspected to be nonsusceptible to a quinolone. The proposed dose is one tablet orally (PO) administered twice daily (BID) for 5 days.
L1601: ## 1.2. Conclusions on the Substantial Evidence of Effectiveness
L1602: The Applicant has not provided substantial evidence of effectiveness for sulopenem for the treatment of uUTI. In the prespecified subgroup of subjects with uUTI caused by a ciprofloxacin-nonsusceptible pathogen in Study 301, sulopenem was found to be superior to ciprofloxacin based on the primary endpoint of overall response (clinical response and microbiological response). However, in the prespecified subgroup of subjects with uUTI caused by a ciprofloxacin-susceptible pathogen in Study 301, sulopenem was inferior to ciprofloxacin. As clinicians usually do not obtain urine cultures when treating uUTI, it may be difficult to identify patients who may benefit from therapy with sulopenem. Additionally, in the related indications of complicated urinary tract infections (cUTI) (Study 302) and complicated intraabdominal infections (cIAI) (Study 303), sulopenem was not noninferior to the active comparator based on the primary efficacy endpoints in each trial. Of note, sulopenem was inferior to the active comparator in Study 302. Nonclinical PK/PD data suggest that the Applicant's proposed dose of sulopenem is suboptimal which may provide an explanation for the Phase 3 study results.
L1603: In order to provide substantial evidence of effectiveness, the Applicant should conduct at least one additional successful study in uUTI and consider using a different active comparator drug in the study(ies) that is more reflective of currently recommended treatment for uUTI. Additionally, the Agency recommends that the Applicant conduct further investigation to determine the optimal sulopenem dosing regimen for the proposed treatment indication(s).
L1604: ## 1.3. Benefit-Risk Assessment
L1605: ## Benefit-Risk Summary and Assessment
L1606: In this NDA, the Applicant seeks approval of sulopenem etzadroxil/probenecid bilayer oral tablet for the treatment of adult women \ge 18 years of age with uncomplicated urinary tract infections (uUTI) caused by designated susceptible microorganisms proven or strongly suspected to be nonsusceptible to a quinolone. uUTI is a common infection that affects most women at least once in their lives. Although there are many antibacterial drugs approved to treat uUTI, antimicrobial resistance may limit their use in certain patients. In addition, many of the antibacterial drugs available to treat resistant pathogens are only available for intravenous administration while oral therapy is preferred in the treatment of uUTI.
L1607: In uUTI Study 301, sulopenem was found to be superior to ciprofloxacin with respect to overall response (clinical response and microbiological response) in the prespecified subgroup of subjects with a ciprofloxacin-nonsusceptible pathogen. Overall response was attained by 77/160 (48%) of sulopenem subjects and 49/149 (33%) of ciprofloxacin subjects with a difference of 15% (95% CI, 4.4% to 26.1%; p-value 0.0062). However, among subjects with a ciprofloxacin-susceptible pathogen, sulopenem was found to be inferior to ciprofloxacin. The overall response was 218/365 (60%) for sulopenem and 296/410 (72%) for ciprofloxacin with a difference of -12.5% (95% CI, -19.1% to -5.9%). Of note, clinicians usually do not obtain urine cultures when treating uUTI. As a result, the role of sulopenem in treating uUTI is unclear and also raises concerns about how to distinguish an appropriate patient population. In addition, in the related indications of complicated urinary tract infections (cUTI) and complicated intraabdominal infections (cIAI), sulopenem was not noninferior to the active comparator based on the primary efficacy endpoints in each trial. Nonclinical PK/PD data suggest that the Applicant's proposed dose of sulopenem is suboptimal which may explain the results of the Phase 3 studies. Overall, there is insufficient evidence to support the findings of benefit for sulopenem in patients with a uUTI caused by a ciprofloxacin-nonsusceptible pathogen.
L1608: The primary safety database for this NDA consisted of 825 sulopenem subjects with uUTI from Study 301. This database was supported by the safety findings from the cUTI Study 302 and the cIAI Study 303; a total of 1855 subjects were exposed to sulopenem in the three Phase 3 trials. Taken together, there was an adequate safety database for this NDA. In Study 301, gastrointestinal adverse reactions, including diarrhea, nausea, and abdominal pain, were common among subjects taking oral sulopenem/probenecid. In particular, diarrhea occurred in 12% of sulopenem subjects in Study 301. However, the diarrhea and other GI adverse events were generally mild and not treatment-limiting. Elevations in ALT, generally less than 5x the upper limit of normal, occurred more commonly among sulopenem subjects compared to ciprofloxacin subjects in Study 301. However, there were no cases that met Hy's Law criteria in Study 301. Hypersensitivity reactions, including angioedema involving the face, were noted uncommonly in the studies. The identified safety issues (e.g., hypersensitivity reactions, GI adverse
L1609: reactions, and elevations in transaminases) can be addressed through labeling and do not preclude approval. Overall, there is an acceptable safety profile for sulopenem/probenecid.
L1610: In summary, while the safety profile for sulopenem is acceptable, there is insufficient evidence to support the effectiveness of sulopenem for the treatment of uUTI. In order to provide substantial evidence of effectiveness, the Applicant should conduct at least one additional successful study in uUTI and consider using a different active comparator drug in the study(ies) that is more reflective of currently recommended treatment for uUTI. Additionally, the Agency recommends that the Applicant conduct further investigation to determine the optimal sulopenem dosing regimen for the proposed treatment indication(s).

L1621: ## 2. Therapeutic Context
L1622: ## 2.1. Analysis of Condition
L1623: Uncomplicated urinary tract infections are characterized by local signs and symptoms including lower abdominal discomfort, dysuria, and urinary frequency that is associated with pyuria and a microbial pathogen on urine culture. uUTI, also referred to as acute cystitis, occur in females with normal anatomy of the urinary tract and are not accompanied by systemic signs or symptoms, such as fever greater than 38 degrees Celsius or costovertebral angle pain/tenderness. Urinary tract infections associated with systemic signs or symptoms, such as fever, and those occurring in males are referred to as cUTI.
L1624: uUTIs are common in women with normal genitourinary tracts. Up to 80 to 90% of women will have at least one uUTI during their life. Risk factors for uUTI include recent sexual intercourse, use of spermicides, and a history of prior UTI.
L1625: The most common bacterial cause of uUTI is *Escherichia coli* (75-95%); other less common pathogens associated with uUTI are *Staphylococcus saprophyticus*, *Klebsiella* species, and *Proteus* species. Rates of antibacterial drug resistance for *E. coli* have been increasing worldwide (see Section 2.2). It is important to note that in clinical practice uUTIs are often diagnosed based on symptoms and, if available, a dipstick urinalysis positive for leukocyte esterase or nitrates; urine culture is not regularly obtained unless there are risk factors for a drug-resistant pathogen.
L1626: Although baseline or follow up urine cultures are not usually obtained in the treatment of uUTI, clinicians generally expect that antibacterial drug treatment will result in eradication of the causative pathogen and sterilization of the urine. The goal of treatment in uUTI is to resolve the acute symptoms but also to reduce the risk of infection progression, including the development of pyelonephritis. Persistent bacteriuria following treatment is generally considered treatment failure. In two randomized studies of antibacterial drugs compared to NSAIDs, the rate of pyelonephritis in patients with uUTIs who were not treated with antibacterial drugs was between 2 to 5% compared to 0 to 0.4% in patients treated with antibacterial drugs (Gagyor et al. 2015; Kronenberg et al. 2017).
L1627: The association between bacteriuria, even when asymptomatic, and infectious complications has been shown in pregnant women. In studies from the 1960s and 1970s, between 20% to 30% of pregnant women with untreated asymptomatic bacteriuria developed pyelonephritis later in the course of pregnancy (Nicolle 2015). In a more recent study from the Netherlands (Kazemier et al. 2015), pyelonephritis occurred in 2.4% of pregnant women with asymptomatic bacteriuria who were not treated with antibacterial drugs, and in only 0.6% among pregnant women who did not have asymptomatic bacteriuria. Among the patients who were treated for asymptomatic bacteriuria, there were no cases of pyelonephritis. A similar finding is noted in the renal transplant literature. In a study of renal transplant patients from a transplant center in New York (Lee et al. 2013), having \ge 10 bacterial colony forming units (CFU)/mL in the urine
L1628: during the 3 months post-transplant was an independent risk factor for subsequent bacteremia (hazard ratio 2.4, 95% CI 1.2-4.8).
L1629: ## 2.2. Analysis of Current Treatment Options
L1630: The decision of which antibacterial drug to use to treat uUTI is often made empirically. However, if culture results are available, they are used to guide treatment choice. When making an empiric treatment choice, clinicians need to consider the local rates of antibacterial drug resistance. Determining the local rate of resistant pathogens for uUTI may be challenging as resistance rates obtained from passive surveillance may overestimate resistance as cultures are obtained more often from patients with risk factors for having a resistant pathogen (Ti et al. 2003). Still, passive surveillance from microbiology laboratories can be helpful, especially in detecting changes in resistance patterns. Two studies found that drug-resistant *E. coli* are becoming more common. In a U.S.-based study from 2000 to 2010, rates of *E. coli* resistance from outpatient urine cultures increased for ciprofloxacin (3% to 17%), TMP/SMX (18% to 24%), nitrofurantoin (0.8% to 1.6%), and ceftriaxone (0.2% to 2.3%) (Sanchez et al. 2012). In Olmsted County, Minnesota from 2005 to 2009, the rate of *E. coli* resistance identified from urine cultures increased for ampicillin (39% to 43%; P=0.02), cefazolin (4% to 7%; P&lt;.001), trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole (17% to 25%; P&lt;.001), fluoroquinolones (7% to 16%; P&lt;.001), fluoroquinolone plus trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole (4% to 10%; P&lt;.001), gentamicin (3% to 7%; P&lt;.001), and extended-spectrum cephalosporins (1% to 3%; P&lt;.001). The rate of nitrofurantoin-resistance did not increase (Swami et al. 2012).
L1631: Table 1 below summarizes the currently available treatment options for uUTI. Clinical efficacy for all the listed treatment options are generally high if the pathogen is susceptible to the antibacterial drug. Current treatment guidelines recommend trimethoprim/sulfamethoxazole, nitrofurantoin, or fosfomycin as first-line options for the treatment of uUTI.

L1641: ## 3.2. Summary of Presubmission/Submission Regulatory Activity
L1642: The development program was conducted under IND 129834 (intravenous [IV] sulopenem; opened 02 Mar 2016), IND 129849 (sulopenem etzadroxil/probenecid; opened 02 Mar 2016),
L1643: (b) (4)
L1644: The Division granted sulopenem qualified infectious disease product designation for uUTI, cUTI, and cIAI on 29 Jul 2016 and fast track designation for these same indications on 15 Mar 2019.
L1645: The Division and Iterum met in July 2017 to discuss the clinical trial design for Study 301 for the treatment of uUTI. The Division emphasized that the clinical response component of the overall response endpoint (combined clinical and microbiological responses) should be defined as the resolution of all UTI symptoms that were present at baseline. The Division also noted that for a noninferiority trial it is essential that only patients with pathogens susceptible to the comparator (ciprofloxacin) be included in the efficacy analysis. The Sponsor was concerned that excluding patients with a ciprofloxacin-resistant pathogen would remove a significant population from their study. In November 2017, Iterum submitted a proposal for statistical hypothesis testing for the uUTI trial in which there would be two analysis populations, one for subjects with a ciprofloxacin-susceptible pathogen at baseline (microbiological modified intent-to-treat susceptible [MMITTS]) and another for subjects with a ciprofloxacin-nonsusceptible pathogen at baseline (microbiological modified intent-to-treat resistant [MMITTR]). Superiority testing would be used in the MMITTR population while noninferiority testing using a 10% margin would be used in the MMITTS population. The following comment was sent to Iterum in response to this study design.
L1646: *We agree with the proposed framework for hypothesis testing and interim analysis. Because the analyses in the MMITTS and MMITTR populations can be viewed as answering separate research questions, we agree that it is not necessary to use alpha sharing or hierarchical testing to control the overall Type I error rate for the two primary analyses at the one-sided \alpha = 0.025 level. However, it is important to note that discordant results in the two primary analyses, for example, if the trial is only able to demonstrate that sulopenem is superior to ciprofloxacin in the MMITTR population, but is not able to demonstrate that sulopenem is noninferior to ciprofloxacin in the MMITTS population can be problematic. We will need to understand the reasons for the discrepant findings. Also, the discordant results may have significant labeling implications, such as, limited use language, limitation of use/warning regarding*

## {sulopenem etzadroxil/probenecid}
L1648: *empiric use. For a clinical condition such as uUTI, where therapy is generally empiric, the utility of a product for which efficacy is not demonstrated in the MMITTS population could be limited.*
L1649: A pre-NDA meeting was held on 28 Sep 2020. The Division reiterated their concern regarding the discordant results between the MMITTS and MMITTR populations and that the results did not support the use of sulopenem for uUTI caused by ciprofloxacin-susceptible isolates. In addition, the Division noted that there are limitations to exploratory analyses of studies that failed to meet their primary endpoint and that the data from Study 302 could not support a labeled indication for cUTI.

L1667: ## 4.2. Product Quality
L1668: The NDA, as amended, has provided sufficient Chemistry, Manufacturing, and Controls information to assure the identity, strength, purity, and quality of the proposed drug product, sulopenem etzadroxil and probenecid tablets. The drug product is a pink, oval-shaped, film-coated, immediate release, bilayer tablet, containing 500 mg sulopenem etzadroxil and 500 mg probenecid. The drug product formulation contains conventional excipients of compendial grade. The proposed commercial packaging configurations for the drug product include high density polyethylene bottles (10-count and 30-count) and aluminum foil blisters (94-count). The stability information submitted in the NDA supports the 24-month expiration dating for the drug product to be stored in the proposed commercial packaging systems at room temperature (20-25°C). Overall, the information provided in the NDA for the drug product (sulopenem etzadroxil and probenecid tablets) and both drug substances (sulopenem etzadroxil and probenecid) was found to be adequate. The manufacturing and testing facilities for this NDA are deemed acceptable and an overall "Approve" recommendation was entered into Panorama by the Office of Pharmaceutical Manufacturing Assessment on May 4, 2021.
L1669: The NDA is recommended for approval by the Office of Pharmaceutical Quality. For details, please refer to the Office of Pharmaceutical Quality Integrated Quality Assessment dated June 1, 2021 in DARRTS.

L1694: ## 4.3. Clinical Microbiology
L1695: Microbiological response analyses related to pathogen isolation, identification, and susceptibility testing with standard culture methods are covered in Section 16.5 of this review. A summary of the clinical microbiology review and recommendations is presented below:
L1696: ## 4.3.1. Mechanism of Action
L1697: Sulopenem, a penem antibacterial drug, inhibits bacterial cell wall synthesis by binding to penicillin-binding proteins (PBPs) resulting in cell death. In *Escherichia coli*, the relative order of affinity towards PBPs was PBP2&gt;PBP1A &gt; PBP1B &gt; PBP4&gt;PBP3&gt;PBP5/6. Similar to other carbapenems, sulopenem showed bactericidal killing by time-kill assay at concentrations \ge 4\times the minimum inhibitory concentration (MIC) against *E. coli* and *K. pneumoniae*.
L1698: ## 4.3.2. Antimicrobial Spectrum of Activity
L1699: Sulopenem demonstrates in vitro activity against both aerobic and anaerobic gram-positive and gram-negative bacteria. The in vitro \text{MIC}_{50/90} values (inhibits the growth of \ge 50\% and \ge 90\% of the isolates) were determined for sulopenem against isolates of relevant pathogens from 3 recent surveillance studies (North American and European isolates) and a single uUTI clinical study (ITO01-301). Against *E. coli* isolates, sulopenem had \text{MIC}_{50/90} values of 0.03/0.03-0.06 \mu\text{g}/\text{mL}; against *K. pneumoniae* isolates, sulopenem had \text{MIC}_{50/90} values of 0.03-0.06/0.06-0.12 \mu\text{g}/\text{mL}; and against *P. mirabilis* isolates, sulopenem had \text{MIC}_{50/90} values of 0.12-0.25/0.25-0.5 \mu\text{g}/\text{mL} reported.
L1700: ## 4.3.3. Resistance
L1701: Sulopenem resistant mutants were selected by conducting in vitro spontaneous mutation frequency studies using two *E. cloacae* isolates at a frequency of 1 \times 10^{-8} with a \le 2-fold MIC. In serial passage mutation studies, MIC values to sulopenem were observed to increase 16-fold during 15 serial passages in two of the three *E. coli* isolates tested and were unchanged for the third isolate. MIC values increased 8-fold during serial passage for one of the two *K. pneumoniae* isolates tested, and MIC values increased from 0.5 to 256 \mu\text{g}/\text{mL} for the other isolate. Resistance occurs primarily due to enzymatic inactivation of carbapenems by carbapenemases, but also can be caused by \beta-lactamase production, efflux pump expression, and changes in porins and/or PBPs. No instance of antagonism was observed in vitro between sulopenem and other routinely used antibacterial drugs against tested *E. coli* and *K. pneumoniae* isolates.
L1702: ## 4.3.4. Clinical Study
L1703: A single Phase 3 clinical study (IT001-301) was conducted to determine the safety and efficacy of a 5-day course of oral sulopenem etzadroxil/probenecid versus a 3-day course of oral ciprofloxacin (comparator arm) for the treatment of women (\ge 18 years of age) with uUTI. The microbiological modified intent-to-treat (mMITT) population comprised all subjects who had at least one or a maximum of two baseline urinary bacterial pathogen(s) identified from urine with \ge 10^5 CFU/mL. Bacterial urinary pathogens were identified from microbiological culture of acceptable urine specimens collected at baseline, and subsequent visits.
L1704: In the mMITT population, uUTIs were predominantly caused by *E. coli* (56.0% in sulopenem treatment group and 58.4% in ciprofloxacin treatment group), *K. pneumoniae* (6.5% in sulopenem treatment group and 6.0% in ciprofloxacin treatment group), and *P. mirabilis* (2.2% in sulopenem treatment group and 2.1% in ciprofloxacin treatment group).
L1705: ## 4.3.5. Breakpoints or Susceptibility Test Interpretive Criteria (STIC) for Sulopenem
L1706: The following is a summary of the Clinical Microbiology team's proposed breakpoints (BPs) rationale and labeling recommendations:
L1707: For setting the MIC BPs for sulopenem against *E. coli*, *K. pneumoniae*, and *P. mirabilis*, the Clinical Microbiology team relied primarily on microbiological eradication rates at each MIC dilution of clinical isolates, and the in vitro MIC data from clinical and surveillance isolates. The pharmacokinetics/pharmacodynamics (PK/PD) target index for sulopenem was predicted to be either T &gt; \text{MIC} or \text{Cmax}/\text{MIC} based on plasma concentration; however, the results are not definitive. Typically, beta-lactam drugs exhibit T &gt; \text{MIC}. The Clinical Pharmacology team has concerns with the validity of PK/PD study results. The microbiological success in relation to MIC values of baseline *E. coli*, *K. pneumoniae*, and *P. mirabilis* isolates from the sulopenem treatment group in mMITT population at test-of-cure (TOC) visit are summarized below:
L1708: ## NDA Multi-disciplinary Review and Evaluation {NDA 213972}
## {sulopenem etzadroxil/probenecid}
L1709: - Among 437 baseline *E. coli* isolates with an MIC range of 0.015 to 1.0 µg/mL, the overall microbiological eradication rate at TOC was 76.4%. The highest sulopenem MIC corresponding to microbiological success was 0.25 µg/mL and 3/5 (60%) isolates were eradicated. There was only one baseline *E. coli* isolate with sulopenem MIC of 1 µg/mL and it was associated with microbiological persistence. No baseline isolate with an MIC \ge2 µg/mL was observed. The MIC50/90 was 0.03/0.06 µg/mL against all *E. coli* isolates from both surveillance and clinical studies. Therefore, a susceptible BP of 0.25 µg/mL appears reasonable and will cover most of the *E. coli* population.
- Among 48 baseline *K. pneumoniae* isolates with an MIC range 0.015 to 8.0 µg/mL, the overall microbiological eradication rate at TOC was 77.1%. The highest sulopenem MIC that corresponded to a favorable microbiological outcome was 0.12 µg/mL and 7/8 (87.5%) isolates at this MIC were eradicated. No baseline isolates were observed with MIC values between 0.25 to 2.0 µg/mL. However, 2 baseline isolates with MIC values of 4 and 8 µg/mL were identified and eradicated. The MIC50/90 was 0.03/0.12 µg/mL against all *K. pneumoniae* isolates from the surveillance and clinical studies. Therefore, a susceptible BP of 0.25 µg/mL appears reasonable and will cover most of the *K. pneumoniae* population.
- Among 17 baseline *P. mirabilis* isolates with an MIC range of 0.03 to 0.25 µg/mL, the overall microbiological eradication rate at TOC was 82.4%. The highest sulopenem MIC that corresponded to microbiological success was 0.25 µg/mL and 10/10 (100%) isolates at this MIC were successfully eradicated. No baseline isolate was available with MIC values \ge0.5 µg/mL. Against *P. mirabilis* isolates from both surveillance and clinical studies, the MIC50/90 values were between 0.12/0.25 to 0.25/0.5µg/mL. Therefore, a susceptible BP of 0.25 µg/mL appears reasonable and should cover most *P. mirabilis* isolates.
L1710: In summary, microbiological success was observed in patients with baseline isolates of *E. coli* and *P. mirabilis* that had MIC values of \le0.015 to 0.25 µg/mL. No baseline *E. coli* isolate had an MIC of 0.5 µg/mL but a single isolate at an MIC of 1.0 µg/mL was associated with microbiological failure. No baseline *P. mirabilis* isolate had an MIC \ge0.5 µg/mL. Microbiological success was observed in patients with baseline *K. pneumoniae* isolates that had MIC values of \le0.015 to 0.12 µg/mL. No baseline *K. pneumoniae* isolates with MIC values between 0.25 to 2 µg/mL were observed; however, two isolates at MIC 4 and 8 µg/mL were observed and eradicated. Therefore, susceptible (S)/intermediate (I)/resistant (R) MIC BPs of \le0.25/0.5/\ge1.0 µg/mL against all three uUTI pathogens appeared to be reasonable and will cover most isolates.
L1711: The Applicant proposed sulopenem MIC BPs (S/I/R) of [REDACTED](b) (4) µg/mL for Enterobacteriales. However, as noted above, the Clinical Microbiology team recommends the revised MIC BPs (S/I/R) of \le0.25/0.5/\ge1.0 µg/mL for sulopenem against *E. coli*, *K. pneumoniae*, and *P. mirabilis* for uUTI indication. The disk diffusion zone diameter BPs have been calculated accordingly. The Clinical Microbiology team's recommended sulopenem MIC and disk diffusion BPs are summarized in Table 5.
