L2757: *M.O. Comment: The incidence of TEAEs in the overall population was 24.8% in the sulopenem arm and 13.9% in the ciprofloxacin arm while the incidence of diarrhea was 12.4% in the sulopenem arm and 2.5% in the ciprofloxacin arm. Subjects with Hispanic/Latino ethnicity, those with BMI &gt;30, and those in the United States were more likely to have a TEAE compared to the overall population. Among these groups, the difference in the incidence of TEAEs between the arms was mostly accounted for by diarrhea as it was in the general population. Review of the demographic data shows that most subjects with Hispanic/Latino ethnicity and BMI &gt;30 were enrolled in the United States. The higher rates of TEAEs and diarrhea in these subjects may be due to different physiological responses based on ethnicity or obesity or could be related to differences in AE reporting by country/site. An example of likely reporting differences is that the rate of TEAEs in Ukraine was notably lower than in Russia or the United States and there were no TEAEs of diarrhea reported from Ukraine.*
L2758: ## 8.2.8. Specific Safety Studies/Clinical Trials
L2759: There were no dedicated safety studies for this NDA.
L2760: ## 8.2.9. Additional Safety Explorations
L2761: ## Human Carcinogenicity or Tumor Development
L2762: In the Phase 3 integrated safety population, there were 5 subjects with a TEAE in the neoplasms SOC, 4 in the sulopenem arm and 1 in the comparator arm. These cases were discussed in the deaths and significant adverse events subsections above. Review of these subjects found that most cases were related to preexisting cancer.
L2763: ## NDA Multi-disciplinary Review and Evaluation {NDA 213972}
## {sulopenem etzadroxil/probenecid}
L2764: *M.O. Comment: Given the short duration of treatment, it does not appear that any of the cases of cancer were related to the study drug. Overall, there is no clinical evidence that sulopenem is carcinogenic.*
L2765: ## Human Reproduction and Pregnancy
L2766: Pregnant women were excluded from all clinical studies of sulopenem. However, there was one pregnancy reported in a patient who received sulopenem in the integrated Phase 3 safety population. The subject had a negative local urine pregnancy test at screening, but the central laboratory test was reported positive 3 days later. The study drug (oral sulopenem/probenecid for uUTI) was stopped at that time. The subject had an uneventful pregnancy and delivered a healthy infant 8 months later.
L2767: *M.O. Comment: There are insufficient data to draw any conclusions regarding the effects of sulopenem on human reproduction and pregnancy.*
L2768: ## Pediatrics and Assessment of Effects on Growth
L2769: There are no data on the safety of sulopenem in pediatric patients less than 18 years of age. The Sponsor submitted an agreed initial pediatric study plan (iPSP) on 21 February 2018. The label for probenecid includes a contraindication for children under the age of 2 years. After consultation with the pediatric team in the Division of Pediatric and Maternal Health, no apparent scientific basis for this pediatric contraindication was found. As a result, no pediatric contraindication will be added to the sulopenem/probenecid label.
L2770: ## Overdose, Drug Abuse Potential, Withdrawal, and Rebound
L2771: Sulopenem does not have known drug abuse potential.
L2772: ## 8.2.10. Safety in the Postmarket Setting
L2773: ## Safety Concerns Identified Through Postmarket Experience
L2774: Sulopenem is not approved for use in any country.
L2775: ## Expectations on Safety in the Postmarket Setting
L2776: If approved, the oral tablet formulation of sulopenem may be used off-label to treat uUTI caused by quinolone-susceptible pathogens and for stepdown therapy for other infections such as cUTI and cIAI. There are no distinct safety concerns regarding this possible off-label use, but the Phase 3 studies for cUTI and cIAI did not meet their primary efficacy endpoints.
L2777: ## 8.2.11. Integrated Assessment of Safety
L2778: The safety data for sulopenem in the treatment of uUTI were derived from Study 301 which evaluated 5 days of oral sulopenem compared to 3 days of oral ciprofloxacin. The subjects in
L2779: ## NDA Multi-disciplinary Review and Evaluation {NDA 213972}
## {sulopenem etzadroxil/probenecid}
L2780: Study 301 were all adult women. Additional safety data were reviewed from Study 302 in cUTI and Study 303 in cIAI which included use of both the IV and oral formulations of sulopenem. The Phase 1 and Phase 2 studies confirmed the safety findings of the Phase 3 studies. The collective safety issues identified from these sources will be summarized in this section.
L2781: Two subjects taking oral sulopenem/probenecid experienced angioedema involving the face and one also had associated dyspnea. One subject was enrolled in Study 301 and another in one of the Phase 1 studies. Both subjects stopped the study drug due to the angioedema events. Both subjects took antihistamine drugs and neither experienced any sequelae from these events. Regardless, angioedema associated with dyspnea suggests involvement of the airway which could be life-threatening. Hypersensitivity is included as a warning in the proposed labeling.
L2782: Gastrointestinal adverse events, including diarrhea, nausea, and abdominal pain, were common among subjects taking oral sulopenem/probenecid. In Study 301, 17% of sulopenem subjects experienced a GI adverse event compared to 8% of ciprofloxacin subjects. In particular, diarrhea was a prominent adverse event associated with sulopenem with 12% experiencing at least one event of diarrhea. However, the diarrhea and other GI adverse events were generally mild and not treatment-limiting. The duration of diarrhea appeared to be reduced when sulopenem was taken with food. GI adverse events and diarrhea will be noted in section 6 of the labeling and the review team will consider recommending that sulopenem be taken with food to reduce the incidence and/or duration of diarrhea.
L2783: Elevations in ALT were more common among sulopenem subjects compared to ciprofloxacin subjects in Study 301. This was also noted in the integrated Phase 3 population which included Studies 302 and 303. In Study 301, the elevations in ALT were generally less than 5x the upper limit of normal. There were no cases of Hy's Law in Study 301. However, there was a subject in Study 302 who met Hy's Law criteria on Day 5, but subsequently had normal liver enzyme tests. The Sponsor reports the cause of the liver test elevations was a drug-drug interaction between valproic acid and sulopenem. (b) (4)
L2784: Elevated transaminases will be noted in section 6 of the labeling.
L2785: Other nonserious adverse events that occurred uncommonly, but more frequently among sulopenem subjects compared to the comparator subjects include dizziness, rash, abnormal urine odor, and vulvovaginal yeast infection. All these adverse reactions will be included in section 6 of the labeling.
L2786: Overall, the safety issues with oral sulopenem/probenecid do not preclude approval; the known risks of sulopenem can be managed by appropriate labeling.
L2787: ## 8.3. Statistical Issues
L2788: One Phase 3 study is included in this NDA for the indication of treatment of uUTI. We have identified the following statistical issues related to this study.
L2789: ## NDA Multi-disciplinary Review and Evaluation {NDA 213972}
## {sulopenem etzadroxil/probenecid}
L2790: ## Late Change of SAP
L2791: After the unblinded interim analysis in October 2019, the conditional power was noted to be less than 40% in the MMITTR (ciprofloxacin-nonsusceptible) population. On March 11, 2020, the SAP was changed to revise the definitions of the MMITT populations and microbiological response based on PCR and antibacterial susceptibility data. The Division did not agree with these changes. Instead, the Division analyzed efficacy based on the original SAP. Although the study results remained significant, they were not as significant as initially reported.
L2792: ## Late Decision of Removing Study Site 202
L2793: Sites 202 and 218 were removed from the efficacy analyses by the Applicant. Site 202 was removed due to unreliable laboratory results. Site 218 was removed due to the concern of study misconduct. For Site 218, the Division agreed with the removal. However, for Site 202, the Division did not find sufficient justifications for its removal. Therefore, Site 202 was included in the Division's efficacy analysis.
L2794: As noted, these changes were made after the unblinded interim analysis for the resistant population and led to a larger treatment effect with a more significant p-value as compared to the Division's analysis using the original SAP.
L2795: ## 8.4. Conclusions and Recommendations
L2796: This NDA contains one Phase 3 clinical trial in uUTI (Study 301) for the proposed indication. The Applicant also submitted the data from one Phase 3 study in cUTI (Study 302) and one Phase 3 study in cIAI (Study 303) as supportive information. The Division has the following conclusions:
L2797: When using the original, agreed-upon SAP and including Site 202 we found there was a lower level of statistical significance for the difference in overall response rate by treatment arm in the ciprofloxacin-resistant (MMITTR) population than was initially reported (p&gt;0.001 vs. p&lt;0.00001) in Study 301.
L2798: Regarding the lack of other evidence of efficacy, we note that in Study 301, significantly inferior results were observed in the overall response rate for sulopenem compared to ciprofloxacin in the ciprofloxacin susceptible (MMITTS) population. In addition, significantly inferior results for sulopenem were observed in the complicated urinary tract infections trial (Study 302) and there was a lack of noninferiority of sulopenem in the complicated intra-abdominal infections trial (Study 303).
L2799: From a safety perspective, there is an adequate safety database for oral sulopenem/probenecid. Identified safety issues include hypersensitivity reactions, elevated liver enzymes, and GI adverse reactions. Overall, the safety issues with oral sulopenem/probenecid do not preclude approval; the known risks of sulopenem can be managed by appropriate labeling.
L2800: ## NDA Multi-disciplinary Review and Evaluation {NDA 213972}
## {sulopenem etzadroxil/probenecid}
L2801: The Division recommends that the NDA receive a Complete Response given the lack of substantial evidence of effectiveness and that the Applicant consider the following future steps:
L2802: - Re-evaluate the proposed dose/dosing regimen given the issues associated with PK-PD/target attainment.
- Conduct a second Phase 3 uUTI study to provide additional evidence of effectiveness.
- Use a more relevant comparator given the current standard of care, such as nitrofurantoin.
L2803: ## 9. Advisory Committee Meeting and Other External Consultations
L2804: No advisory committee meeting was held, and no external consultations were obtained as there were no issues that needed input from external experts.
L2805: ## 10. Pediatrics
L2806: There are currently no clinical data available on the safety and efficacy of sulopenem in children and adolescents &lt;18 years old. Iterum submitted their initial pediatric study plan (iPSP) for sulopenem for the treatment of uUTI, (b) (4) on 19 Sep 2017. (b) (4)
L2807: The Division (b) (4) recommended that Iterum study uUTI in children 2 years and older and consider requesting a partial waiver from studying uUTI in children less than 2 years old. The iPSP was discussed with PeRC on 8 Nov 2017. PeRC agreed with the Division's recommendation for a partial waiver in pediatric patients less than 2 years of age for uUTI (treated using the oral formulation) and with granting a deferral (b) (4) After Division feedback, Iterum resubmitted their pediatric study plan on 21 Feb 2018 including revisions based on Agency feedback. The Division confirmed agreement of the iPSP on 26 Feb 2018. Of note, PeRC also reviewed the revised iPSP in February 2018 and reiterated their agreement with the partial waiver in pediatric patients less than 2 years of age for uUTI and with granting the deferral of all pediatric studies as presented in the Agreed iPSP.

L2871: ## Human PK Studies in Healthy Volunteers
L2872: ## Single Ascending Dose
L2873: Study A8811001 was a single ascending dose study to characterize the PK, safety, and tolerability of two sulopenem oral prodrugs, PF-03678685 and PF-03709270 (i.e., sulopenem etzadroxil) in healthy adult volunteers. Eighteen male subjects aged 21 to 52 years with a mean body mass index (BMI) of 24.0 kg/m2 were enrolled and randomized to 2 cohorts to receive one of the two sulopenem oral prodrugs or placebo according to the schematic in Table 118.
L2874: **Table 118. Treatments Received in Cohorts 1 and 2**
L2875: Sequence	N	Period 1	Period 2	Period 3	Period 4
Cohort 1
1	3	Placebo	1000 mg	2000 mg	600 mg
2	3	400 mg	Placebo	2000 mg	600 mg
3	3	400 mg	1000 mg	Placebo	Placebo
Cohort 2
1	3	Placebo	1000 mg	2000 mg	
2	3	400 mg	Placebo	2000 mg	
3	3	400 mg	1000 mg	Placebo
L2876: Source: Tables S2 and S3 of Applicant's ISR A8811001
L2877: All doses were administered following an 8 h fast; subjects were required to refrain from eating or drinking anything except water for another 4 h post-dosing. Sulopenem prodrugs were administered as oral powders (supplied as 100 mg, 300 mg, and 500 mg dose strengths) for reconstitution. Dose escalations within each cohort were based upon available preliminary safety, tolerability, and PK from previous dosing periods. Whole blood and plasma PK samples were collected pre-dose and at pre-specified times post-dose for measurement of sulopenem, sulopenem prodrugs and formate (a by-product of prodrug hydrolysis) using validated liquid chromatography with tandem mass spectrometry (LC-MS/MS) methods. Pharmacokinetic assessments included: Cmax, Tmax, area under the curve (AUC) and t1/2.
L2878: Per the Applicant, this study was expected to inform the selection of an appropriate sulopenem prodrug for future studies. Both prodrugs were well-tolerated and there were no study discontinuations due to adverse events (AEs). One subject in the sulopenem etzadroxil cohort was no longer willing to participate and withdrew from the study after receiving single doses of 400 and 1000 mg in Periods 1 and 2, respectively. Following Period 1, all subjects from the PF-03678685 cohort were discontinued from the study because exposures of sulopenem from the 400 mg dose were considered too low to warrant further study. Because PF-03678685, sulopenem etzadroxil and formate were not detected in whole blood or plasma samples at any dose level, PK parameters are only summarized for sulopenem (Table 119).

L2891: ## Single and Multiple Ascending Dose
L2892: Study A8811003 was a PK, safety, and tolerability study of single and multiple ascending doses of sulopenem etzadroxil that also evaluated the effect of probenecid on sulopenem exposure. Seventy-two healthy male adult subjects were planned for enrollment into 6 cohorts (N=12/cohort). Dose escalation was contingent upon the absence of serious AEs and dose-limiting intolerance. The planned dosing schemes for Cohorts 1 through 6 are summarized in Table 121 and Table 122. Subjects in the multiple dose cohorts were dosed for 10 days using a sulopenem etzadroxil powder in bottle formulation at dose strengths of 600 mg and 2000 mg.

L2904: All doses were administered under fasted conditions. Blood samples were collected pre-dose and at pre-specified times post-dosing for measurement of sulopenem, formate and 2-ethylbutyric acid. Pharmacokinetic assessments included: Cmax, Tmax, AUC0-inf, AUC0-last, AUC0-tau, Rac and t1/2. A 24 h urine collection was also performed for subjects in the multiple dose cohorts on Day 6. Blood and urine samples were assayed using validated LC-MS/MS methods.
L2905: *Reviewer's Comment: In addition to the release of sulopenem, hydrolysis of the sulopenem etzadroxil prodrug ester bond yields formate and 2-ethylbutyric acid as by-products.*
L2906: Ultimately, 11 male healthy volunteers aged 22-48 years (mean = 30.6 years) were enrolled in Cohort 1, where 2 of 5 study discontinuations were due to treatment-emergent adverse event (TEAEs). Each subject in this cohort reported at least 1 TEAE, with diarrhea being most frequently reported. Single doses of 2000 mg and 4000 mg were considered well-tolerated while doses of 6000 mg and 8000 mg were poorly tolerated due to a greater frequency and severity of AEs. Twenty-four healthy volunteers aged 23-51 years (twenty-three males and one female), were enrolled in Cohorts 2 and 3, three of whom discontinued the study due to AEs. Overall, 12 of the 24 subjects in Cohorts 2 and 3 reported at least 1 adverse event. As with the single ascending dose portion of this study, diarrhea was the most frequently observed AE, occurring in 18 (75%) of subjects. Due to the prevalence and severity of treatment-related gastrointestinal AEs observed in Cohort 2 (where sulopenem etzadroxil 2000 mg twice daily [BID] was administered), Cohorts 4 through 6 of this study were not enrolled. Multiple dose administration of 1200 mg sulopenem etzadroxil with 1000 mg probenecid (Cohort 3) was better tolerated than multiple doses of 2000 mg sulopenem etzadroxil.
L2907: ## NDA Multi-disciplinary Review and Evaluation {NDA 213972}
## {sulopenem etzadroxil/probenecid}
L2908: Following oral administration of single doses of 2000 mg to 8000 mg, AUC increased in an approximately dose proportional manner while C_{max} increased less than dose proportionally (Table 123). Mean sulopenem exposures in Cohort 3, where subjects received 1200 mg sulopenem etzadroxil with 1000 mg probenecid BID were moderately higher than exposures observed in Cohort 2 following administration of 2000 mg sulopenem etzadroxil BID (Table 62). The terminal half-life of sulopenem was ~1.44 h with probenecid and 1.27h in the absence of probenecid. Interindividual variability was moderate (18 to 26%) for both AUC and C_{max} on Days 1 and 10 with and without probenecid. Mean accumulation ratios were below 1 for both Cohorts 2 and 3 due to an inexplicable reduction in both AUC and C_{max} on Day 10 compared to Day 1. This reduction was less pronounced when sulopenem etzadroxil was administered with probenecid (6%) versus without (30%).
L2909: The 24-hour urinary excretion accounted for approximately 16 to 17% of the total parent dose (i.e. active sulopenem component) in both Cohort 2 and 3. In the presence of probenecid, Cl_r decreased by ~65% compared to administration of sulopenem etzadroxil alone. Formate was unquantifiable at any dose levels evaluated in this study and concentrations of 2-EBA were below the lower limit of quantification (LLOQ) at most time points.

L2920: ## Absolute Bioavailability and Food Effect
L2921: Study IT001-105 was an open label, single-center, four sequence, three period study to assess the safety, tolerability, and absolute bioavailability of the to-be-marketed sulopenem etzadroxil and probenecid bilayer tablet in the fed and fasted state. This study also evaluated the PK, safety, and tolerability of two other sulopenem formulations: an oral powder-in-bottle (PIB) sulopenem etzadroxil formulation and intravenous (IV) sulopenem. Additionally, this study was used to bridge the probenecid layer of the bilayer tablet and commercial probenecid by comparing the PK of probenecid following administration of the bilayer tablet to that of
L2922: ## NDA Multi-disciplinary Review and Evaluation {NDA 213972}
## {sulopenem etzadroxil/probenecid}
L2923: probenecid, USP tablet (an FDA-approved generic drug version of Benemid). Shown in Table 125 are the details of drug administration in each cohort of the study.

L2926: Reviewer's Comment: Per the Applicant, the objective of including Cohort 2 was to investigate the effect of a single 500 mg dose of sulopenem etzadroxil on the PK of sulopenem when separated by a 7-day washout period. Given the decrease in sulopenem exposure following multiple dose administration of sulopenem etzadroxil (in Study A8811003), this evaluation was deemed necessary to determine whether a period effect may explain this observation. However, it is the reviewer's opinion that given sulopenem's short half-life, the dosing regimen indicated for Cohort 2 is insufficient to address the stated question.
L2927: Per the Applicant, the proposed dosing regimen for Study Period 2 of Cohort 4 was intended to evaluate any potential food effect on the PK of IV sulopenem. Given that food does not impact the absorption of parenteral administration, no food effect is expected.
L2928: Both oral sulopenem etzadroxil formulations contain 366 mg of the sulopenem active component. For this reason, 366 mg IV sulopenem was used to assess the absolute bioavailability of the oral formulations. Drug administration across cohorts proceeded as described below:
L2929: - Period 1 - After an overnight fast of at least 10 h, subjects received their assigned single dose treatments and continued fasting for at least 4 h post-dosing.
- Period 2 - Following a 7-day washout, subjects were readmitted into their assigned cohorts to receive the same treatments as indicated for Period 1. With the exception of Cohort 2, all other cohorts were provided a standard high-fat breakfast (~800-1000 kCal total, 50% fat) 30 min before dosing. Subjects in Cohort 2 received their assigned treatment under the same fasted conditions outlined for Period 1.
- Period 3 - Following another 7-day washout period, subjects were readmitted into their assigned cohorts. Cohorts 1-3 received 366 mg sulopenem IV infused over 1 h while Cohort 4 received 1000 mg sulopenem IV infused over 3 h in combination with a 500 mg oral probenecid tablet.
L2930: ## NDA Multi-disciplinary Review and Evaluation {NDA 213972}
## {sulopenem etzadroxil/probenecid}
L2931: ## *PK Sampling and Assessments*
L2932: Plasma PK samples were collected on Day 1 at pre-dose and at pre-specified times through 12 h post-dosing. The following plasma PK parameters of sulopenem were calculated: C_{max}, T_{max}, AUC_{0-last}, AUC_{0-inf}, AUC_{extrap}, V_z, V_z/F, clearance (CL), and t_{1/2}. Plasma samples were assayed for sulopenem and formate using validated LC/MS/MS methods. Whole blood samples were also assayed for PF-03678685 and PF-03709270 (sulopenem etzadroxil) using a validated LC-MS/MS method.
L2933: The PK population was comprised of subjects who received any study drug and had sufficient data to calculate at least 1 pre-planned PK parameter. Absolute bioavailability was calculated for both the bilayer tablet and PIB under fasting conditions using 366 mg IV as reference. The effect of food on the PK of sulopenem was also determined using a paired t-test on the natural-log transformed C_{max} and AUCs of the fed versus fasted state. Similarly, for Cohorts 2 and 4, paired t-test on the log transformed C_{max} and AUCs was used for comparison of Periods 1 and 2.
L2934: ## *Demographics*
L2935: Forty-six healthy male and female subjects with mean age 35.8 years and BMI of 25.76 kg/m2 were enrolled in this study. The majority of the subjects (87%) were male and Black (67.4%). No previous or concomitant medications were recorded for any subjects in this study. Although the study's inclusion criteria indicated that subjects with estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) \ge 85 mL/min/1.73m2 were to be enrolled in the study, three subjects in Cohort 1, one subject in Cohort 2 and one subject in Cohort 3 with eGFR values in the range of 75 mL/min/1.73m2 to 83 mL/min/1.73 m2 participated in the study.
L2936: *Reviewer's Comment:* Of the five subjects indicated as having an eGFR in the range of 75 mL/min/1.73m2 to 83 mL/min/1.73 m2 under protocol deviations, individualized eGFR values ranged from 94 mL/min to 113 mL/min. Individualization of eGFRs for all other subjects enrolled in this study identified only two subjects (both in Cohort 1) whose eGFR fell within the range of 83 to 88 mL/min and would thus be categorized as having mild renal impairment according to the FDA's guidance on pharmacokinetics in patients with impaired renal function. L2942: ## *Results*
L2943: All formulations of sulopenem were well-tolerated. Of the 46 subjects enrolled in the study, 2 subjects discontinued the study (for reasons unrelated to AEs). In the fasted state, 2 subjects (14.3%) in the bilayer tablet cohort and 7 (35.0%) in the PIB cohort experienced TEAEs. Only 1 of these AEs were gastrointestinal (GI) in nature; all others were characterized as abnormal urine odor. In the fed state, only 1 subject receiving sulopenem etzadroxil reported TEAE, which again was abnormal urine odor.
L2944: The absolute bioavailability of sulopenem for the PIB formulation was 31% in the fasted state and 38% in the fed state. Absolute bioavailability for the bilayer tablet (i.e., sulopenem etzadroxil in combination with probenecid) was 40%, as shown in Table 127. During Period 2, a subject in Cohort 1 registered unusually low plasma concentrations of sulopenem and probenecid in the fed state in spite of having adequate concentrations of both drugs in the fasted state. No definitive explanation for this observation could be provided, except for potential subject non-compliance. Therefore, this subject was re-dosed in the fed state. When PK data from redosing this subject in the fed state was included in analyses, it was determined that a high fat meal increased the mean absolute bioavailability of sulopenem for the bilayer tablet to 64.4% (Table 128). Sensitivity analysis conducted by exclusion of data from this subject resulted in a similar estimated bioavailability (i.e. 64.6%) in the fed state.

L2960: ## ADME
L2961: ## Study A8811006
L2962: Study A8811006 evaluated the metabolic profile, safety, tolerability, and routes of excretion of sulopenem in 4 healthy adult male subjects following administration of a single 2000 mg oral dose of [^{14}C]sulopenem etzadroxil containing ~200 \mu Ci of radiocarbon under fasted conditions. Blood samples were collected pre-dose and at 0.5, 1, 1.5, 2, 3, 4, 5, 8, 12, 24, 48, 72 and 96 h post-dosing into heparin-coated tubes for determination of plasma CP-70429 (sulopenem) concentrations. At these same timepoints, blood samples were also obtained for measurement of total plasma radioactivity. For profiling and identification of [^{14}C]sulopenem etzadroxil metabolites in plasma, blood samples were obtained pre-dose and at the 0.5, 1, 3, 6 and 12 h post-dosing.
L2963: Urine samples were collected pre-dose and pooled (per subject) at intervals of 0-8, 24-48, 48-72, 72-96, 96-120, 120-144 and 144-168 h post-dosing for analysis of total radioactivity and identification of metabolites. The daily urine collections were considered complete if the 24 h urinary excretion of creatinine was 20 to 25 mg/kg. A pre-dose fecal sample was obtained on Day 0 and post-dosing feces were collected (and pooled by subject at 24 h intervals) until up to
L2964: ## NDA Multi-disciplinary Review and Evaluation {NDA 213972}
## {sulopenem etzadroxil/probenecid}
L2965: 168 h. All toilet papers that came into contact with feces was also collected. Subjects were discharged before Day 7 if either ~90% of the administered radioactivity was recovered from urine and feces, or 24 h urine and fecal samples from 2 consecutive collections each had radioactivity levels amounting to ~1% of the total administered radioactivity.
L2966: ## *Analytical Methods*
L2967: Quantitation of sulopenem in plasma was performed using a validated LC-MS/MS method with an LLOQ of 25.0 ng/mL and upper limit of quantification of 5,000 ng/mL. Radioanalysis of plasma and urine sample was conducted using liquid scintillation counting (LSC) for at least 5 min or 100,000 counts. For radioanalysis of feces, samples were combusted and analyzed by LSC. Oxidation efficiency was evaluated daily by analyzing a commercial radiolabeled standard both directly in scintillation cocktail and by oxidation. Acceptance criteria were combustion recoveries of 95 to 105%. The sensitivity of detection of radioactivity was 100 dpm.
L2968: For metabolite profiling, plasma samples were pooled per the Hamilton method (i.e. across timepoints for each subject). For urine, samples were pooled from 0-48 h for each subject and for feces, fecal homogenates containing the highest levels of excreted radioactivity (i.e. samples obtained between 0-120 h) were pooled per subject for analysis. Metabolite quantification was performed by measuring the areas of individually separated high-performance liquid chromatography (HPLC) peaks by HPLC with radio-detection. Identification of the metabolites from HPLC column eluent was performed by mass spectrometry.
L2969: ## *Results*
L2970: PK parameters for sulopenem and total radioactivity were determined from plasma concentration-time data. Quantitation of metabolites in biological matrices was expressed as percentage of dose in urine and feces, and percentage of sample for plasma. The mean of total recovered radioactivity was 85.1% (range 80.2 to 95.0%), most of which was recovered within the first 72 h (Table 70). Although the mean total recovered radioactivity was &lt;90%, both urine and fecal samples from 2 consecutive collections had radioactivity levels approximately less than 1% of the total administered dose for all subjects. The percentages of radioactivity recovered in urine and feces were similar, i.e., 44.3% vs. 40.8%, respectively (Table 132).

L2976: *Reviewer's Comment: By 48 h, 43% of total radioactivity was recovered in urine. Within the first 48 h, fecal recoveries were highly variable; 2 subjects had unusually low fecal recoveries (mean = 3.13%) compared to the other 2 (mean = 31.2%). No dosing or sampling issues were reported that could explain these observations.*
L2977: The prodrug, sulopenem etzadroxil, was undetected at any timepoint. The proposed biotransformation pathway of the prodrug is provided in Figure 5. Based on AUC_{0-last}, sulopenem accounted for 32% of circulating plasma total radioactivity (Figure 6) and the mean observed terminal half-life of sulopenem in plasma was 1.1 h. Quantifiable levels of radioactivity were observed in plasma through 96 h post-dose. However, this collection interval was insufficient to estimate the terminal half-life of total radioactivity in plasma. Aside from sulopenem, major circulating metabolites were the 2 diastereomers, M1a and M1b, accounting for 21.8% and 43.6%, respectively. These inactive metabolites are formed by hydrolysis of the sulopenem \beta-lactam ring (Figure 5). Sulopenem was the major metabolite recovered in urine, accounting for 26.9% of the administered dose (based on 0-48 h pooled urine). In feces, sulopenem only accounted for 3.1% of administered dose (based on 0-120 h pooled feces). In feces, the majority of metabolites are proposed to be derived from sulfoxide reduction by gut microbial activity. In urine, M1a and M1b accounted for 7.4% and 2.5%, respectively, of the administered dose.
L2978: *Reviewer's Comment: In vitro studies evaluating the stability and release of sulopenem in human blood, and simulated gastric and intestinal fluids provided the following key observations:*
L2979: - *In human blood, sulopenem concentrations did not exceed ~30% of sulopenem etzadroxil input, indicating possible biotransformation in blood.*
- *Sulopenem etzadroxil was slowly degraded in simulated gastric fluid containing pepsin; however, this did not produce detectable concentrations of sulopenem, suggesting the formation of other degradants.*
- *In enzyme-free simulated intestinal fluid, sulopenem etzadroxil was stable. However, in simulated intestinal fluid containing porcine pancreatin, sulopenem etzadroxil was rapidly degraded.*
- *It was observed that in porcine small intestinal fluid, sulopenem etzadroxil was rapidly degraded, and sulopenem was undetectable.*
L2980: Although these studies did not elucidate the structural identity of the other degradants from the prodrug, the observations lend some additional insight on the fate of sulopenem etzadroxil and sulopenem. The low percentage of plasma radioactivity attributable to sulopenem may be explained in part by substantial and rapid degradation of the prodrug both by gastric enzymes and in blood.

L2986: ## Renal Impairment
L2987: Study A8811009 was an open-label, 2-way crossover study which evaluated the PK, safety, and tolerability of IV sulopenem and oral sulopenem etzadroxil in subjects with varying degrees of renal function. Mass balance studies indicated that renal clearance accounted for ~50% of total sulopenem excretion. Because of the apparent importance of renal clearance and the likelihood that sulopenem will be administered in patients with renal impairment, this study was necessary to determine the impact of renal impairment on the PK of sulopenem.
L2988: The study was designed to enroll 8 subjects per renal function group (except for the severe renal impairment cohort, where N=5). Subjects were selected based on their estimated CLcr based on the Cockcroft Gault equation and were classified as follows:
L2989: - Group 1: Normal Renal Function (CLcr &gt;80 mL/min)
- Group 2: Mild Renal Impairment (CLcr &gt;50 and ≤80 mL/min)
- Group 3: Moderate Renal Impairment (CLcr ≥30 and ≤50 mL/min)
- Group 4: Severe Renal Impairment (CLcr &lt;30 mL/min)
L2990: Reviewer's Comments: The Applicant's classification of renal function groups was based on the 1998 FDA Guidance on Pharmacokinetics in Patients with Impaired Renal Function – Study Design, Data Analysis, and Impact on Dosing and Labeling. Reclassification of renal function groups according to the 2020 version of the guidance displaces 4 subjects from the mild to the moderate impairment group. Notably, subjects with kidney failure, classified as having CLcr &lt;15 mL/min were omitted from this study.
L2991: Subjects were required to have stable renal function, defined as having 2 serum creatinine values obtained within 7-14 days which differed by ≤20% (for subjects with renal impairment) and ≤25% for subjects with normal renal function. Subjects in Groups 1 through 4 participated in 2 treatment periods with dosing in these periods separated by a washout period of 14 days. Subjects fasted for 8 h before and 3 h after dosing. On Day 1 of each treatment period, subjects received a single dose of study drug as follows:
L2992: - Period 1: 800 mg sulopenem 1.5h IV infusion, except in Group 4, where only 1 subject was administered 800 mg and all others received 200 mg sulopenem 1.5 h IV infusion.
- Period 2: 1000 mg (2 X 500 mg) sulopenem etzadroxil immediate release (IR) tablets.
L2993: Reviewer's Comment: An interim analysis of PK data from 1 subject in the severe impairment group during the IV dosing period indicated higher sulopenem exposures than predicted. To maintain IV exposures within the Applicant's observed maximally tolerated dose (MTD) for IV dosing, the protocol was amended to administer 200 mg sulopenem for the remaining severely renally impaired subjects.
L2994: Subjects with normal renal function who received any prescription drugs, vitamins, and dietary supplements within 7 days or 5 half-lives (whichever was longer) prior to the first dose of study drug were excluded. Renally impaired subjects on any immunosuppressive drugs (including cyclosporine, tacrolimus and sirolimus) and drugs known to affect estimation of CLcr (including cimetidine, trimethoprim and cibenzoline) were also excluded.
L2995: ## NDA Multi-disciplinary Review and Evaluation {NDA 213972}
## {sulopenem etzadroxil/probenecid}
L2996: ## PK Sampling and Assessments
L2997: Plasma samples for assessment of sulopenem PK and metabolites were collected pre-dose and at pre-specified times post-dosing. Urine samples were also obtained pre-dose and at intervals of 0-6, 6-12 and 12-24 h post-dose. The following PK parameters were calculated: AUC_{0-24}, AUC_{0-\text{last}}, AUC_{0-\text{inf}}, C_{\text{max}}, T_{\text{max}}, V_z, V_z/F, CL/F, CL, CL_r, CL_{\text{nr}} t_{1/2}, and Ae_{24}. Plasma protein-binding was not determined in this study. A one-way ANOVA model with group as a fixed effect was used to compare log-transformed AUC_{\text{inf}}, AUC_{\text{last}} and C_{\text{max}} for mild, moderate, and severe renal impairment groups to the normal renal function group.
L2998: *Reviewer's Comment: Because the plasma protein binding of sulopenem is 11%, changes in protein binding resulting from impaired renal function are expected to be low. Therefore, use of total concentrations is appropriate.*
L2999: ## Results
L3000: ## *Study Population*
L3001: With the exception of race and renal status, overall mean demographic characteristics were similar across renal function groups. Seventeen male and twelve female subjects aged 38 to 78 years with a mean BMI of 27.7 kg/m2 were enrolled in this study and a majority of the subjects (86.2%) were White. One subject in the severe impairment group discontinued the study after Period 1 (i.e., following administration of IV sulopenem) due to AEs, leaving twenty-eight PK evaluable subjects.
L3002: ## *Protocol Deviations*
L3003: Twelve subjects did not have metabolite assays performed and three subjects (two in the normal renal function group and one in the severe impairment group) did not save all urine for processing.
L3004: *Reviewer's Comment: Overall, the implications of these protocol deviations are considered to be minor. Consistent with the observations from the single ascending doses (SAD) and multiple ascending doses (MAD) studies, concentrations of 2-EBA and formate were below LLOQ at most timepoints in subjects for whom metabolites were evaluated.*
L3005: The Applicant did not specify which intervals of urine collection may have been impacted by the lapses in urine collection and analysis. The reviewer's analysis of raw urine PK data for the 2 subjects from the normal renal function group with incomplete urine collection yielded no indication of which (or how many) urine samples were impacted by the protocol deviation. Exclusion of urine PK data from these subjects had only a modest effect, which was an increase in the estimated mean urine concentration for the 0-6 h collection interval from 177.45 µg/mL to 201.2 µg/mL.
L3006: ## NDA Multi-disciplinary Review and Evaluation {NDA 213972}
## {sulopenem etzadroxil/probenecid}
L3007: ## *Pharmacokinetics*
L3008: Following administration of a single 1000 mg oral dose of sulopenem etzadroxil, AUC of sulopenem increased 7.4-fold in subjects with severe renal impairment compared to those with normal renal function, and C_{max} increased 2.9-fold (Table 133). Sulopenem half-life increased with worsening renal function, but remained short (i.e. 2.8 h) in subjects with severe renal impairment. Sulopenem etzadroxil was well-tolerated and the incidence of AEs was comparable across renal function groups.
L3009: *Reviewer's Comment: The bioavailability of sulopenem in this study increased progressively from 22% with normal renal function to 35% in subjects with severe renal impairment. The mechanism underlying this increase is unknown, but may be due to gastroparesis (delayed gastric emptying) observed in severe renal impairment and more commonly, in end-stage renal disease (Kumar 2021). Because sulopenem is poorly soluble (Biopharmaceutical Classification System Class IV), slowed gastric emptying may provide additional time and opportunity for drug dissolution and thus result in absorption of a larger proportion of the administered dose.*
L3010: It has been reported that renal impairment results in downregulation of renal OAT transporter expression and function (VanWert et al. 2010) and the probenecid USPI notes that probenecid may not be effective when GFR \le 30 mL/min. Because probenecid requires functional OAT transporters to exert its effect, chronic renal impairment diminishes probenecid's effectiveness as an OAT3 inhibitor. Therefore, concomitant administration of probenecid with sulopenem etzadroxil is not expected to further increase sulopenem exposures in subjects with severe renal impairment. The single 1000 mg dose of sulopenem etzadroxil used in the renal impairment study is intended to be the total daily dose for the treatment of uUTI administered 500 mg BID for a total duration of 5 days. Given that sulopenem exposures increase approximately dose proportionally (within the dose range of 400 mg to 2000 mg), administration of a 500 mg dose of sulopenem etzadroxil in subjects with severe renal impairment is anticipated to yield a sulopenem AUC_{0-inf} of ~23995 ng\cdoth/mL. The AUC_{0-inf} at the MTD of 4000 mg from SAD studies is 26900 ng/mL. In MAD studies, dose escalation beyond the starting 2000 mg BID dose of sulopenem etzadroxil was infeasible due to the occurrence of severe adverse events at higher doses. 1200 mg sulopenem etzadroxil in combination with 1000 mg BID probenecid appeared to be well tolerated and yielded moderately higher exposures than the 2000 mg BID sulopenem etzadroxil regimen. Day 10 AUC_{tau} for 1200 mg sulopenem etzadroxil plus 1000 mg was 18800 ng\cdoth/mL, which is 28% lower than the exposure anticipated for 500 mg in subjects with severe renal impairment. Given sulopenem's short half-life even in the setting of severe renal impairment (i.e., 2.75 h) and the short treatment duration of 5 days, the proposed dose is expected to be safe in subjects with severe renal impairment. However, because sulopenem PK has not been evaluated in subjects with CL_{cr} &lt; 15 mL/min or subjects on dialysis, the sulopenem etzadroxil/probenecid bilayer tablet cannot be used in this population.

L3017: Successful treatment of urinary tract infections is expected to be contingent upon the achievement of adequate concentrations of study drug in urine (Gilbert 2006). Thus, in patients with renal insufficiency, sufficiently high urine concentrations may be difficult to achieve. Where sulopenem is concerned, the cumulative amount excreted in urine following a single oral dose was generally comparable across the renal function groups studied (Table 133).
L3018: Reviewer's Comment: CLr decreases with decreasing renal function, thus the rate of sulopenem elimination is expected to be fastest with normal renal function and slowest with severe renal impairment. This may result in variable sulopenem concentrations across urine collection intervals, which may have implications for efficacy. However, for a short half-life drug like sulopenem, regardless of the differences in sulopenem concentrations at the various urine collection intervals, the resulting amount of sulopenem recovered is similar across renal function groups. Of note, the higher 24 h urine recovery of sulopenem in the severe impairment was driven by a single outlier whose urine recovery was 365000 \mug; exclusion of this subjects brings the Ae24 to 126877 \mug, which is in closer agreement with the values observed in other renal function groups.
L3019: ## Clinical Drug-Drug Interactions
L3020: Study IT001-102 was a Phase 1, randomized, open-label single-dose, 4-way crossover study to evaluate the effect of gallic acid, tannic acid, and probenecid on the plasma PK of sulopenem. Sulopenem was administered as the etzadroxil prodrug in a PIB formulation. Probenecid is an OAT3 inhibitor commonly used in this capacity to increase the plasma exposures of \beta-lactam antibiotics. Gallic acid and tannic acid are phenolic compounds that are structurally similar to probenecid and suggested to also inhibit OAT3.
L3021: Thirteen healthy male and female subjects were enrolled in this study. The 4 treatment periods were as follows:
L3022: - Period 1 – 500 mg sulopenem etzadroxil alone
- Period 2 – Sulopenem etzadroxil 500 mg + probenecid 500 mg
L3023: ## NDA Multi-disciplinary Review and Evaluation {NDA 213972}
## {sulopenem etzadroxil/probenecid}
L3024: - Period 3 - Sulopenem etzadroxil 500 mg + gallic acid 400 mg
- Period 4 - Sulopenem etzadroxil 500 mg + tannic acid 400 mg
L3025: A 3-period probenecid sub-study was also conducted in 12 additional male and female subjects in which a single 500 mg dose of sulopenem etzadroxil PIB was administered with probenecid. The treatment periods were as follows:
L3026: - Period 1 – Concurrent administration with a single 500 mg dose of probenecid
- Period 2 – Staggered with administration of probenecid occurring 1 h after sulopenem etzadroxil dosing
- Period 3 – Concurrent administration of sulopenem etzadroxil with 250 mg probenecid, followed by a second 250 mg dose of probenecid 1 h later.
L3027: All doses were administered in the fasted state, and a washout period of 6 days was used between treatment periods. Blood samples for PK analysis were obtained pre-dose and at pre-specified times post-dosing for 12 h. PK parameters estimated included AUC_{0-\text{last}}, AUC_{0-\text{inf}}, C_{\text{max}}, T_{\text{max}}, CL/F and t_{1/2}. The mean difference between test and reference treatments, geometric mean ratios and their 90% CIs were determined.
L3028: ## Results
L3029: No prior medications were reported and concomitant medications were limited to administration of over-the-counter Tylenol severe cold and flu to treat a viral syndrome in one subject. All treatments were well tolerated and of the 3 discontinuations from the primary study, none were due to AEs. An approximately 33% increase in sulopenem AUC was observed when administered with 500 mg probenecid, which exceeds the 5% increase observed with gallic acid (Table 134). Inexplicably, sulopenem exposure with coadministration of tannic acid (a precursor to gallic acid) resulted in a ~12% reduction in sulopenem AUC. Results of the probenecid sub-study indicate that the maximum benefit of probenecid is observed with simultaneous administration of sulopenem etzadroxil (Table 135).

L3040: ## *Study IT001-101*
L3041: Study IT001-101 was a Phase 1, randomized, double-blinded, placebo-controlled, multiple dose study of two sulopenem prodrugs (PF-04064900 and PF-03709270) with and without probenecid (under fed and fasted conditions) or gallic acid (under fasted conditions). The study objectives included:
L3042: - To evaluate the safety and tolerability of sulopenem prodrugs following multiple dose administration
- To evaluate the effect of food on PK, safety, and tolerability of the sulopenem prodrugs
- To characterize the PK of sulopenem and its prodrugs when coadministered with probenecid
- To estimate the relative oral bioavailability of the sulopenem prodrugs
- To evaluate the effect of different doses of probenecid when co-administered with a single dose of sulopenem etzadroxil
- To evaluate the effect of gallic acid on the PK of sulopenem when coadministered with sulopenem etzadroxil
L3043: Two hundred and forty healthy adult male and female subjects aged 20-60 years with CLr ranging from 91 to 156 mL/min were randomized to 5 treatment groups as indicated in Table 74. Of these, 192 subjects were enrolled in Treatment Groups 1-4 and 48 subjects were enrolled in Treatment Group 5. For both prodrugs, an oral powder in bottle formulation was used.
L3044: Blood samples were obtained pre-dosing and at pre-specified times post-dosing to assess sulopenem and sulopenem prodrug PK parameters. Urine samples were also obtained pre-dose and post-dosing on Days 2 and 7 of treatment for assessment of sulopenem urine PK. On Day 1, urine was collected at 2 h intervals through 12 h post-dosing, and at 6 h intervals on Day 7 through 24 h post-dosing. For plasma, parameters of interest included: C_{max}, T_{max}, AUC_{last}, AUC_{tau} on Days 1 and Day 7, t_{1/2} and R_{ac}. For urine, Ae_{24} and CLr were calculated.
L3045: *Reviewer's Comment: Given that sulopenem etzadroxil (PF-03709270) was the prodrug selected for marketing, and probenecid was the OAT3 inhibitor of choice for the to-be-marketed formulation, the study results will focus on observations made following administration of this prodrug in the presence and absence of probenecid. Additionally, because food effect and bioavailability were determined under IT001-105 for the to-be-marketed formulation, the effect of food on sulopenem exposure will not be covered under the review of this study.*

L3050: ## Results
L3051: Five subjects were reported as having major protocol deviations, one of which belonged to the sulopenem etzadroxil treatment groups. One subject did not receive study drug on Days 5 through 7 due to the development of angioedema and pruritis, and was subsequently withdrawn from the study. With the exception of this subject, treatments were generally well tolerated. Most TEAEs were graded as mild (97.3%) for Treatment Groups 1-4. In Treatment Group 5, all TEAEs were regarded as mild. No subjects were excluded from either the safety or PK populations for Treatment Groups 1-5.
L3052: As observed in Study A8811003, there was an unexplained decline in sulopenem exposure following multiple dose administration of sulopenem etzadroxil that was mitigated by coadministration of probenecid (PK summary under fed conditions provided in Table 137). Consistent with sulopenem's short half-life, accumulation was minimal (based on AUC, R_{ac} = 1.06) following multiple dose administration of sulopenem etzadroxil (even in combination

L3068: ## Study IT001-103
L3069: Study IT001-103 was a Phase 1, 2-period, 4-sequence, parallel study to evaluate the effects of multiple dose administration of itraconazole (a P-gp inhibitor) on the PK of sulopenem in healthy adult subjects. The rationale for this study is that in vitro, sulopenem etzadroxil was identified as a P-gp substrate. This review focuses on the two study cohorts wherein the to-be-marketed bilayer tablet was used.
L3070: Thirty-two adult male and female subjects were enrolled in the cohorts of interest. Drug administration was as follows:
L3071: - Period 1 - Single 500 mg sulopenem etzadroxil/500 mg probenecid bilayer tablet under fed (Cohort 2) and fasted (Cohort 3) conditions
- Period 2 - Following a washout period of 3 days, 200 mg of itraconazole (2 X 100 mg oral capsules) was administered once daily for 4 days in the fasted state for both Cohorts 2 and 3. On Day 4, itraconazole was coadministered with a single oral dose of the bilayer tablet under fed (Cohort 2) and fasted (Cohort 3) conditions.
L3072: Blood samples for PK assessment were obtained pre-dosing and at pre-specified times through 12 h post-dosing. Plasma PK parameters such as AUC_{0-t}, AUC_{\text{extrap}}, AUC_{0-\text{inf}}, C_{\text{max}} and t_{1/2} were summarized descriptively. The C_{\text{max}} and AUCs of sulopenem in the bilayer tablet administered alone in the fasted and fed states, respectively, were compared to the exposures achieved in
L3073: ## NDA Multi-disciplinary Review and Evaluation {NDA 213972}
## {sulopenem etzadroxil/probenecid}
L3074: the presence of itraconazole using a paired t-test for the natural-log transformed C_{max} and AUCs.
L3075: Reviewer's Comment: The itraconazole dose (200 mg) used in this study provides adequate exposure for P-gp inhibition. Because sulopenem etzadroxil is rapidly hydrolyzed to sulopenem after oral administration, a clinically significant drug-drug interaction (DDI) with P-gp inhibitors such as itraconazole is unlikely.
L3076: ## Results

L3084: ## Study IT001-104
L3085: Study IT001-104 was a Phase 1, open-label, 2-period, 3-sequence, parallel study designed to evaluate the effects of multiple-dose administration of IV sulopenem, sulopenem etzadroxil/probenecid bilayer oral tablet or sulopenem etzadroxil oral tablet on the steady-state PK profile of valproic acid in healthy adult subjects. The rationale underpinning this study is the observation that carbapenems may decrease the plasma concentrations of valproic acid.

L3122: Reviewer's Comment: The significant reduction in sulopenem AUC and C_{max} observed with the administration of aluminum hydroxide appears to be driven by lower sulopenem exposures with concomitant administration of the antacid for 1 subject. The Applicant does not offer an explanation for the lower exposures observed for sulopenem etzadroxil + aluminum hydroxide in this subject. When data from the subject are excluded from the analysis, the reduction in AUC and C_{max} improve to 7% and 14%, respectively. According to the FDA guidance on evaluating gastric pH-dependent drug interactions, results of an interaction study with a proton-pump inhibitor (PPI) present the worst-case scenario for pH-dependent DDIs due to the long-lasting effect of this class on gastric pH. Therefore, a negative result with a PPI, as is the case here, is indicative of a lack of pH-dependent DDI.
L3123: The main goal of the probenecid portion of the study was to inform probenecid dose selection for use in combination in a fixed-dose tablet. The doses evaluated (500 mg and 1000 mg) are consistent with the standard doses of probenecid generally recommended for coadministration with \beta-lactams to improve their plasma exposures. Both sulopenem AUC and C_{max} increased approximately 1.4-fold with a 2-fold increase in the dose of probenecid (Table 145). The amount of sulopenem recovered in urine over 12 h decreased by 9% with a 2-fold increase in the dose of probenecid.

L3131: ## Summary of In Vitro ADME
L3132: ## Absorption
L3133: Studies 17IT001-2017_03_14_Iterum Therapeutics(b)(4) and 17IT002-2017_06_30_Iterum Therapeutics(b)(4)-00 evaluated the permeability of sulopenem, PF-03709270 (sulopenem etzadroxil) and PF-04064900 across Caco-2 cell monolayers in the presence and absence of probenecid. Sulopenem's permeability was 0.08 to 0.09 x 10-6 cm/s at concentrations of 20 µM to 1mM. The permeability of sulopenem etzadroxil was also low in the A-B direction (0.07 to 0.31 x 10-6 cm/s) and moderate in the opposite direction (3.59 to 8.73 x 10-6 cm/s) at concentrations of 20 µM to 1mM. Therefore, the efflux ratio for sulopenem etzadroxil was &gt;2. The addition of probenecid had no effect on Papp or efflux ratio of sulopenem or sulopenem etzadroxil.
L3134: ## Distribution
L3135: Study DM2004-070429-013 evaluated the extent of sulopenem binding to human plasma proteins at concentrations of 1, 10, 50 and 100 µg/mL using ultrafiltration. Sulopenem plasma protein binding was low, with bound (unbound) fraction of 10.7 (0.893±0.200) and was concentration-independent over the range of 1 to 100 µg/mL.
L3136: ## Metabolism
L3137: ## *CYP450 and UGT Reaction Phenotyping*
L3138: The metabolic stability of sulopenem in the presence of human recombinant UGTs (UGT1A1, 1A3, 1A4, 1A6, 1A9, 2B7 and 2B15) and CYPs (1A2, 2A6, 2B6, 2C9, 2C19, 2D6, 3A4 and 3A5) at concentrations of 1 and 10 µM in Study Iterum-03-09Aug2019. No metabolism was observed when sulopenem was incubated with recombinant UGT or CYP enzymes. For unspecified reasons, the Applicant states that in vitro metabolism of sulopenem could not be characterized sufficiently using human liver microsomes or hepatocytes. No in vitro metabolism studies were conducted for sulopenem etzadroxil because it is expected to be rapidly hydrolyzed to the active sulopenem moiety.
L3139: *Reviewer's Comment: The review team postulates that the inability to illustrate in vitro metabolism of sulopenem using human liver microsomes or hepatocytes is because sulopenem may be susceptible to non-CYP and UGT-mediated biotransformations in these in vitro test systems. Thus, the Applicant's use of recombinant CYP and UGT enzymes elucidates the involvement (or lack thereof) of these enzymes in the disposition of sulopenem.*
L3140: ## In Vitro Drug-Drug Interaction Studies
L3141: ## CYP Inhibitory and Induction Potential
L3142: Studies DM2006-070429-029 and 17081086ITX evaluated the inhibitory potential of sulopenem and sulopenem etzadroxil on pooled human liver microsomal activity of CYP1A2, CYP2B6, CYP2C8, CYP2C9, CYP2C19 and CYP3A4/5. Sulopenem was found to not be a direct or time-dependent inhibitor of CYP isoforms tested up to 150 µM. Sulopenem etzadroxil was found to be a time-dependent inhibitor of CYP3A4/5, but an IC50 could not be calculated within the concentration range studied, and was estimated to be &gt;150 µM. The potential of sulopenem to induce the activities of CYPs 1A2, 2B6 and 3A4 were evaluated in Study 17081087ITX using pooled human hepatocytes. No induction of enzyme activity was observed using sulopenem concentrations of 0.07 to 150 µM. The induction potential of sulopenem etzadroxil was not evaluated.
L3143: ## Transporter Studies
L3144: Studies 17081088ITX and Iterum-02-08-Mar2019-A1 evaluated sulopenem and sulopenem etzadroxil both as substrates and inhibitors of human BSEP, P-gp, MRP2, MATE1, MATE2-K OAT1, OAT3, OATP1B1, OATP1B3, OCT1 and OCT2 transporters. Bidirectional permeability was evaluated using MDCKII or HEK293 cells expressing the respective uptake transporters. Sulopenem was a substrate of OAT3 with over 34-fold accumulation in cells expressing OAT3 and inhibitor of OAT1 with IC50&gt;150 µM. Sulopenem was neither a substrate or inhibitor of BCRP, P-gp, BSEP, MRP2, MATE1, MATE2-K, OAT1B1B1, OAT1P1B3, OCT1 or OCT2. Sulopenem etzadroxil was a substrate and inhibitor of P-gp (IC50=1.91 µM) and BCRP (IC50=20.4 µM), and an inhibitor of OAT1 (IC50=93.6 µM) and OAT3 (IC50=34.8 µM). However, inhibition of OAT1 and

L3146: OAT3 by sulopenem etzadroxil is not expected to be clinically relevant given that it is rapidly hydrolyzed following oral administration and not detected systemically.
L3147: Reviewer's Comment: At 150 \mu\text{M} (i.e. 52.4 \mu\text{g}/\text{mL}), only 34% OAT1 inhibition was observed in vitro for sulopenem. Given the sulopenem C_{\text{max}} (for the bilayer tablet) in fed state = 2.66 \mu\text{g}/\text{mL} and \text{IC}_{50} &gt; 52.4 \mu\text{g}/\text{mL}, I_{\text{max},u}/\text{IC}_{50} &lt; &lt; 0.1. L3149: ## Identification of PK/PD Index of Sulopenem
L3150: The pharmacokinetics/pharmacodynamics (PK/PD) index of sulopenem was evaluated with dose-fractionation in a murine thigh infection model using 2 strains each of *E. coli*, *K. pneumoniae*, *S. pneumoniae* and *S. pyogenes* with sulopenem minimum inhibitor concentration (MIC) in the range of 0.0078 - 1 \mu\text{g}/\text{mL}. Immunosuppressed mice were used in studies involving *E. coli* while all other dose-fractionation studies were conducted in immunocompetent mice. Sulopenem total daily doses in the range of 3.125 - 200 \text{ mg}/\text{kg}/\text{day} were administered according to q3h, q6h, q12h and q24h dosing regimens 24h post-inoculation of murine thigh muscles to delineate the PK/PD driver of sulopenem's antibacterial activity. Accompanying PK studies were conducted for sulopenem single doses of 4.69, 18.75, 75 and 300 \text{ mg}/\text{kg}. Because protein binding of sulopenem in mouse plasma was determined to be 0.01 and concentration independent, adjustment of PK parameters for protein binding was negligible. The correlation of \text{AUC}/\text{MIC}, C_{\text{max}}/\text{MIC}, and T &gt; \text{MIC} to the PD data (i.e., change in \log_{10} CFU) was determined by non-linear least-squares regression analysis using a Hill-type model. Based on the coefficient of determination (r^2), results presented for *S. pneumoniae* in Figure 8 suggest that \text{AUC}/\text{MIC} is the PK/PD index that best correlated with sulopenem's antibacterial activity.

L3155: *Reviewer's Comment: Although the Applicant's Summary of Clinical Pharmacology described 2 sets of nonclinical PK/PD studies, the original NDA submission provided only an abbreviated nonclinical PK/PD study report (for Study 810-00081) which offered limited information on PK/PD index and target determination in a murine thigh infection model. Therefore, an IR (dated 02/11/2021) was issued to the Applicant, seeking clarification on which of the studies described in the Summary of Clinical Pharmacology was used to inform PK/PD targets for probability of target attainment (PTA) analysis. In response to this IR, the Applicant provided an unpublished manuscript, an abstract presented at 2 scientific conferences and laboratory notebook pages. Per the Applicant, information contained in the report for Study 810-00081, abstract and laboratory notebook pages were integrated into the unpublished manuscript. Therefore, the manuscript served as the Applicant's primary source of information for the identification of a PK/PD index and target for sulopenem.*
L3156: *Per the reviewer's assessment, the integrity of PK and PD information provided by the Applicant is questionable due to discrepancies in the data and results summarized in the Study 810-00081 report, abstract and unpublished manuscript. Key issues identified by the reviewer include: a) incongruity of the best PK/PD index for sulopenem suggested by Study 810-00081 and the unpublished manuscript, b) differences in values of PK parameters reported in the abstract compared to the unpublished manuscript, and c) inconsistencies in the methodology described within the unpublished manuscript. Study report 810-00081 briefly outlined dose-fractionation studies conducted with a single isolate each of K. pneumoniae* and *S. pneumoniae* in a murine thigh infection model. In this report, T &gt; MIC was identified as the relevant PK/PD driver for sulopenem's activity, which is consistent with the known PK/PD driver for other penem (i.e. \beta-lactam) antibacterial drugs. Although data from Study 810-00081 were purportedly integrated into the unpublished manuscript, results presented in the manuscript conclude that AUC/MIC (and not T &gt; MIC) is the relevant PK/PD driver. The Applicant's explanation for these contradicting observations is that both concentration and T &gt; MIC are relevant to sulopenem's activity. Additionally, inconsistencies in the values of PK parameters summarized in the abstract compared to the manuscript render the PK data unreliable. Ultimately, a dearth of details, questionable data and ambiguities regarding study methodology and PK/PD analyses render the results of the nonclinical PK/PD studies uninterpretable. Because raw data from these studies were not available, the reviewer was unable to conduct independent analyses to confirm T &gt; MIC as the PK/PD driver of sulopenem's antibacterial activity.
L3157: ## Determination of PK/PD Target of Sulopenem
L3158: In an unconventional approach, the previously described dose-fractionation studies were also used by the Applicant to suggest PK/PD targets for the pathogens evaluated. Individual estimates of T &gt; MIC values for each isolate by dosing frequency are summarized in Table 84. For PTA analyses, the Applicant computed mean T &gt; MIC values of 17% and 20% as the targets required for net stasis and 1-\log_{10} CFU reduction, respectively across Gram negative species (Table 146).

L3164: *Reviewer's Comment: Although the Applicant failed to show definitively that T &gt; MIC best predicted sulopenem's antibacterial activity, the unpublished manuscript summarized the magnitude of T &gt; MIC required for various PD endpoints. Of note, the Applicant's results indicate that larger magnitudes of T &gt; MIC were required with increased dosing frequency, which is inconsistent with T &gt; MIC being the driver of antibacterial activity. Additionally, T &gt; MIC values were inappropriately averaged across different experimental conditions (i.e., immunocompetent vs. immunosuppressed murine models) and pathogens. Interestingly, the values suggested for net stasis and 1-log10 CFU reduction approached those described for other carbapenems (i.e., 20-30% T &gt; MIC). Nonetheless, because these data (and ensuing results) are questionable, the PK/PD targets from these studies cannot be used for PTA analyses.*
L3165: Nonclinical PK/PD studies were also conducted using a single strain each of *K. pneumoniae* and *S. pneumoniae* to compare the magnitude of T &gt; MIC for sulopenem and meropenem required to achieve net stasis, 1-log10, 2-log10 CFU reduction and EC80 in an immunosuppressed thigh infection model. L3169: *Reviewer's Comment: The method described in the manuscript for this study indicated that comparisons of T &gt; MIC estimates for meropenem and sulopenem were conducted in both immunocompetent and immunosuppressed murine thigh infection models, yet results were described solely for studies in immunosuppressed mice. L3170: ## Population PK Analysis
L3171: ## Review Summary
L3172: The Applicant's population PK (PopPK) analysis reasonably describes the time-concentration profiles of sulopenem in healthy subjects and subjects with uUTI. Parameters for clearance were estimated with acceptable relative standard errors (RSE) less than 20%. There was no notable bias in goodness-of-fit (GOF) plots and the visual predictive check (VPC). The ETA shrinkages for PK parameters for clearance and volumes of distributions are modest (25% to 57%). The PopPK model is acceptable to be used to derive the summary exposure parameters (AUCtau, Cmax) for healthy and uUTI infected patients. Limitations of the popPK model were noted in describing covariate effects (such as renal function, food status, and formulations). These should be carefully considered when interpreting the model derived covariate effects and using the model for simulations for target attainment analysis.

- Assess the impact of clinically relevant covariates on the PK of sulopenem

L3204: Following oral administration, there were a second peak in the observed concentrations after some oral doses. This was described using an absorption model with two parallel chains of transit compartments. T_M and concentration for half maximum rate of elimination (K_M) were estimated to 2540 \mug/h and 77.9 \mug/mL. V1, V2, and V3 were estimated to 12.6 L, 7.40 L and 4.49 L, respectively.
L3205: Inter individual variability (IIV) for T_M, V1, V2 and V3 were 16.1%, 20.2%, 25.3% and 21.2%, respectively. The IIV for the parameters related to absorption were 23.0%, 71.1% and 189% for mean transit time for first transit chain (MTT1), number of transit compartments for first transit chain (NTR1) and the fraction of dose going into the fast or slow absorption chain, respectively. The inter occasion variability estimated for MTT1 was 26.0%.
L3206: The bioavailability (F) of sulopenem etzadroxil was estimated to 21.2%. Food increased F by 32.6% for the PIB and monolayer tablet formulation, and 47.2% for the bilayer tablet. Food prolonged absorption and MTT1 by 63.0% for the monolayer tablet and PIB formulation. PIB formulation also showed a faster overall absorption as compared to mono- and bilayer tablet, 20.1%. There was also a statistically significant effect on F following multiple oral dosing without probenecid, predicting a 24.7% lower F on day 7.
L3207: Administering IV sulopenem and oral sulopenem etzadroxil with probenecid reduced T_M by 32.4% at probenecid dose ranging from 250-500 mg and with 52.0% at the higher probenecid dose (1000 mg). Probenecid was also found to be a covariate on the volumes of distributions (reducing the volumes by 12.2%). Creatinine clearance (CL_{Cr}) had an impact on T_M, resulting in 8.35% decrease in T_M for every 10 ml/min change in CL_{Cr}. Refer to Applicant's PopPK report, Table 9 and 10 (parameter estimates of the Phase 1 popPK model), Figures 10, 11, 12, 13 (GOF plots), and Figure 14 and Figure 15 (prediction corrected VPC plots).

L3210: **Final PopPK model:** The structural model of the final model is the same as Phase 1 PopPK model. L3242: Reviewer's Comment: In general, the Applicant's final PopPK model acceptably describes the observed PK data collected from Phase 1 and Phase 3 studies. Most PK parameters were estimated with acceptable precision (%RSE &lt;20%) and IIVs were estimated with %RSE &lt;50%. ETA shrinkages for TM, V1, V2, and V3 were modest (25%, 57%, 48%, and 49%). The GOF plots by route of administration did not show any obvious bias. The VPC plots showed that the model predictions are in agreement with the observed concentrations for both Phase 1 and Phase 3 studies. Therefore, the reviewer agrees that this model can be used to derive the summary exposure metrics such as AUC and Cmax for the study populations.
L3243: Body weight, and sex minimally impact sulopenem exposure and these impacts are not considered clinically meaningful. With decreasing CLcr from 116 to 48 mL/min, there is a 2-fold increase in sulopenem AUC0-12h following a 500 mg bilayer tablet. The model predicted magnitude of CLcr impact is somewhat smaller than those observed in the dedicated RI study. In the RI study, sulopenem AUCinf increased in subjects with mild, moderate, and severe renal function by 210%, 350% and 740% after a single oral dose of 1000 mg sulopenem etzadroxil, and 170% (mild RI) and 250% (moderate RI) after an 800 mg IV dose. Note that a different formulation (tablet without probenecid) was used in the RI study from the proposed formulation (bilayer tablet with probenecid). The impacts of renal impairment on probenecid and the associated impact on sulopenem exposures were not incorporated in the Applicant's PopPK model.
L3244: The complexity of the structural model and the potential interactions between intrinsic/extrinsic factors that are correlated to each other (i.e., renal function, food effects, and formulations (with or without probenecid) make it difficult to interpret the model-estimated covariate effects. Therefore, this limitation should be carefully considered when this model is used for simulations for target attainment analysis. One example is food effect. The model-derived food effect on bilayer tablets is mainly driven by the data from the food effect study (IT001-105) which showed
L3245: ## NDA Multi-disciplinary Review and Evaluation {NDA 213972}
## {sulopenem etzadroxil/probenecid}
L3246: a significant food effect (approx. 50% higher exposure vs. fasted). While most subjects (90.7%) from Phase 3 studies were recorded as in a fed status during dosing, the model predicted exposures for Phase 3 subjects are generally lower than those observed in healthy subjects with fed status and more close to those observed in fasted status. It is not clear whether the lower exposures observed in the Phase 3 studies are due to the inherent PK difference between patients (uUTI, cUTI) vs. healthy subjects, or the way food status was recorded in the Phase 3 studies (i.e., inaccurate record of food status, or the consumed food ([planned] meal/snack) different from those (high-fat meal) consumed in Study IT001-105.
L3247: Because of the deficiencies in the determination of PK/PD targets noted by the Clinical Pharmacology reviewer (See Appendix 16.3), the Applicant's target attainment analysis could not be evaluated by the reviewer. In the Phase 3 efficacy trial (IT001-301) supporting the proposed indication, PK samples were collected in a subset (n=118) of intent-to-treat (ITT) population (n=787). Therefore, the exposure-response for clinical efficacy/safety was not further evaluated by the reviewer.

L3274: ## 16.5. Clinical Microbiology
L3275: ## 16.5.1. In Vitro Information
L3276: ## 16.5.1.1. Mechanism of Action
L3277: Sulopenem is a penem antibacterial drug that inhibits bacterial cell wall synthesis by binding to penicillin-binding proteins (PBPs). A competitive binding assay was conducted with 3H-penicillin in *E. coli* strain W-7 that showed sulopenem (CP-65,207) had the highest affinity for PBP2, with concentrations as low as 0.004 µg/mL (Figure 14) (Gootz 1989). It has also shown that the relative order of affinity towards PBPs of sulopenem in *E. coli* was PBP2&gt;PBP1A &gt; PBP1B &gt; PBP4&gt;PBP3&gt;PBP5/6. Additionally, it was determined through a hydrolysis study that CP-65207 was highly stable to some cephalosporinases, including plasmid-encoded enzymes TEM-1, SHV-1, and PSE-2.
L3278: **Figure 14. Autoradiograph of Competitive Binding of Unlabeled CP-65,207 Versus 3HPenicillin G for *E. coli* W-7 PBPs**
L3279: ## 16.5.1.2. Bactericidal Activity
L3280: The bactericidal activity of sulopenem was demonstrated in several time-kill studies. Sulopenem exhibited bactericidal killing in one study (Uppsala 2018-10-11), at concentrations \ge 4\times the MIC against *E. coli* and *K. pneumoniae* isolates (Table 155).

L3299: ## 16.5.1.3. Mechanisms of Resistance
L3300: The development of resistance to sulopenem was evaluated in spontaneous mutation frequency studies using two *E. cloacae* isolates and in serial passage studies using clinical isolates of *E. coli* and *K. pneumoniae*.
L3301: In a spontaneous mutation frequency study, colonies were isolated at a frequency of 1 \times 10^{-8} with a \le 2-fold increase in MIC from the parent strain. In the serial passage mutation studies, MIC values increased 16-fold during 15 serial passages in two out of the three tested *E. coli* isolates and were unchanged for the third isolate. MIC values increased 8-fold during serial passage for one of the two *K. pneumoniae* isolates tested, and MIC values increased from 0.5 to 256 \mu\text{g}/\text{mL} for the other isolate.
L3302: ## NDA Multi-disciplinary Review and Evaluation {NDA 213972}
## {sulopenem etzadroxil/probenecid}
L3303: Similar to other carbapenems, resistance to sulopenem occurs primarily due to enzymatic inactivation by carbapenemases, but also can be caused by \beta-lactamase production, efflux pump expression, and changes in porins and/or PBPs (Papp-Wallace et al. 2011; Papp-Wallace 2019).
L3304: ## 16.5.1.4. Interaction With Other Antimicrobials
L3305: Interactions of sulopenem with nine other antimicrobial agents were evaluated in a checkerboard assay using four *E. coli* and two *K. pneumoniae* isolates (JMI final report 17-ITR-01 Part 3). The antimicrobial drugs that were tested in combination with sulopenem were amoxicillin, aztreonam, ceftriaxone, doxycycline, gentamicin, levofloxacin, nitrofurantoin, trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole, and vancomycin (Table 157). No instance of antagonism was observed in vitro between sulopenem and other antibacterial drugs against tested *E. coli* and *K. pneumoniae* isolates. Only, two instances of synergy were observed, both with trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole, against *E. coli* ATCC 35218 (TEM-1) and *E. coli* 937054 (ESBL, CTX-M-15).

L3311: ## 16.5.1.5. In Vitro Spectrum and Activity
L3312: In vitro susceptibility testing was performed to determine the MIC by following the Clinical Laboratory Standard Institute guidelines (CLSI M07, M11, and M100). Sulopenem demonstrated in vitro activity against aerobic and anaerobic gram-positive and gram-negative bacteria in profiling, surveillance, and clinical studies. The in vitro MIC50/90 values (inhibits the growth of ≥50% and ≥90% of the isolates) were determined for sulopenem in all studies but this review only focuses on relevant uUTI pathogens from 3 recent surveillance studies and a single uUTI clinical study (IT001-301).
L3313: The activity of sulopenem was evaluated in a large collection of clinical isolates (UTI and IAI infection sources) from the US, Europe, and Canada. The first study was conducted by testing 873 aerobic clinical isolates collected from 2013-2015 (International Health Management Associates [IHMA]; Study IHMA_2757); the second study was conducted by testing 1,918 aerobic clinical isolates collected from 2016-2017 (JMI; Study 17-ITR-05); and a third
L3314: ## NDA Multi-disciplinary Review and Evaluation {NDA 213972}
## {sulopenem etzadroxil/probenecid}
L3315: surveillance study was conducted by testing 3,126 aerobic clinical isolates collected from 2016 in Canada (the Health Sciences Centre; CANWARD 2016).
L3316: ## In Vitro Activity Against Aerobic Gram-negative Bacteria
L3317: Sulopenem exhibited in vitro activity against Enterobacteriales including uUTI-relevant pathogens and *H. influenzae* but had poor or no activity against *P. aeruginosa* and *A. baumannii*. A summary of the MIC50/90 values for sulopenem against gram-negative aerobic bacteria has been presented in Table 158.
L3318: Against *E. coli* isolates, sulopenem had MIC50/90 values of 0.03/0.06, 0.03/0.03, 0.03/0.06, 0.03/0.03 µg/mL against US-European isolates from 2013-2015, 2016-2017, Canadian (2016) and US (2019) isolates, respectively. The MIC50/90 value was 0.03/0.06 µg/mL against uUTI clinical study isolates (N=900).
L3319: Against *K. pneumoniae* isolates, sulopenem had MIC50/90 values of 0.06/0.12, 0.03/0.12, 0.06/0.12, and 0.03/0.06 µg/mL against US-European isolates from 2013-2015, 2016-2017, Canadian (2016) and US (2019) isolates, respectively. The MIC50/90 value was 0.06/0.12 µg/mL against uUTI clinical study isolates (N=96).

L3372: ## 16.5.1.7. Susceptibility Testing Methods
L3373: Studies were conducted to determine the in vitro susceptibility testing methods for sulopenem by following the CLSI guidelines (CLSI M23; CLSI M07) (Study (b) (4) 615). These include the following:
L3374: - Evaluating the impact of potential variation of test parameters in standard broth microdilution MIC testing;
- Development of a disk diffusion susceptibility testing;
L3375: ## NDA Multi-disciplinary Review and Evaluation {NDA 213972}
## {sulopenem etzadroxil/probenecid}
L3376: - Evaluating the correlation between broth microdilution relative to disk diffusion and agar dilution methods; and
- Establishing quality control (QC) parameters.
L3377: ## Effect of Test Parameters on MIC Values
L3378: The effect of different test parameters on the activity of sulopenem was evaluated using QC isolates from American Type Culture Collections (ATCC). The evaluated parameters included: test medium cation content, test medium pH, inoculum density, inclusion of lysed horse blood in test medium, and incubation atmosphere (ambient vs. 5% CO2).
L3379: ## Effect of Divalent Cations on the Activity of Sulopenem
L3380: The in vitro activity of sulopenem was tested using cation-adjusted Mueller-Hinton broth (CAMHB) containing varying concentrations of calcium and magnesium cations against the four QC strains, *E. coli* ATCC 25922, *P. aeruginosa* ATCC 27853, *E. faecalis* ATCC 29212, and *S. aureus* ATCC 29213. Sulopenem did not appear to show significant variation in the in vitro MIC values. (Table 161).

L3401: ## **Effect of Testing in Medium With Lysed Horse Blood and Varied Incubation**
L3402: The effects of supplementing test medium with 3 – 5% lysed horse blood compared to the standard CAMHB and the impact of incubating at 5% \text{CO}_2 as opposed to the standard ambient atmosphere on the activity of sulopenem were evaluated against the QC strains (Table 164).
